Burnham tells cabinet to tackle living costs at first meeting

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 20:09:03 GMT

Andy Burnham has promised to lead a "cost of living government," as he chaired his first cabinet meeting as prime minister.

He told his newly-assembled top team that he wanted to make living expenses a key priority, and give people a "sense that help is coming" on costs.

It comes after he announced a VAT cut to household energy bills from October, in his first major announcement since taking office.

But his plan to pay for the policy by scrapping Sir Keir Starmer's digital ID scheme led to an early row over whether the plan was properly funded.

Downing Street said the estimated £850m cost of the VAT cut over the rest of the financial year could come from £1.8bn earmarked by the previous government to roll out the digital ID scheme in the next three years.

But Darren Jones, who was among a clutch of Starmer loyalists sacked from the cabinet on Monday, said the ID programme was "unfunded" and Burnham would need to set out where the money would be found.

Opposition parties also seized on the announcement, pointing out the government's budget watchdog has previously said the money to fund digital ID was due to be found from within existing budgets.

"We are only one day in and already Labour are playing fast and loose with the public finances," said Conservative shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride.

The PM's spokesman insisted the policy would be funded by redirecting "savings" identified by departments to cover the cost of the ID scheme.

Burnham was given a round of applause by his senior ministers earlier, as he opened the first meeting of his new cabinet after appointing his top team on Monday.

Appointments below cabinet rank are expected to follow on Tuesday evening, including Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar, who is set to be given a seat in the House of Lords so he can join Burnham's government.

It is thought Sarwar, who rocked Starmer's premiership when he called for him to resign in February, will become a business minister.

New rules mean he would have to quit his seat in the Scottish Parliament, although a by-election to replace him will not be required as he was elected on the regional list system.

Monday's wide-ranging reshuffle saw Starmer loyalists such as Rachel Reeves and David Lammy out of government, with Ed Miliband promoted to foreign secretary and Burnham ally Louise Haigh given a big job running the Cabinet Office.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, a Burnham ally promoted into the cabinet as energy secretary, denied he had led a purge of Starmer supporters, telling BBC Newsnight "no one has a right" to be in the cabinet, which contained a "diversity of views".

Speaking to staff at the Treasury, new chancellor John Healey said discipline over tax and spending would be his "first duty", as he recommitted to the tax and spending rules set by his predecessor.

But he added that government would seek to make the "fullest possible use of public investment" within the framework, alongside making the most of private and international investment.

Speaking at the start of the cabinet meeting attended by broadcasters, Burnham said the cost of living would be an early priority, with further measures to be announced in the coming days.

He said he would be asking ministers to come up with suggestions to lower costs to households, adding: "There are things can be done, big and small."

He insisted his government would always show "how we are going to pay for" policies, adding "discipline" on spending would be required.

But he conceded that funding new announcements ahead of his first Budget, where big tax decisions are made, would require ministers to be "prepared to reprioritise" how they allocate their budgets.

This was also reflected in Burnham's first announcement on Monday, a further £340m to tackle rough sleeping over five years, which is expected to be funded within "uncommitted" spending at the housing department.

In a later development on Tuesday, Burnham agreed to allow British military bases to be used for US defensive strikes against Iran - a continuation of the same policy under Sir Keir's government.

Sources stressed bases at Diego Garcia and RAF Fairford would only be used for what the UK deems to be defensive operations.

The announcement on energy bills, which will see VAT on household electricity reduced from 5% to zero in England, Wales and Scotland, is estimated to save the typical household about £45 a year.

It will not apply in Northern Ireland due to post-Brexit rules agreed by the previous Conservative government, with ministers at Stormont instead offered extra money from the Treasury to use on cost of living measures.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both previously called for the measure, with Nigel Farage calling it a benefit of Brexit but insisting it would not "address the real issue of the cost of living" and taking aim at green levies on bills.

Meanwhile, further details have been confirmed of Burnham's plan for a new Downing Street unit in Manchester, known as No 10 North.

The government says the unit, expected to be initially set up in a building currently housing intelligence service GCHQ, will be given control of aspects of local economic growth and devolution strategy.

Alongside this, a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet will be created to ensure departments remain focused on "top strategic priorities", according to a statement announcing the changes.

Civil servants working in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move north, it is understood, with Downing Street saying Burnham would try to work from No 10 North "at least one day a week".

Additional reporting by Harry Farley.

Zelensky sacks Ukraine's top army commander after days of protests

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 19:57:38 GMT

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has dismissed the country's army commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

It comes just days after the removal of popular Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov - a move that triggered street protests across the country.

Initial rumours that the end of Fedorov's tenure was related to a conflict between him and Syrskyi were soon confirmed.

Fedorov, 35, has been widely praised for energising the ministry and transforming the armed forces, as well as leading a drive against corruption. Syrskyi, 60, is seen by many in Ukraine as a Soviet-school commander reluctant to implement radical changes in the army.

He was replaced by Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, who is a popular, battle-hardened general.

In a video post on social media late on Tuesday, Zelensky thanked Syrskyi for his military campaigns, including his role in successfully defending the capital Kyiv during the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Zelensky also revealed that earlier in the day, he met Fedorov and offered him a "worthy position in power", but did not say whether the offer had been accepted.

Fedorov was last week replaced by Yevhenii Khmara, a former top official at Ukraine's Security Service (SBU).

"All decisions will be formalised tomorrow," Zelensky added in his post.

Meanwhile, Fedorov congratulated Drapatyi with his new job, describing his appointment as a "new hope in the fight of free people for freedom and justice".

He said it was "the voice of change that could not be ignored".

Fedorov also revealed that he had called Syrskyi to thank him for the defence of the Kyiv region and other "historic battles".

"But we need to move even faster and write new chapters correcting all previous mistakes," he added.

Fedorov, 35, had been appointed defence minister only in January - but has been widely praised for using data to analyse and try to improve performance on the front line.

A former minister of digital transformation, he was active from the early days of the full-scale invasion by setting up a volunteer "IT Army of Ukraine" to launch cyber-attacks against Russia.

Later, he led a successful fundraising campaign called the Army of Drones and brought in elements of "gamification" to the war, designing a system that awarded Ukrainian military units with credits for hitting Russian assets.

Fedorov's ousting prompted six days of widespread protests, with Zelensky coming under mounting pressure to dismiss Syrskyi.

Zelensky appeared to have bowed to that pressure by replacing him with Drapatyi, who is seen as a younger, more innovative commander. Drapatyi is also thought to be a close friend of Federov's.

Federov's clear endorsement of Drapatyi is likely to go some way towards defusing the political crisis of the past week.

For the time being, acting Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara remains in the position. President Zelensky has asked him and Drapatyi to come up with a new defence strategy, covering key issues like reforming the military corps system, weapons supply and drones.

Syrskyi has so far not publicly commented on the latest developments.

On Monday, he wrote an op-ed for the Militarny website, saying of his relationship with Fedorov: "I perceived our relationship as a working one".

"If I offended anyone, Mykhailo Albertovych [Fedorov], I'm sorry."

On the protests that have been held in several Ukrainian cities, the general wrote that the issues of military contracts, procurement and mobilisation currently being aired in the press and boiled down to pithy slogans by protesters were a great deal more complicated than most people realised.

"Decisions on which people's lives depend are not made with slogans," he said. "Real work, not the public drama surrounding it, wins the war," Syrskyi wrote.

Protesters will still want to see Fedorov backing a position of real authority, where he can continue to drive forward innovation in Ukraine's battle with Russia.

If he gets such a position, Zelensky will have repaired the immediate damage. But many will not forgive him for making what they saw as the wrong choice in the first place.

'They want us gone' - Man Utd fans' fury over ticket ultimatum

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 19:05:39 GMT

Manchester United have 46,800 season-ticket holders at Old Trafford

Manchester United fans have reacted with fury after "thousands" had their season-ticket accounts restricted.

The action follows an attempt by United to identify potential ticket touts and those breaking the club's ticketing terms and conditions.

But supporters have told BBC Sport that those who have been informed their season tickets are now at risk of being revoked include many of the club's most loyal followers, and insist that the majority have done nothing wrong.

"I feel angry about it - they just want us gone," Andy, a season ticket holder for more than 35 years, who was informed his account has been restricted on Monday night, told BBC Sport.

"My dad has been a season-ticket holder since 1974, when we were in the second division. He is a pensioner now and I have to help him with all the online stuff since digital tickets became a thing.

"Going the match is our bond. Things like that are what keep older people alive sometimes.

"It's stressful enough for my own mental health but I think it could make my dad ill."

Manchester United declined to comment on the process or fan reaction when asked to do so.

In one email sent to a supporter, seen by BBC Sport, Manchester United said: "We have identified patterns linked to your ticketing account that we need to understand more clearly.

"We need to establish whether there is a straightforward explanation for the activity identified."

As it stands, those under suspicion have had restrictions placed their online accounts, preventing them from buying and transferring tickets.

Those whose accounts have been flagged have been asked to submit evidence to the club to defend themselves if they feel they have been wrongly accused.

United have not revoked any tickets so far and an appeals panel will make a final decision on each case before their Premier League season begins on 22 August.

But supporters such as Andy say they have not been told explicitly what they are being accused of, that the lack of information feels like they are being invited to incriminate themselves, and that the confusion is causing significant anxiety.

"They have already taken my season ticket money," Andy says.

"They don't care about how it affects people, their relationships, maybe their health and mental health. There is no empathy.

"I feel like people are punished for their loyalty. They don't want fans, they want customers."

Old Trafford is the biggest home club football stadium in the UK, and the fourth biggest in Europe

In a social media post, Manchester United Supporters' Trust said the club has "been sending out account suspensions and season-ticket cancellation notices to thousands of supporters".

"We have been overwhelmed with requests for help [and] have sent out individual advice to hundreds," the trust added.

"Clearly the scale of this has caused huge concern among fans.

"We are increasingly concerned that the current approach risks causing significant unintended consequences."

Physical season tickets are a thing of the past in the Premier League.

Clubs now use digital systems where fans download tickets to their phones. The change has been accompanied at many clubs by stricter rules on how, and how often, ticket holders can transfer their tickets to other people.

At Manchester United, for example, fans can have their season ticket revoked if they do not attend or forward their ticket to approved friends and family members for at least 16 out of 19 Premier League fixtures.

Last season, the club moved 500 season ticket holders from seats they had used for years in order to accommodate an increase in hospitality tickets.

The Red Devils have made sweeping cuts to their workforce since the partial takeover by Ineos in 2024, including those working in ticketing.

The method of identifying suspicious accounts United have employed uses third-party software and is largely automated.

In a message sent to the club fans' forum last week, after the first restrictions were sent out to supporters, United defended their approach and insisted the vast majority of those facing potential sanctions have misbehaved.

"Our recent operation focused on instances where multiple accounts displayed patterns of activity indicating they may have been centrally controlled, coordinated by the same individual, or operated using automated software," they said.

"We are confident that the vast majority of accounts identified for misuse have been correctly flagged with the appropriate action taken."

United conducted a crackdown on touting last season, cancelling 22,000 tickets for the first five home games of the season.

They regard that figure as "the tip of the iceberg" and believe around 10-15% of season tickets are controlled by touts.

A joint statement signed by United supporter organisations, fan clubs and fanzines acknowledged the need to crack down on touting but said the issue must be tackled appropriately.

"The club and its supporters share the same objective: ensuring tickets are used fairly by genuine Manchester United supporters while protecting the integrity of the ticketing system," said the statement.

"That objective will only be achieved through trust, transparency, proportionate enforcement, better-designed systems and meaningful engagement.

"Taking time to review the current approach, engage with supporter representatives and restore confidence is in the interests of both the club and its supporters."

Manchester United fans have protested against rising ticket prices and rule changes in recent years

"Every single one of our members with a season ticket has had the email," says the secretary of a United supporters' club in Northern Ireland - a fan for more than 50 years, who asked not to be named.

"If one of our members can't go to a game for some reason, they'll usually offer it to another member and lots of our accounts are linked together. Everything is fair and done for face value. But the club don't seem to understand that, or want to understand it.

"It's just so disappointing. Everybody is really angry."

Fans told BBC Sport they believe some of Manchester United's most loyal matchgoers have been erroneously targeted because they are more likely to ask friends or family members to log in to their account, for example to purchase tickets for away matches as a group or for help when busy with work or childcare, which they say the club is conflating with touting.

"It feels like you're not allowed to help your mates out and pass your ticket on to them, because the club will accuse you of touting," Andy says.

"But you can sell your ticket back to them and they'll sell it to someone else at a much higher price than you paid by adding on some free drinks or food.

"It's all wrong."

Touting - illegally reselling match tickets at an inflated price - is a widespread issue in the Premier League.

Last season, BBC Sport exposed the black market of top-flight tickets available for resale online, which circumvent UK laws against ticket touting by being based abroad.

Manchester United insist that revoked season tickets will be repurposed as new ones for supporters on the waiting list.

But some fans believe that clubs - particularly the wealthiest - want fewer season-ticket holders in their stadiums, because selling seats for matches on an individual basis generates more revenue per ticket.

In theory, fans who are tourists visiting infrequently are more likely to spend money in the stadium and in club stores than regulars who attend every match.

"Season ticket rules are definitely a concern," says Thomas Concannon, Premier League network manager at the Football Supporters' Association.

"We've all benefited from passing a ticket on to a mate for face value, and fans worry that even something like that is now deemed against the rules. We need a proper consensus on the rules across all clubs.

"Taking a season ticket away harms the atmosphere and means you're losing that fan for life.

"We stand behind protecting season-ticket holders and having as many of them as possible."

Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 18:39:47 GMT

A Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 46 miles (74km) south of Plymouth on Monday.

The Royal Navy monitored the exercise and is tracking "the vessel's activity closely", a Ministry of Defence spokesperson said.

The BBC has been told that, prior to opening fire, Russian frigate Neustrashimy (English: Dauntless) had informed the Royal Navy Offshore Patrol Vessel, HMS Tyne, of its intention to conduct gunnery activity.

Newly appointed Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the exercise "performative and irresponsible". The Kremlin has signalled there was no link between the exercise and Andy Burnham taking office as prime minister.

"All [military] exercises and all actions undertaken by our warships are carried out in strict compliance with international and maritime law," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told BBC News.

"Therefore, there is no need to see any signals in this," he said.

However, Peskov added that Burnham had sent signals to Russia, saying: "One of the first things the new British prime minister did as he took office was to declare his unconditional support for Ukraine and, accordingly, declare the UK's intention to continue doing everything it possibly can to continue the war."

Streeting said Russia "should be in no doubt about the resolve" of the new government and prime minister.

UK defence sources would not comment on whether the incident might have been timed to coincide with the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

The live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The Russian warship requested that the Royal Navy's HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did.

The Russian frigate was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

BBC Verify has analysed flight and ship-tracking data which shows the position of HMS Tyne and several British military aircraft operating in and around the Channel near Plymouth on Monday.

Flight data on ADS-B Exchange indicates at least four Royal Air Force and Royal Navy aircraft were flying off the coast of Dorset mostly above the UK's territorial waters, including two Eurofighter Typhoons, a Voyager air refuelling tanker and a Super Lynx helicopter.

A French military H160M Guépard helicopter also flew out and over the Channel during the afternoon. It is not clear if this is the aircraft which made contact with the Russian warship.

Data on ship-tracking service MarineTraffic shows HMS Tyne began to broadcast its location about 40 miles off Plymouth at 13:57 BST on Monday. It remained in that location for around two hours before departing at 15:56 to return to Plymouth.

HMS Tyne has been tracking Neustrashimy since at least 16 July when both vessels were also captured in the North Sea about 36 miles miles from the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk on a satellite image.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they had not been on a "collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

Tom Sharpe, a retired Royal Navy commander, told BBC Radio 4's World At One programme it was "very unusual" to conduct a gunnery exercise so close to the south coast.

"It is entirely allowable but in my mind it is a signal," he said.

Apart from the warning to HMS Tyne, the Russian vessel did not put any safety measures in place before firing a 100mm cannon, he said.

"One of the issues with firing a weapon of that calibre is that it can ricochet for miles, perhaps over ten miles beyond its intended landing point," Sharpe added.

"You are in the busiest shipping lane in the world and who knows where it is going?"

Asked how the UK should respond, the retired commander said: "You could argue that this was them responding to us because we've upped the ante in the Channel, we boarded the [MV] Smyrtos, one of their dark fleet ships, which is now at anchor off the south coast.

"So we are in this tit-for-tat, which is kind of Cold War normality. We've just forgotten that this sort of stuff used to happen all the time but we need to acknowledge that it is getting closer and closer to the UK."

Additional reporting by Ella Kipling, Barbara Metzler, Thomas Spencer and Patrick Jackson

Lebanese army says troops deploying in 'pilot zone' after Israeli withdrawal

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 18:07:34 GMT

Lebanon's army says its troops are deploying to a "pilot zone" in the south of the country following the withdrawal of Israeli forces under a US-brokered agreement reached last month.

Engineering units entered the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh in Nabatieh district on Tuesday morning, the army command announced.

Later, it said Israeli forces had opened fire in the vicinity of the troops. Israel's military said warning shots had been fired after the troops crossed into the Israeli-declared "security zone".

The pilot zone plan should see Israeli troops pulling out of a small part of the territory occupied during their conflict with Hezbollah and the disarmament of the Iran-backed Lebanese group.

Tuesday's deployment began ahead of a meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and his Lebanese counterpart, Joseph Aoun.

Aoun was expected to urge Trump to put pressure on Israel to withdraw from the rest of southern Lebanon and support the Lebanese army in taking full control of areas where Hezbollah holds sway.

"I told him [Trump] I need two things from you: political support and supporting the LAF [Lebanese Armed Forces]," Aoun told reporters in the Oval Office.

Speaking alongside Aoun, Trump vowed that the US would provide help to Lebanon which had been "hit hard" for decades.

"It's been a very badly treated place and country, and we're going to have it properly treated," he said. "And treated with the respect it deserves."

The US state department announced on Monday afternoon that "pilot zone operations" had begun in Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh and two other Lebanese villages, Froun and Srifa, in line with the Trilateral Framework agreed by Israel, Lebanon and the US at the end of June.

It said the "milestone" was the direct result of discussions last week between Israeli and Lebanese representatives in Rome.

Later on Monday, an Israeli military official confirmed the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) would "adjust its force posture in one of the pilot areas" to allow the Lebanese army to carry out its mission, while also "safeguarding the security of IDF soldiers and preserving its right to self-defence and to remove threats".

"The objective of the pilot and the agreement is the disarmament of the Hezbollah terrorist organisation and the removal of its illegal weapons," the official said.

They also reiterated that the IDF would remain in the "security zone" - the 10km (six-mile) deep strip of occupied Lebanese territory running along the border - for "as long as necessary" to defend northern Israeli communities.

On Tuesday, the Lebanese army's command said its units had begun deploying to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh "based on ongoing communications with the Military Co-ordination Group for Lebanon", referring to the trilateral body created to support implementation of the framework.

The statement also called on Lebanese citizens "not to head to the village until the security situation stabilises, and to comply with the instructions of the deployed military units for their own safety".

Later on Tuesday, the army command said Israeli forces had "opened fire in the vicinity of these units" and warned that the "attack hinders the implementation of deployment steps in the pilot zones".

The IDF said its soldiers had fired "warning shots into the air" after the Lebanese troops and an engineering vehicle "crossed approximately 150m (490ft) into the security zone and breached the barriers" in the neighbouring area of Zawtar al-Sharqiyeh.

The Lebanese troops "withdrew from the area, and no injuries were reported", it added.

The Lebanese army said its troops were already carrying out missions in nearby Froun and Srifa following Monday's US announcement.

An Israeli source also told Haaretz newspaper that there were no Israeli troops in those villages.

Also on Tuesday, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency said Israeli forces were behind two large explosions near the villages of Beit Yahoun and Kounine, in Bint Jbeil district. It also reported blasts from Israeli controlled demolitions in the town of Majdal Zoun, in Tyre district.

In areas still occupied by Israeli forces, many villages have been completely destroyed by Israeli strikes or demolitions.

The Israeli military says it has been destroying Hezbollah infrastructure, but human rights groups say some of what has happened there amounts to the deliberate destruction of civilian infrastructure, a possible war crime.

Hezbollah has rejected the agreement between Lebanon's government, Israel and the US, saying the provisions linking Israel's withdrawal to the group's disarmament crossed "all red lines". Israel has said it will not fully withdraw from the country until the group is fully disarmed.

According to Trump, the US has "concrete plans" to help Lebanon build the capacity to disarm Hezbollah, but he provided no details.

"They're also becoming much more self-sufficient," Trump said of the Lebanese army.

Additionally, Trump said he would speak directly to representatives of Hezbollah if requested by Aoun.

Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.

Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south.

More than 4,300 people have been killed in Lebanon, including almost 800 children, women and medics, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Israeli authorities say 37 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed on both sides of the border during the conflict.

How a former Blue Peter presenter stunned America's Got Talent judges

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 17:44:04 GMT

A 50th birthday gift from her fellow Spice Girls, a picture of a dog and a mobile phone.

Those were the prized possessions that three America's Got Talent judges watched a former Blue Peter presenter appear to smash with a hammer.

But like all magic tricks, everything was not quite as it seemed and moments later the treasured items returned.

Joel Mawhinney, known as Joel M, said the "risky" trick was "the scariest experience" of his life.

But as he reminded the judges: "Everything that disappears must reappear."

Going into the judges dressing rooms and taking some of their prized possessions might not be the best way of getting them on your side.

Smashing those items with a hammer is even less likely to help your chances.

Yet that is exactly what Mawhinney did, leaving Mel B, Sofía Vergara and Howie Mandel stunned before revealing that every item had somehow survived.

Mandel's phone appeared inside a locked box that had been sitting in front of the judges throughout the audition.

The phone then began receiving texts from Mawhinney revealing where the other judges missing valuables had ended up.

Vergara's framed picture of her dog was hidden inside her seat cushion, while Mel B's bracelet was concealed in one of the famous Got Talent red buzzers.

"I don't know how you do it. I believe in magic but I loved it," Mel B said when giving her verdict, which was a yes.

Vergara laughed and said the "magic was very impressive". She also voted yes, adding: "I don't know if this was necessary, but it was very exciting."

Mendel called Mawhinney "charming, you've got a good look", but it was a no from the comedian, calling the performance "too slow".

Simon Cowell agreed on the length of the performance and said "you can't do that on a live show".

"Our audience love magic, which is exactly the reason I'm going to say yes."

With three yeses, Mawhinney progressed to the next stage and remains in with a chance of winning the cash prize.

Mawhinney said that when he entered the judges' dressing rooms he didn't know what he would have ended up with.

"I knew the plan was to take prized possessions, or whatever I could find, but it just so happened that the jewellery was there," he told BBC Good Morning Ulster programme.

"It's a hard and set rule that if I'm performing magic, I don't borrow possessions of people.

"I don't like taking phones. I don't like borrowing rings because I've just heard so many horror stories.

"But I thought, it's America's Got Talent, I have to do something. So I sort of went for it."

The former presenter said producers had been inviting him to audition for America's Got Talent since 2020, but he always felt it sounded like "a massive risk" and his "gut instinct was always no".

"But then I left Blue Peter this year and wanted to establish myself as a magician again, because that's what I'm doing now.

"And I thought, you might as well kick the whole thing off with something a bit extreme, so I'll fly to the States and do that."

Mawhinney, from Bangor in Northern Ireland, first appeared on Blue Peter in 2018 and later became the iconic children's show's 41st presenter.

After more than three and a half years on the show, he announced in July that he was leaving to focus on magic.

He said his experience presenting live television proved invaluable during the audition.

"The live training of Blue Peter meant I would've really struggled in that audition because there were so many different elements going on at once.

"I'm really glad I did it, but I mean, yeah, it's the most nervous I've been for quite a while because you're putting yourself into a massive risky position."

Carney looking at 'all options' as Trump announces 50% tariffs on Canada

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 17:33:22 GMT

US President Donald Trump has imposed a 50% tariff on a wide range of goods imported from Canada, in retaliation for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

Everyday consumer items like wine and hockey sticks, as well as industrial goods such as cement, are on the target list. Several key exports, though, will be spared, including energy, potash, critical minerals and fish.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had spoken to Trump and both leaders agreed to "intensify" trade talks in a bid to calm growing trade tensions between the North American neighbours.

But he warned "all options" were on the table in terms of how Canada could respond to the fresh tariff threat.

Since the tariff war broke out more than 18 months ago, Carney said, Canadians have "stood together" by buying home-produced goods and agreeing new trade routes with other countries.

"[The] country is stronger, stronger because we are united, and we will remain united," he told reporters.

Tensions between the major trading partners have been simmering since Trump returned to office in January last year and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs, sometimes to pursue objectives not directly linked to trade.

Tariffs are taxes on imported goods that are paid to the government by companies bringing in the foreign products.

Asked about the latest tariffs, which the White House says will take effect in 30 days, on Tuesday, President Trump said Canada had been "very, very tough on us over the years" and "no other presidents done anything about it".

"I love Canada, I love the people of Canada, many friends that live in Canada," he said. "Without us, there's no way they can survive."

The latest move by Trump comes after the US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that many of the tariffs imposed globally under emergency powers were illegally enacted. The president has since sought other legal avenues to push through his flagship trade policy, as seen in Monday's announcement.

Trump has said the levies will boost American manufacturing and jobs, but some economists have warned that higher charges on imported goods risks pushing up prices for consumers.

This new round of duties on Canadian goods has also fuelled speculation about a potential wider tariff announcement by the US on countries across the world. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Tuesday that he expected to "see some action soon", when asked on CNBC about the possibility of forthcoming levies.

Canada, which is one of the US's closest trading partners, was one of the few countries to retaliate last year against Trump's tariffs, placing a 25% levy of its own on about C$30bn (£16bn; $21.7bn) worth of US goods.

Carney later dropped some of them.

The new US tariffs add to trade barriers already in place between the two nations.

The US has been maintaining active tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on Canadian steel, aluminium and copper. It also charges a 35% tariff on Canadian softwood lumber, alongside a 25% tax on non-US parts in cars.

Meanwhile Canada has its own 25% counter-tariff on selected imports of American steel, aluminium and vehicles.

A White House fact sheet said the new tariffs announced this week applied regardless of whether the product was included under the existing free trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA.

But Carney said the move was the "latest in a series of unilateral US trade actions that began with the US imposing a series of tariffs in direct violation" of the USMCA.

The prime minister also cited "threats to Canadian sovereignty", possibly in reference to Trump's repeated calls to make America's northern neighbour the 51st US state.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said that if the US goes ahead with its latest threat, "Canada should respond tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar".

The BBC has contacted the White House and the Canadian government for further comment.

As part of his executive action announcing the new tariffs, Trump issued three proclamations, relating to to cars, dairy products and alcohol.

Monday's announcement also comes in the wake of President Trump's threat to impose tariffs over Canadian wildfire smoke drifting into US cities, though this issue has not been officially mentioned as the justification for the move.

Earlier this year, the US chose not to renew the USMCA in its current form - while Canada and Mexico sought a renewal - as it aimed to make changes to the agreement, which was reached during Trump's first term in office.

Despite the recent US action, the treaty will continue to govern North American trade over the next decade on a rolling basis, but it will require annual reviews.

The recently announced tariffs highlight the Trump administration's opposition to USMCA, said Michael Devereux, a professor of economics at the University of British Columbia.

"It is a significant escalation because it directly targets goods that were previously exempt under the US, Canada, Mexico trade agreement that President Trump negotiated and signed himself in 2018," he added.

In February, the US Supreme Court struck down sweeping international tariffs imposed by Trump through the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) of 1977, saying he had exceeded his authority under a law reserved for national emergencies.

The White House then vowed to invoke other mechanisms to impose import taxes, and in recent week has announced fresh tariffs on a range of countries under a different law commonly called "Section 301". That included a new levy on Brazil, which has vowed to retaliate.

Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 17:14:44 GMT

Shortly after Andy Burnham telephoned a number of Keir Starmer's allies to sack them from the cabinet on Monday afternoon, John Healey received the signal to head to Number 10.

Wearing a suit and one of his many red ties, the former defence secretary left parliament alone via a back entrance next to a pub.

"I'm on my way to a meeting," he said with a slight smile as he marched down Whitehall.

Healey's imminent appointment as chancellor was a surprise - to him, to his Labour colleagues, and to the British public.

It was a consequential moment among a flurry of announcements from the new prime minister, including today's cut in VAT on energy bills, that demonstrate the new government's intention to move at breakneck speed - at least for now.

The Conservatives support that tax cut but have questioned its funding.

Five weeks earlier Healey had weakened Keir Starmer's grip on Downing Street by quitting as defence secretary in a row over military spending.

Soon he would be back around the cabinet table alongside two others whose recent resignations had also damaged Starmer - new defence secretary Wes Streeting and new energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Were they rewarded for rebelling and hastening Burnham's path to office? Possibly.

But all three are also widely seen as skilled operators taking on complex roles.

John Healey's elevation to the second most important job in government has delighted senior figures in the Ministry of Defence, who are relieved to have someone in the Treasury who is committed to increasing military spending.

"It's brilliant for us," said an insider.

Yet the same MOD source is also relieved Healey is not returning.

"We were dreading him coming back", they said. "He's a difficult person".

Even some senior Conservatives think Healey's appointment as chancellor was clever. "For a number of reasons", explains one former Tory cabinet minister.

"He's not Ed Miliband, he's hard to attack, and he's Treasury-literate." Healey served as a minister in the department for five years during Tony Blair's premiership.

Burnham ally Anneliese Midgeley has the difficult task of trying to keep Labour MPs - including those sacked as ministers - loyal to the government.

Former chief secretary to the prime minister Darren Jones's public swipe at Burnham's energy bills policy is a sign not all will play nice.

One Labour MP claims that those sacked by Burnham can be divided into three groups.

"Some went because of their politics, others just weren't good, and then there are those disliked in the parliamentary Labour party," said the MP.

Behind the scenes, many in Westminster are talking about the possibility of Burnham taking advantage of a possible bounce in the opinion polls and calling a snap general election.

Nigel Farage wants one and argues it is necessary since Burnham has no mandate.

But with the Reform leader facing both a by-election and questions over his finances, some in his party worry that if Burnham moves too fast, Farage could miss his one great chance to become PM.

"We are really worried about a snap election," said the Reform source, grinning.

"Which is why we're calling for a snap election."

Across all the parties at Westminster, plans are being put in place in case a snap contest is called.

"We've started preparing," said a senior Liberal Democrat aide.

Burnham has appeared to rule out heading to the polls.

It would certainly anger some Labour MPs who could lose their seats.

Yet it would also offer the new PM an opportunity to get a fresh mandate for more radical policies, as well as secure his position for a full five year term.

"There is economic pain coming down the horizon", says the former Conservative cabinet minister.

"And it's about how far he [Burnham] gets ahead of it. He faces a choice between going for an election, and a slow decline as we saw with Gordon Brown."

That former PM was dubbed "bottler Brown" in 2007 after considering going to the polls before deciding against it.

Yet Brown got to Number 10 with a mixture of patience, caution, guile and ruthlessness, whereas Burnham's speedy rise was largely due to one major electoral gamble.

After his success in Makerfield and then the Labour leadership contest, will Burnham fancy another throw of the dice?

Two French firefighters die tackling blaze near Bordeaux airport

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 16:44:30 GMT

Two firefighters have died while battling a huge blaze near Bordeaux's airport in south-west France, officials have said.

Reports in French media say the blaze, near one of the parking lots at the airport, originated from a brush fire and then spread to a building.

Pictures shared on social media show passengers getting off a plane as a massive plume of smoke rises nearby. A number of flights scheduled to arrive at Bordeaux–Mérignac airport have been delayed.

Some 100 firefighters, backed by specialist aircraft, are reported to be trying to extinguish the blaze.

The country's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had been informed about the deaths by officials in the Gironde department.

Speaking during Tuesday's question-and-answer session at the French parliament, Nuñez also said he would travel to Gironde "as soon as possible" to oversee the firefighting efforts.

Gironde is one of several French departments ravaged by wildfires in recent days, due to a series of unusual and prolonged heatwaves.

Also on Tuesday, a huge fire broke out in the south-eastern Var department.

The blaze in the Pontevès commune "is currently out of control and is evolving rapidly", said the PSFDF volunteer association, which monitors fires across France.

It said 600 firefighters and rescuers had been deployed to contain the fire, and 150 people had already been evacuated.

France has registered nearly 11,000 fires since the beginning of the year, with President Emmanuel Macron saying last week that there had not been so many blazes in the country since World War Two.

Tuesday's satellite data from the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis) shows that more than 42,000 hectares (103,784 acres) burned in France between January and mid-July, surpassing the previous record set in 2022.

Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world, and Europe is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires.

The record-breaking temperatures across Europe this summer have led to major wildfires, most notably in Spain where at least 13 people have been killed.

Some 29,000 hectares of land have been destroyed by a massive wildfire north of the Spanish capital Madrid.

Consortium in talks to buy Liverpool minority stake

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 16:37:11 GMT

Amit Bhatia is part of one of the world's wealthiest families

A consortium led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia has expressed an interest in buying a minority stake in Liverpool.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of the Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal, was director and co-owner at QPR for 18 seasons but stepped down from the board and relinquished ownership of the club on Tuesday afternoon.

Amit Bhatia is a former investment banker who worked for Morgan Stanley on Wall Street before becoming an entrepreneur.

He operates businesses in construction, real estate, and private equity.

The construction company he founded at 32 is now the largest independent building materials business in the UK with more than 5,000 employees, and his real estate firm builds homes, student housing and offices across the country.

Londoner Bhatia, 46, was awarded the young entrepreneur of the year award in 2013, and sits on the advisory board of the Saudi Arabian government's cultural affairs and international relations unit.

He was a director and co-owner of QPR before his unexpected departure on Tuesday, and a stand at Loftus Road bears his surname.

He married Vanisha Mittal Bhatia in 2004, in a six-day ceremony in France costing more than $55m (£41m), which at the time was recognised by Guinness World Records as the most expensive of all-time.

Vanisha is the daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, whose net worth has been estimated at more $30bn (£22bn).

Liverpool finished fifth in the Premier League last season, and have hired ex-Bournemouth boss Andoni Iraola for the new campaign

FSG originally made clear in 2022 that it would be open to new investment in Liverpool, either from minority shareholders or a potential full sale.

It said at the time: "FSG has frequently received expressions of interest from third parties seeking to become shareholders in Liverpool.

"FSG has said before that under the right terms and conditions, we would consider new shareholders if it was in the best interests of Liverpool as a club."

The full sale never materialised but the agreement with Dynasty in 2023 was valued at between £82m and £164m, and was hailed by FSG as helping offset bank debt accrued from infrastructure projects including the redevelopments of the Main Stand, Anfield Road end, and the club's Kirkby training ground.

At the time of that deal, FSG president Mike Gordon said: "Our long-term commitment to Liverpool remains as strong as ever.

"[We want] to further strengthen the club's financial position and sustain our ambitions for continued success on and off the pitch."

Since then, FSG has explored the possibility of purchasing a second club in continental Europe to add to its portfolio.

The multi-club model would have followed the examples of Chelsea and Manchester City, whose owners also operate clubs in other territories.

But after examining potential purchases including Spanish sides Malaga and Getafe and French club Bordeaux, FSG did not proceed with any of the deals and is now understood to have moved away from the model.

That decision to eschew the approach led to the departure of Michael Edwards last month - the former Liverpool sporting director had been rehired by FSG in order to lead the multi-club project.

Current sporting director Richard Hughes is managing the club's transfer strategy this summer and has a contract lasting until summer 2027, but is believed to be open to a move to Saudi Arabia in the near future.

Liverpool principal owner John W Henry has taken a back seat on matters relating to the club in public since acknowledging and apologising for his role in the widely derided European Super League project in 2021.

Angela Rayner: Cabinet comeback for one of Labour's biggest names

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 16:12:23 GMT

Earlier this year, Angela Rayner was weighing up whether to reach for the Labour crown if Sir Keir Starmer's leadership was challenged.

The resolution of an HMRC investigation into her tax affairs, long seen as a barrier to any leadership bid, cleared a path for the former deputy prime minister to take part in any contest to replace her old boss.

But in the end she added her name to the wave of Labour MPs nominating Andy Burnham as leader, propelling the former Greater Manchester mayor into Downing Street uncontested.

Now she has made a return to the cabinet, with Burnham giving her back the job of housing secretary from which she resigned in September last year, after admitting she did not pay enough tax on the purchase of a new home.

It is a role in which she will play a key part in his drive to devolve power away from Westminster and deliver a major programme of council house building.

Her against-the-odds story, personality, and ability to connect with parts of the electorate other politicians have struggled to reach are likely to make her a prominent voice within Burnham's top team.

Born Angela Bowen in Stockport, Greater Manchester, in 1980, Rayner grew up on one of the area's poorest council estates and from an early age was caring for her mother, who had bipolar disorder and suffered from depression.

Both Rayner's parents were unemployed and speaking in 2017, she remembered having to grow up very quickly.

"My mum was a really vulnerable person. I remember, at 10, my mum being suicidal and me sleeping like a dog on the end of her bed, just to try and stay next to her so she didn't do any harm to herself," Rayner said.

She has also recalled going to her grandmother's flat on Sundays, so the family could take it in turns to have a bath there. Hot water was too expensive for them to use at home.

Rayner has often spoken about being told she would "never amount to anything", after she left school without any qualifications.

But after having her first child at 16, Rayner studied part-time at college, learning British sign language and gaining a vocational qualification in social care.

She spent a number of years as a care worker in Stockport, mainly looking after elderly people in their own homes, while also rising quickly through the ranks of the union, Unison.

She has described herself as "mouthy", someone who would "take no messing from management".

In her 20s, she became a full-time union official and eventually, after battles over working conditions and zero-hour contracts, rose to the most senior elected role in Unison in north-west England.

It was at Unison she met Mark Rayner, a fellow union official whom she married in 2010 and divorced in 2023. The couple went on to have two sons, one of whom was born so prematurely he is registered blind and has special educational needs.

At the age of 37, the mum-of-three became a grandmother, sparking the nickname "Grangela".

She credits the trade union movement with encouraging her to enter politics and taking her from - in her own words - "the girl on a council estate" to "a woman who feels like she can conquer the world".

Those ambitions started to be realised in 2015, when she was elected as the MP for Ashton-under-Lyne - a seat not far from her hometown. She later said she had only stood to make the point that "people like me can't get elected" and had "accidentally" won the seat.

A self-described "proper working-class" woman, Rayner rose quickly in Westminster, taking up the women and equalities and education briefs in the shadow cabinet of former Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.

When Corbyn stood down in 2020, following Labour's worst general election result since 1935, Rayner did not run for the leadership, and backed her ally Rebecca Long-Bailey, who came second to Sir Keir.

Instead, Rayner stood for the deputy leadership and won election to that post comfortably - going on to be a central figure in Sir Keir's bid to remake the party.

However, relations between Sir Keir and Rayner were sometimes tense. After Labour lost control of eight English councils and lost the seat of Hartlepool in a parliamentary by-election in May 2021, the deputy leader was removed from her post as party chairwoman.

She pushed back, and was appointed shadow first secretary of state among other titles.

By that point, Rayner had a strong support base and a powerful role likened to that of John Prescott, who was seen as a political bridge between the working class and the New Labour project during Tony Blair's premiership.

Rayner heavily leaned into that role and tried to use it to her party's advantage in the years before Labour's general election win in 2024.

Outspoken and combative at times, Rayner repeatedly accused the Conservatives of being "out of touch", and hammered the party with lines such as "one rule for them and another rule for us" during the scandal over pandemic parties in Downing Street.

Sometimes Rayner admitted she had gone too far, once apologising for describing senior Conservatives as "a bunch of scum".

Her prominence and the venom of her political attacks had put a target on her back and attracted unwanted headlines.

In 2021, Rayner lashed out at "sexism and misogyny" in politics, after a newspaper reported that she crossed and uncrossed her legs during prime minister's questions to distract Boris Johnson.

And in 2024, she was investigated by the police over the tax paid on the sale of her council house, again following a slew of reports by unfriendly newspapers, cheered on by the Conservatives. She was not found to have committed a criminal offence.

Her tendency to brush through political controversies gave her an air of untouchability, with some dubbing her "Teflon Ange".

Her stock had risen further still as deputy prime minister, leading on one of Labour's key pledges to build 1.5 million homes by 2030, and helping Sir Keir quell a rebellion by Labour MPs over welfare cuts.

But the political optics of a housing secretary admitting she had not paid enough when buying her £800,000 flat in Hove were not easy on the eye.

Rayner faced charges of hypocrisy and calls for her to stand down, and she did so after admitting arrangements on her family home in Greater Manchester meant she should have paid a higher rate.

She resigned from government after the prime minister's ethics adviser Sir Laurie Magnus declared that she had breached the ministerial code.

HMRC launched an investigation, and almost 10 months later, as a leadership crisis engulfed her party, a conclusion was reached.

Rayner announced she had settled £40,000 in unpaid stamp duty, and had been "exonerated" of the accusation she had "deliberately sought to avoid tax".

In an interview with the Guardian, the prime minister's former deputy did not rule out running in any Labour leadership race but said she would not "trigger" a contest.

Pressed over whether the prime minister should step aside, Rayner said: "Keir will have to reflect on that."

Prior to his downfall as Labour leader, Sir Keir had suggested he could bring Rayner back into his cabinet, adding she had the "best social mobility story this country has ever seen".

It is a story she will be hoping to continue after her return to cabinet, as Labour heads in a new direction under Burnham.

Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 16:11:14 GMT

While the UK government has announced it will cut VAT on domestic electricity this October from 5% to zero in an attempt to help with the cost of living, British households are still paying more for power than many other European nations.

Comparing UK prices with the EU shows that medium-use households here paid the fourth-highest electricity prices in the second half of last year including taxes and levies, although the government has taken steps to reduce bills since then.

Here are three key reasons why British electricity prices are high.

The price energy suppliers pay for electricity is set by a bidding process with each generating company saying what it would be willing to accept to produce one unit of electricity.

Once built, the cost of generating power from renewables like wind and solar is relatively low, so these typically come in with the cheapest bid. Nuclear might come next.

Gas generators often have the highest costs because they have to buy fuel to generate electricity as well as paying a "carbon price" - a charge for emissions.

The wholesale cost is set by the last unit of electricity needed to meet demand from consumers.

This means that even if gas only generates 1% of overall electricity at a given time it can often set the overall wholesale price which gets paid to every type of generator.

That raises prices for households - particularly because the wars in Iran and Ukraine have increased the cost of gas.

Northern Ireland operates on a separate system to the rest of the UK, being part of the Single Electricity Market with the Republic of Ireland.

Analysts say that one of the reasons why electricity prices are higher in the UK than some other countries is because we generate a relatively high share of our electricity from natural gas.

In 2025 31% of the UK's electricity was produced from burning natural gas.

This compares with just 3% in France, which generated the majority of its electricity - 69% - from nuclear power.

The US has a higher share of natural gas in its electricity generation mix than the UK - 40% - but American wholesale gas prices are considerably lower thanks to the shale gas production boom of the past 20 years.

Higher wholesale gas prices have pushed up UK domestic electricity bills this year.

The wholesale energy costs contribution to a typical household bill in Great Britain rose from £311 in 2024-25 to £320 in 2025-26.

But bills have also been pushed up in recent years by state subsidies to encourage private firms to build wind and solar farms and also national electricity grid network investment costs, which previous governments have added to household electricity bills.

These network costs have been driven by the need to expand and modernise the grid to accommodate new wind and solar farms and transmit their power to homes and businesses.

The network costs contribution to a typical bill rose from £136 in 2019-20 to £250 in 2026, an increase of £113.

"We've probably underinvested in the last decade and now we're trying to catch up so there's quite a lot of spending," says Frankie Mayo, an energy analyst from Ember Energy.

The generation subsidies contribution to a typical bill rose from £127 in 2019-20 to £159 in 2026, an increase of £32.

Network costs are projected to increase further by 2030, adding another £48 to a typical bill, according to calculations by energy analyst Ben James.

However the government and some energy groups also argue that reducing our national reliance on volatile international gas prices via the government's 2030 clean power policy will keep down the UK's wholesale electricity costs and mean household bills will be lower than they would otherwise have been.

This would be by reducing the amount of time in each year that gas sets the wholesale electricity price.

A great deal though depends on future wholesale gas prices which are impossible to accurately forecast.

Some analysts, including the government's Climate Change Committee, also say the government should go further to remove policy costs from household electricity bills and meet them through general taxation instead, in order to avoid discouraging people from using electricity rather than gas to heat their homes.

"The way you allocate those costs matters," says Mayo.

"They may be being put on bills or they may be being paid by consumers in other ways that are less visible, such as taxes."

Whitehall officials offered move to No 10 North in Manchester

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 16:01:00 GMT

Civil servants working for government departments based in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move to the North of England, the BBC understands.

It comes as the first details are emerging about the new No 10 North, which Downing Street says is already up and running.

The BBC has been told that the Northern branch of Downing Street will be overseen by cabinet minister and ally of Burnham, Louise Haigh.

Haigh, who is the first secretary of state, is thought to have been asked to lead a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC), which will give her control of key decision-making bodies across government.

The OPMC will include No 10, No 10 North and teams within the Cabinet Office.

Addressing his cabinet for the first time, Burnham said No 10 North was "not a gimmick" and that the "time for resisting devolution was over".

A No 10 spokesman said the prime minister was expecting to work from No 10 North "at least one day a week" subject to government business.

Announcing the changes, which will also establish a new AI taskforce, Leader of the House of Lords, Baroness Angela Smith said No 10 North would be a "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

It is understood that the initial location of No 10 North will be Heron House in central Manchester, in the same building which houses offices for the intelligence service GCHQ. Specialist police officers have been seen guarding the building.

It is likely that the longer term base for No 10 North will be at a new government "Digital Campus" which is under construction in the Ancoats area of Manchester. It is not due for completion until 2032.

However, a good indication of what it could look like comes from a new report, released on Tuesday.

The blueprint has been authored by the Re:State think tank which Burnham was involved with until he stepped down as mayor of Greater Manchester.

It sets out a possible recruitment plan that would bring in new hires from across Greater Manchester and the wider North of England.

In total, the report suggests around 300 staff should be employed within 18 months.

It proposes transferring teams from Whitehall departments, including the Treasury, Cabinet Office, and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government – all of which are now being led by ministers who represent constituencies in the North of England.

Successive governments have sought to move more civil servants out of London and last year a target was set to cut the number of roles in the capital by 12,000.

According to the most recent figures, 19.6% of civil servants are based in London and the number has been gradually decreasing for the past four years.

The percentage of senior civil servants based outside of London stands at 13.5% compared to 34.7% in London.

Whitehall officials willing to move to Manchester have been told they will be offered relocation packages, the BBC understands.

It's also likely there will be a significant movement of staff from Burnham's former mayoral team at the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA).

The BBC has been told that at least three senior figures are understood to have agreed to work at No 10 North. Some GMCA staff expressed surprise at only finding out their colleagues would be moving after seeing them on TV greeting the new prime minister in Downing Street.

No 10 North will lead on a key plank of Burnham's agenda; handing power from Whitehall and Westminster to regions across the country.

It means strategic decisions about devolution and local economic growth will shift out of the Treasury, now led by Chancellor John Healey, and Angela Rayner's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government - though both departments will have some "remaining functions" in these areas.

Brazil's Amazon sees sharp decline in size of area burned in 2025

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:57:29 GMT

The area burned in Brazil's Amazon in 2025 was far smaller in size than the previous year, according to the deforestation monitoring group MapBiomas.

A MapBiomas report states that 3.1 million hectares of Brazil's Amazon were burned last year, compared with a record-breaking 15.8 million hectares in 2024.

The amount of land burned in the world's largest rainforest last year covered the smallest area since MapBiomas records began in 1985.

Protecting the Amazon was one of the pledges President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made when he was running for office four years ago. These latest figures will be seen as a boost to his campaign for re-election in October.

In 2024, the Amazon rainforest experienced its worst forest fires in over two decades, which the Copernicus Climate Change Service put down to "climate extremes and human activity".

"The 2025 figures are significant and show that it is possible to reduce the burned area in the country," Vera Arruda, a researcher at the Amazon Environmental Research Institute (IPAM) and co-ordinator at MapBiomas, told the BBC.

"The 31% drop compared to the historical average - driven primarily by the lowest number of fires recorded in the Amazon in 41 years - is positive news, but it does not yet allow us to conclude that this is an established trend or to scale back prevention efforts," Arruda added.

The MapBiomas report shows a dramatic drop in area burned not just in the Amazon, but across the whole of Brazil in 2025.

Figures show around 12.7 million hectares burned in Brazil in 2025, compared to 30 million hectares in 2024.

The highest number of hectares burned in Brazil since records began was in 2007, when 30.7 million were recorded across the country.

The decline in the 2025 figures partly reflects an easing of the unprecedented fires of 2024, helped by cooler La Niña conditions instead of the warmer El Niño.

But MapBiomas warned the natural weather pattern of El Niño, which pushes up global temperatures, could extend this year's dry season and increase the risk of forest fires.

Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species, and in a healthy state they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.

They have come under increasing pressure as a result of decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create the conditions for bigger fires to spread.

When he took office, President Lula promised to reverse the deforestation which occurred during the presidency of his predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro argued that more farming and mining in the Amazon would reduce poverty in the region and environmentalists accused him of allowing deforestation to accelerate.

Three years into Bolsonaro's four-year term, the amount of trees cut down in the Amazon rainforest went up by 75%.

On his first day in office, on 1 January 2023, Lula insisted that "our goal is to achieve zero deforestation in the Amazon".

While that pledge was warmly welcomed by environmentalists, there has been widespread criticism of Lula's decision to approve oil exploration at the mouth of the Amazon river, which activists say flies in the face of his promise to protect the Amazon region.

At least 12 Palestinians, including six members of one family, have been killed in three separate Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip, according to local medics.

The brother of Firas al-Masri told the BBC that he had been burnt to death along with his wife, Salsabeel, and their three daughters and son, Faryal, Salma, Amira and Naim.

The Israeli military said its target was a Hamas operative and that it was still looking into the results of the attack.

The Israeli military has not yet commented on those strikes.

According to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, at least 1,168 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect last October.

Four Israeli soldiers have been killed in Palestinian attacks in Gaza over the same period.

The UN's human rights office condemned on Tuesday the recent intensification of Israeli military attacks in Gaza.

Between 13 and 20 July, at least 57 Palestinians, including six children and eight women, were killed in strikes on residential buildings, a tent camp for displaced families, and other crowded areas, spokesman Thameen Al-Kheetan said.

Thirty-four of those people were "killed far away" from the so-called Yellow Line, which marks territory in Gaza controlled by Israeli forces, he added.

Israel responded by launching a massive military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,290 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

Lindt's Easter chocolate sales fall after price hike

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:37:58 GMT

Lindt has partially U-turned on its decision to hike prices after Easter chocolate sales dropped.

The Swiss chocolate maker said a "necessary groupwide" price surge of 11.8% was one of the reasons revenue shrank in the first half of this year, particularly in the UK, Germany, and Switzerland.

It also blamed weaker Easter demand and a drop in tourism from Asia and the Middle East "due to geopolitical uncertainties". In response, it said it has adjusted prices and boosted marketing in certain regions for the second half of the year.

Around Easter, Lindt is known for its chocolate rabbits wrapped in gold-coloured foil and decorated with a red ribbon and bell on their necks.

Overall, the company's sales dipped 0.9%, with European sales down by 2.1%. It added that "performance was impacted by more price-sensitive and mature markets such as Germany, Switzerland and the UK".

By volume, meaning the amount of chocolate sold rather than the money it made, overall sales sank 7.5%. Pre-tax profit fell 1.5%.

Meanwhile, sales of Lindt chocolate in airports decreased "due to ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, and therefore declining passenger traffic".

Lindt said its sales picked up in North America, Australia, China, and Japan, though these countries account for a much smaller slice of its sales than Europe, where it makes over half its revenue.

Lindt chief executive Adalbert Lechner said: "The actions we have initiated focus on volume recovery in the second half of 2026 and lay the foundation to regain volume growth momentum in 2027."

Lindt is not the only chocolate firm which has been putting prices up.

Experts say climate change has led to extreme rainfall and droughts which have decreased cocoa farmers' crops.

This pushes up costs of making chocolate, and companies have chosen different ways to react to this, with some reducing chocolate content or sizes rather than raising prices.

According to the latest official data, the annual rate of chocolate and sweet price rises is 7.9% – much higher than the general rate of UK inflation at 2.8%.

Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:35:08 GMT

Ann Widdecombe was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch in an attack that was caught on camera, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man charged with her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.

Kerry, who prosecutors say was in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer in her kitchen, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off.

The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.

At the Old Bailey hearing, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the attack on Widdecombe had been carried out with a "ferocity of violence".

Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.

The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.

Malik told the chief magistrate that security camera footage from her home in Haytor, Devon, showed she had been fatally attacked the day before.

He added that police were still investigating whether there was a terrorism connection or political motivation for the attack.

Kerry, from Rotherham, was charged with one count of murder on Monday night following an investigation led by counter-terrorism detectives.

He appeared emotionless in the dock and spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during the short hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court. He was not asked to indicate a plea.

Later on Tuesday, he also appeared at the Old Bailey. It is expected that he will be remanded at HMP Belmarsh in south-east London.

He will next appear at the same court on 9 October for a case management hearing.

A provisional trial date has been listed for 8 June 2027.

The court heard that a pathologist had given a provisional cause of Widdecombe's death as a blunt force injury to the head.

An earlier inquest hearing, that was opened and adjourned on Tuesday, heard that emergency services were called on the day Widdecombe was found, but she was pronounced dead at 12:20.

The hearing was also told that while a post-mortem examination had taken place, "at this stage the precise medical cause of death has yet to be established".

Widdecombe's career in politics spanned decades.

She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

She later represented South West England as a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for the Brexit Party and in 2023 she joined Reform UK as a party spokeswoman.
