Teenagers jailed for murdering 16-year-old in beach knife attack

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 14:42:07 GMT

Three teenagers have been jailed for murdering a 16-year-old boy during a confrontation between rival groups on a beach in North Ayrshire last year.

They were convicted of stabbing apprentice painter and decorator Kayden Moy from East Kilbride on Irvine Beach on 17 May 2025.

Cole Turley, 18, who had pleaded guilty to the murder, and Jay Stewart, 19 were given life sentences and told they will serve a minimum of 16 years.

A third teenager - a 15-year-old who cannot be named for legal reasons - will be detained for a minimum of 14 years.

Speaking outside the High Court in Glasgow, Moy's father said his family's grief meant they were themselves enduring a life sentence.

Paul Moy said: "While today's outcome brings a measure of justice, it does not bring peace, it does not bring our son back.

"Kayden was more than a name in the courtroom or a headline in the news, he was our son, he was loved beyond words and had his whole life ahead of him.

"We hope today's sentence sends a clear message that violence has a devastating and irreversible consequences.

"One moment of violence has destroyed so many lives and no family should ever have to endure the pain that we now live with every day."

Passing sentence, Judge Lord Scott said Moy's death was "pointless and unnecessary".

He said the attackers "travelled to Irvine, armed, intent on a reprisal for some slight".

He added: "It could have been anyone but Kayden slipped and fell."

The court heard that Stewart and the 15-year-old - while acting with Turley - chased Moy and repeatedly stabbed him with a lock knife after he fell to the ground.

Stewart brandished his baton and was heard to shout "Murray Boys". He then told a witness at the scene that his victim "deserved it."

After running from the scene, Turley stuck the knife into the grass and was overheard boasting that he "just done him."

Turley also shouted "One-nil."

CCTV showed the trio running down a road near to the beach - stopping momentarily to embrace each other.

They also went on to create a rap song mocking Moy who at the time was fighting for his life in hospital, and Turley acted out the murder on the couch of a friend whose flat was used as a hide-out.

That friend, Fraser Wallace, told the court the teenagers were "over the moon" after the attack.

He said: "I have never seen people as happy in my life."

The witness stated that the 15-year-old told him that he gave the murder weapon to Turley before the stabbing

Stewart and the younger boy had both denied murder but were found guilty last month after a trial at the High Court in Glasgow.

Prosecutor Liam Ewing KC said the group's apparent congratulations to each other after the stabbing were "the actions of those who have accomplished what they came to do".

The trial heard the attackers were members of the Murray Boys gang from East Kilbride, while Moy was a member of the rival Himshie group.

The trio had travelled to Irvine beach after a fight between the groups earlier that day.

Stewart, who was also armed with an extendable baton, had previously made threats towards Moy on social media.

The boys threw rocks at Moy and his friends - which prosecutors said was intended to draw them into a fight.

After the stabbing, which led to scenes of chaos on the beach, they took a taxi back to East Kilbride.

Earlier, Donald Findlay KC spoke in mitigation for Stewart. He told the court that Stewart and Kayden Moy had been "close friends at one time".

He added: "But two groups were formed and took to behaving in the way that they did. Violence was commonplace."

He said Stewart regrets what happens and has been "very affected" since his conviction.

Stewart was subject to a community payback order at the time for possession of a machete which was imposed four days before the murder.

His other previous conviction was a breach of the peace with a knife.

Mark Stewart KC, representing Turley, said the 18-year-old "didn't intend to kill or want to kill Kayden Moy but he accepts that he did".

Iain Duguid KC for the third teenager said he was 14-years-old at the time of the murder and his "immaturity" had been highlighted in criminal justice social work reports.

He said the teenager had a "traumatic upbringing" and has since engaged in education projects while in secure accommodation.

He will be detained in secure accommodation before being transferred to prison when he is an adult.

Moira Orr, who leads on homicide for the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal service said: "The three accused, all teenagers, made themselves potential murderers the moment they armed themselves with at least one knife.

"And murderers they became. One of them - Cole Turley - struck the fatal blow but prosecutors proved that all three were part of the planning and execution of the crime.

"It is difficult to adequately express the devastation caused by their decision to carry a bladed weapon."

Why Iran is risking so much over the Strait of Hormuz

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 14:36:47 GMT

After 10 days of exchanging strikes with the US over control of the vital Strait of Hormuz waterway, Iran's leaders may appear to have three choices. None offer a clear route to victory.

The first is to accept much of what Washington wants: guarantee free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz by ending attacks on commercial shipping, give up or dilute Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium, and accept intrusive inspections by the global nuclear watchdog.

In return, Tehran would seek an end to the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, and protection from further attacks.

This is probably the least costly option, but also the costliest politically.

Reopening Hormuz without securing a recognised Iranian role in managing the waterway would mean surrendering what some in Tehran increasingly see as a newly discovered deterrent, one that may now appear more effective than Iran's missiles, regional proxies, or even its nuclear programme.

For the first time, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated its ability to impose immediate costs on the global economy for an attack on its territory by its enemies.

The nuclear programme, meanwhile, has long been presented as a right that Iran cannot be forced to abandon.

Conceding to demands for tight restrictions on nuclear activities after months of attacks would allow hardliners to argue that American military pressure had worked. It could also open the door to further demands over Iran's missile programme and its relationships with Hezbollah in Lebanon, Iraqi Shia groups and Yemen's Houthis.

The second option is escalation. Iran could intensify its attacks on American bases in the region, shipping, and vital infrastructure in Gulf Arab states, hoping that higher energy prices and wider disruption would force Washington and its allies to compromise.

This carries the greatest military risk. An attack causing mass casualties or serious damage to Gulf infrastructure could draw Iran's neighbours more directly into the conflict and leave it facing a broader coalition.

The third option is to preserve the current instability: enough pressure on shipping and energy markets to retain leverage, but not enough to trigger a return to all-out war with the US.

This seems to fit the Islamic Republic's established thinking. Iran does not need to defeat a stronger enemy if it can survive for longer than that enemy is willing to fight. Survival itself can be presented as victory. But sanctions, war damage and inflation are steadily increasing pressure at home.

And as time goes on, a paradox may emerge: The more Iran uses the Strait of Hormuz as a weapon, the less powerful it could become if countries find new ways to export energy and other goods out of the region.

Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has acknowledged the contradiction, arguing that the value of Hormuz lies in increasing the volume of shipping through it rather than reducing it. A permanently unsafe waterway encourages the world to find ways around Iran.

Complicating matters further is the uncertainty surrounding Iran's decision-making process.

Under Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike at the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February, disputes between elected politicians, clerical institutions and the Revolutionary Guards were ultimately settled by the supreme leader. After months of war and under the new leadership of Khamenei's son Mojtaba, that balance of power is less clear.

President Masoud Pezeshkian and his diplomats may favour a settlement to ease economic pressure and restore stability. Hardliners in parliament, powerful unelected institutions, and conservative media outlets, meanwhile, may fear that major concessions would undermine the ideological foundations of the Islamic Republic and alienate its core supporters.

The biggest question concerns the armed forces, particularly the Revolutionary Guards. Iran's missile programme, regional alliances and strategy in the Strait of Hormuz are central to the Revolutionary Guards' influence, yet it remains unclear how much weight commanders carry in decisions over escalation and negotiations.

The three options facing Tehran do not impose the same costs on different parts of the system. Pragmatists may favour a deal, hardliners may prefer endurance, while some military commanders could see escalation as strengthening Iran's bargaining position.

The question, therefore, is not only which path Iran chooses, but who has the authority to make that choice.

The leadership's idea of endurance looks very different to those required to endure it.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June to halt military operations and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days. But three weeks after it was signed, US President Donald Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in Hormuz, and US strikes in response.

One woman in Iran told BBC Persian that she was "very, very saddened" when the fighting resumed.

She had hoped the MoU would give the two sides time to resolve the remaining disputes and restore stability. Instead, she fears the destruction of infrastructure and the deaths of civilians and military personnel.

She blamed hardliners inside the Iranian system for imposing destructive policies, while also condemning opposition figures abroad who, in her view, had encouraged war.

Another woman in Tehran said the foreign-trade company where she worked had closed, leaving her unemployed for four months despite holding a doctorate and having 17 years of experience.

"No-one is hiring because nobody knows what will happen," she said. She described soaring prices, power and water cuts, increased theft, and occasional gunfire at night. She now limits how often she travels around the city.

These accounts do not point to a single political conclusion. Foreign attacks can produce anger against the United States and Israel even among opponents of the Islamic Republic. But they also illustrate the limits of asking the public to endure indefinite hardship in the name of resistance.

Trump faces difficult choices of his own: widen the war, continue military and economic pressure, or accept a settlement allowing Iran a restricted civilian nuclear programme under stronger supervision. None offers a clear path to victory.

The confrontation could continue for months through cycles of attacks, mediation and temporary ceasefires. The decisive question is how long Iran's leaders can preserve Hormuz as leverage without provoking an all-out war, renewed unrest or the construction of alternative routes that make the strait matter less.

VAT to be cut from household electricity bills in October

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 14:25:22 GMT

VAT will be cut from household electricity bills, the government has announced, as part of new Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge to help with the cost of living.

The reduction from 5% VAT to zero will come into effect on 1 October, saving a typical household about £45 a year.

Ministers said it would be funded by savings from the cancellation of the digital ID programme, which was going to cost £1.8bn over the next three years. The government estimated it will cost £850m this financial year.

But Labour's Darren Jones, who was sacked as chief secretary to the prime minister on Monday, accused the government of announcing an unfunded tax cut.

Jonathan Reynolds, the new business secretary, said the cut would give people some "breathing space".

He said it was funded until "the end of the financial year" in March 2027 and any changes beyond that would have to be announced in the next Budget.

Suppliers have been told the VAT reduction should be passed on to all household customers, including those on fixed tariffs, as was the case when some charges were taken off bills in April.

The cut will take effect in England, Scotland and Wales, but equivalent funding would be given to Northern Ireland, which is regulated differently, the government said.

The reduction could not be automatically be applied in Northern Ireland due to EU rules limiting the range of goods which can be sold without VAT. Following Brexit, England, Scotland and Wales are not bound by these restrictions.

Small businesses who qualify for the domestic energy VAT relief and are not registered for VAT, as well as charities and residential care homes eligible for the reduced rate, will also benefit.

Cutting VAT is a relatively basic tool to reduce an energy bill - with larger households likely to save more as they use more electricity.

However, some vulnerable households are also high electricity users, such as for running medical equipment.

Jones, who was also previously chief secretary to the Treasury, wrote on X that the Digital ID programme was unfunded.

While praising the VAT cut as "good", he said "the government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget".

Conservative Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride also criticised the use of the Digital ID budget to fund the VAT cut.

"The cuts to the Digital ID card budget are not real because the money was never provided in the first place.

"We are only one day in and already it is smoke and mirrors on the public finances."

Reynolds told the BBC's Today programme a VAT cut to electricity bills would be funded through a "straightforward switch spend" redirecting money for digital ID.

He said money for digital ID "would have had to have been found" and that scrapping the scheme removed "pressure" from the budget allowing the government to "give real help to people".

But the Office for Budget Responsibility said last November that digital ID would have to paid for out of savings from government departments and these had not yet been identified.

The spending watchdog said bringing in Digital ID had "provisionally forecast to cost £1.8bn in total over the next three years".

Government sources have insisted that departments have been working to find savings to fund Digital ID since the OBR made its forecast in November and this money would now be reallocated to fund the VAT cut.

Household energy prices rose by 13% for millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales at the start of July, under regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Price rises were driven by the higher cost of gas, but have a relatively limited impact owing to warm weather and lower energy use during the summer months.

However, higher energy prices caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has constrained global supplies of oil and liquified natural gas, are likely to persist into the winter, according to analysts.

The VAT cut only applies to the current financial year — any decision to keep it in future years would have to be made in a Budget.

The government expects it will lower inflation by 0.1 percentage points.

In his first speech as the UK's prime minister, Burnham vowed to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living.

On Tuesday, he said the VAT cut would "put more money in people's pockets".

The VAT cut is the second intervention on energy bills by the government in six months.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves removed one levy and shifted others onto general taxation to lower bills in April.

Speaking to the BBC, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "I think we'll have a summer of these little headline grabbing small announcements.

"What we need is the big picture so people know they are getting real help with the cost of living."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the VAT cut was "something that is only allowed because of Brexit".

But he said it would not "address the real issue of the cost of living" and of running a home, because "most houses are heated by oil or gas" and bills were being inflated by green levies.

The End Fuel Poverty Coalition welcomed the reduction, but said it "does not address the scale of what households are facing".

Simon Francis, the group's co-ordinator, said Burnham's government must "go even further" with targeted support for those most in need.

He added: "This breathing space is also not a cure. The only way to bring bills down for good is to change how they are set."

Parts of the UK move closer to drought

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:46:05 GMT

Dry, cracked earth is already evident in some parts of the UK, such as here in Cambridgeshire

Parts of southern, central and eastern England are now close to drought, according to the National Drought Group, external.

As of Monday, East Anglia, the West Midlands, Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Hertfordshire and London, Wessex, Thames, Solent and the South Downs, are in "prolonged dry weather", the stage before drought.

The group, which brings together the Met Office, the National Farmers' Union, water companies and other expert bodies, made the announcement on Tuesday.

It comes as a further 10.1 million people are to be impacted by a hosepipe ban, as Thames Water announces a hosepipe ban for all its customers from Thursday.

The latest announcement means that more than 20 million people will be living under hosepipe bans by the end of this week. Agriculture and wildlife are also experiencing consequences.

Drought - simply defined as a lack of water - has no official threshold criteria, but the National Drought Group will assess conditions to decide if one should be declared.

This assessment will consider lack of rainfall, impacts on agriculture and wildlife, the likelihood of wildfires, and low reserves of water and river levels.

As well as a lack of rainfall, a contributory factor is high temperatures which evaporate water from soil. It can be influenced, too, by human activity such as deforestation, intensive farming and excessive consumption.

According to the Met Office, external, unlike most other extreme weather, drought tends to build up over time and can last from as little as a few weeks to several years.

There is pressure on public water supplies with demand increasing by up to 30% on the hottest days this July. Seven water companies have implemented or announced future hosepipe bans to reduce the strain on treatment works and storage during peak demand.

A hosepipe can use a thousand litres of water an hour, more than a family of four will use in a day.

Farmers have had to begin their harvests early and there have been warnings that cereal yields may be affected by the lack of rain.

Farmers and growers are "working around the clock to harvest crops which have come early, keep fruit and vegetables watered, and care for their livestock", according to Paul Tompkins, deputy president of the National Farmers' Union.

"Parts of the country, particularly in the east and south, have seen exceptionally low rainfall this spring and summer," he said, which could mean, "another difficult and expensive harvest after extreme weather impacts in both 2024 and 2025".

Farmers in many parts of the UK are having to adapt to protect livestock and crops

River flows have decreased in recent weeks in England according to the Environment Agency, external, with 87% of catchments now at "below normal to exceptionally low levels".

The Rivers Avon in Hampshire, Cam, Derwent in Yorkshire, Swale, Tone, Wye and Yare are exceptionally low.

National reservoir storage is 5% lower than the long-term average. Groundwater levels are seeing a usual seasonal decline but there are notably low levels in the Cotswolds and Wessex Downs.

According to the National Drought Group, by 2055 England will need to find an additional 5 billion litres of water a day to meet demand for public water supply. Water companies are investing in ten new reservoirs and exploring desalination which involves treating seawater.

Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

In Wales, where just 5% of July rainfall has fallen, Natural Resources Wales has moved the worst affected regions in the north and south-east into "prolonged dry weather status", the first step in its drought plan.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

As the effects of human-induced climate change continue, the Met Office expects our summers to become hotter and drier, external in the future. In fact, by 2070, our summers could be up to 60% drier and 1-6C warmer compared to 1990.

The week ahead brings very little rainfall to most places away from north-west Scotland

High pressure stays in charge for the rest of this week, meaning no significant rainfall for at least the next five days. We could see a few midweek showers especially near coasts in south-east England and East Anglia, as well as northern Scotland.

Through the weekend, rain-bearing weather fronts will try to move in from the north-west, but most of this rain is likely to fall across parts of Northern Ireland and Scotland. As the fronts push south, they may fizzle out, meaning little or no rainfall for the places that need it most, in the south and east.

As for the rest of summer, it is too far off to know for sure, but there are hints that things could stay mainly dry and warm, especially in the south, although summer thunderstorms are possible.

Keep up to date with the latest forecast on the BBC Weather website or app.

Ferguson says Keegan built Newcastle's greatest team

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:21:54 GMT

Keegan and Ferguson were involved in managerial battles while in charge of Newcastle United and Manchester United respectively

Former Manchester United manager Sir Alex Ferguson said Kevin Keegan "carried the love of the game on his sleeve" as he paid a fond tribute to his former rival.

Keegan's death aged 75 was announced on Monday and Ferguson, recalling their managerial battles, praised the former Newcastle United manager for the impact he made with the Tyneside club.

"I had the utmost respect for him," Ferguson, whose team famously beat Newcastle to the Premier League title in 1995-96, told Track Radio.

"We had many duels when he was manager of Newcastle, but I have to say the job he did at Newcastle was fantastic."

Keegan's first stint as Magpies boss was between 1992 and 1997. He guided the club to promotion to the Premier League in 1992-93 before they went on to finish as runners-up to United three years later.

"He re-energised that club and he brought that enthusiasm and fanaticism that great supporters can give. That's the job he did," said Ferguson.

"And he also brought three great players to the club – [David] Ginola, [Faustino] Asprilla, Philippe Albert - and added a bit of class to the team, and I must say the challenges we had with Newcastle at that time at United were huge.

"Kevin carried the love of the game on his sleeve, there's no question about that, and that carried right on to the fans, to the players.

"That period at Newcastle was of emotion, it was excitement. They brought these great players to the club too and they added to it, and it gave Newcastle - I think - their best ever team."

Keegan famously said "I will love it if we beat them" in a TV outburst aimed at Ferguson as Newcastle gave up a 12-point lead when they were beaten to the title by United in 1996.

That reaction came after Ferguson questioned whether Leeds and Nottingham Forest would try as hard against Newcastle as they would against Manchester United.

Ferguson recalled that the pair bumped into each other at Wentworth Golf Club a few weeks after the end of the season and there was no animosity as they spent time together.

"The great thing about him, he held no grudges. That was a fantastic quality he had and we had a great night," said Ferguson.

"All aside whatever happened in previous weeks, that was soon forgotten. I really respected him for that."

This video can not be played

'I'm proud of it' - Kevin Keegan reflects on some of his career highlights

Gifted, charismatic and passionate amid highs and lows - Keegan obituary

Ferguson joined the floods of tributes being paid to former England captain and manager Keegan, who enjoyed a stellar playing career which involved spells at Scunthorpe United, Liverpool, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle.

He claimed three league titles, the European Cup, two Uefa Cups and the FA Cup during a six-year spell from 1971 to 1977 at Liverpool.

He helped Hamburg win the Bundesliga and earned back-to-back Ballons d'Or in 1978 and 1979. Keegan remains one of only four English players to have won the award to date.

As a manager, he was also in charge at Fulham and Manchester City in addition to England and Newcastle.

Keegan signed Alan Shearer for a world record £15m fee for Newcastle in 1996 and also took charge of England at a time when the striker was captaining his country.

"He was my friend. A man everyone loved. For his passion. For his energy but most of all for his friendship. He loved football and he loved Newcastle more than anything," said Shearer.

"I'm so honoured to have known him. We will miss you Kevin."

Newcastle United's current manager Eddie Howe got in touch with Keegan when he was appointed by the Magpies in 2021.

"Kevin was an inspiration to me as a young player and, I'm honoured to say, a friend whose guidance and support meant a great deal in recent years," said Howe.

"He showed me incredible warmth and generosity. He had already given so much to this football club, yet he immediately made me feel welcome.

"Kevin understood better than most the privilege and responsibility of leading Newcastle United. He was always willing to share his wisdom, offer encouragement and provide support, and I will always be grateful for that."

Former Scotland and Liverpool forward Sir Kenny Dalglish described Keegan as "one of the very best players of his generation" who "wore Liverpool's famous number seven shirt with great distinction".

"His achievements on the pitch were exceptional, but he was also a wonderful person and genuine gentleman," added Dalglish, who was signed from Celtic to replace Keegan at Liverpool in 1977, and later also succeeded him as manager of Newcastle.

"He gave so many people wonderful memories and his teams played the game in a way that supporters loved to watch.

"Football has lost one of its true greats."

This video can not be played

Keegan scores brace to inspire Liverpool to 1974 FA Cup final win

Phil Thompson described his former England and Liverpool team-mate as the "best of all the people I have known in football and in sport".

"He was a lovely man and that is above all his footballing exploits," said former defender Thompson. "Humility poured out of Kevin's veins."

He added: "When he came to Liverpool, he was a star waiting to happen. We got a superhero in 1971 and he was a revelation. He was inspirational."

Former Liverpool forward David Fairclough made his first-team debut for Liverpool in 1975 and said he "looked up" to Keegan and "started to do things the Kevin Keegan way".

"I remember going home after training, having been an apprentice, and telling my friends how close I had been to Kevin Keegan," Fairclough told BBC Radio Merseyside. "I would tell them about the fact he had even addressed me.

"As a young kid, it was so nice that he had noticed me. I remember my mates being gobsmacked about it because he was the top man at Liverpool at that time."

Keegan scored 21 goals in 63 games for England between 1972 and 1982, and went on to manage them from February 1999 until October 2000.

Fernandez defends Argentina as Messi questions remain

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:19:17 GMT

Enzo Fernandez played in seven of Argentina's eight 2026 World Cup matches

Midfielder Enzo Fernandez has claimed Argentina represented their nation "in the best possible way" during the World Cup, despite ugly scenes during and after their final loss to Spain.

Fernandez was sent off late in normal time for two yellow cards and Spain won 1-0 after extra time on Sunday in New Jersey.

His first booking was for showing dissent towards Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic and Fernandez was later dismissed for catching Pau Cubarsi with a challenge that sent the defender cartwheeling in the air.

But, in a statement on social media, the Chelsea midfielder did not mention the red card and said: "As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result.

"For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn't just about winning; it's about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up.

"It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment."

Keeper Martinez may 'step aside' from Argentina

Fifa opens investigation into Argentina post-final trouble

This video can not be played

Fight breaks out between Spain and Argentina players at full-time

Members of the Argentina team and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain players who had begun to celebrate their World Cup success.

Fifa's disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened and any player or coach involved could face suspension, while the Argentine Football Association may also be fined.

Nahuel Molina, Leandro Paredes, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala all appeared to be involved, with Paredes pushing Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat.

Spain's Gavi tried to intervene, but was forced to the ground by Almada, before Paredes pushed Gavi to the turf by putting his hand in the Spaniard's face.

Ayala then looked to be holding Garcia around the throat, before appearing to strike Spain midfielder Dani Olmo.

While the match ended with ugly scenes broadcast around the world, questions remain over what happened behind closed doors prior to kick-off.

There has been widespread speculation on social media about what was said in the Argentina dressing room before the game, including whether Lionel Messi informed his team-mates that the final would be his last match for the national side.

It comes after Argentine television company RLC Noticias posted footage appearing to show Messi urging his team-mates to stay calm on their walk to the tunnel - and "forget about everything else".

In the footage, which has not been verified by the BBC, Messi is seen saying: "Let's go, boys, [let's keep] calm people, calm. The main thing is for us to remain calm, boys, that we remain calm.

"Let's just concentrate on playing, nothing else - calm, OK? Forget everything else.

"Let's just play, let's just concentrate on playing. Let's go."

Enzo Fernandez was on a yellow card when he challenged Pau Cubarsi

The actions of the Argentina players on the pitch were heavily criticised by former England internationals.

Ex-England captain Alan Shearer said: "Paredes threw two or three haymakers into someone's face. He went for them. There is no place or space for that.

"We know how much it means to them and we know how much it hurts to lose, but there is a way to lose. Too many times we have seen that from Argentina. The reaction after the final whistle is terrible."

Former England goalkeeper Joe Hart added: "The game's done, they can have absolutely no complaints about what happened. Disgusting behaviour."

Argentina manager Lionel Scaloni attempted to calm the situation down in his post-match interview.

He said: "We are gracious in victory, and we must be gracious in defeat. Today, we are showing that we know how to lose.

"We lost the match, and we accept it, but that doesn't mean we stop living or forget everything we did to get here."

Argentina, the World Cup winners in 1978, 1986 and 2022, won their first seven matches in North America, beating Algeria, Austria, Jordan, Cape Verde, Egypt, Switzerland and England before losing to Spain.

Against Egypt, Argentina were 2-0 down before scoring three late goals to win and in the semi-final with England, the Three Lions led 1-0 until the 85th minute before goals from Fernandez and a Lautaro Martinez header gave them a 2-1 win.

Several media outlets in Argentina have suggested the final could be Scaloni's last in charge and called it the end of an era, with talisman Lionel Messi, in tears at the end, unlikely to play at another World Cup.

"The pain is immense, and this wound will take time to heal. But I also hold onto all the good things," Messi wrote on social media.

Argentina fans lined the streets to welcome the team home

However, the team were still greeted by thousands of Argentina fans with an open-top bus parade through the streets of Buenos Aires.

Scaloni and 16 of his 26 players returned to the country and were welcomed by a red carpet and military band at Ezeiza International Airport.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who made 11 saves during the final, was among the players in Argentina, but Messi was one of those who did not make the trip, instead returning to Miami where he plays club football for Inter Miami.

Ryanair broken window may have been caused by 'foreign object'

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:10:49 GMT

An incident on a Ryanair flight which saw a passenger partially sucked out of a plane window may have been caused by "foreign object damage" to an engine, said the airline's boss.

Michael O'Leary said an initial investigation into the incident on 10 July between Greece and Germany suggests "it looks like a foreign object damage to the engine on takeoff at Thessaloniki but ... we can't say that definitively".

He insisted that the engine on the 18-year-old Boeing 737 plane had been fully serviced and overhauled in the past two years.

Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the plane's window, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".

His wife Svetlana Grković Maksimović told BBC Serbia that she and two other passengers held on to his legs for several minutes.

She said: "We pulled him back together. His entire face was deformed and blood was pouring from his nose and mouth."

He was taken to hospital after the plane made an emergency landing.

Passengers told local media they heard "some kind of explosion" on board.

The aircraft was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.

Confirmation that the damage was caused by an external object could affect Ryanair or Boeing's liabilities over the incident.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. O'Leary said that a draft report would be issued in about 28 days.

Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for 10 million

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 12:45:44 GMT

Thames Water has announced a hosepipe ban affecting 10.1 million customers after an "exceptionally warm and dry spring".

The restrictions mean, from Thursday, hosepipes should not be used for watering gardens or allotments, cleaning cars, filling paddling pools or swimming pools, or cleaning windows.

The water company said its region had seen 40% of average rainfall, and more days at or above 34C this year than ever recorded before.

Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources, said: "We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment."

The ban applies to all customers that Thames Water supplies with drinking water and comes into effect on Thursday.

The company provides water to customers across parts of Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Surrey, the Thames Valley, Greater London, and the surrounding areas.

It provides water and wastewater services to 16 million customers overall.

It said water use was currently 10% above normal in the Thames Valley and Home Counties and 7% above normal in London, which amounted to an extra 100 million litres of water every day.

Muncaster added: "Recent heatwaves and a very dry spring and summer have led to sustained high demand.

"While there is enough water for essential use, we need to reduce non-essential outdoor demand to keep taps flowing."

He said teams were "working 24/7 to keep water moving, fix leaks and support customers" and that the situation would be kept "under close review", with restrictions lifted when safe to do so.

The company said this year's hot weather had meant during peak periods "water has been used faster than it can be treated and moved through parts of the network, placing additional pressure on local supplies".

"Customers should continue to use water for essential needs such as drinking, cooking, washing and hygiene," it said.

"Buckets and watering cans can still be used, and there are exemptions, including where water use is necessary for health and safety reasons or for customers with severe mobility problems."

Thames Water is about £20bn in debt.

The government recently rejected a rescue proposal, and the BBC understands the company's main lenders are preparing a legal challenge in case the new Andy Burnham-led government takes the firm into public hands.

Source: Thames Water

Elsewhere, South East Water has announced that a hosepipe ban currently in force in Kent will be extended to parts of Surrey, Sussex, Hampshire and Berkshire from Saturday.

Other companies with bans in force include Southern Water, which affects about one million customers across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, and South West Water, covering Mid Devon and other parts of the county, and Lyme Regis in Dorset.

A ban affecting 33,000 properties in west Wales was introduced last weekend by Welsh Water.

Cambridge Water, Anglian Water and Affinity Water, which all supply to much of the East of England, have implemented "temporary use bans".

The UK's summer has seen a number of records broken - including some which date back to the notorious summer of 1976 in which a drought was declared and a minister appointed to deal with water problems.

A lack of rain has also been a big part of this summer with some places in southern England seeing no measurable rain for more than four weeks.

Correction: The earlier figure in this story has been amended to 10 million because only Thames Water's water supply customers, and not waste water customers, are affected.

Owners of viral TikTok blue lagoon warn people to stay away

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 05:13:10 GMT

Owners of a "blue lagoon" that went viral on TikTok during the Covid pandemic have warned people not to enter the site, particularly during the current hot weather.

Brombil Reservoir in Margam in Neath Port Talbot attracted thousands of visitors, which caused traffic problems and littering.

To reach the 30m-deep (100ft) reservoir, visitors must walk up a steep 900m (2,953ft) public footpath.

Leisure Estate Investments Ltd, which bought the secluded site at auction for £20,000 in 2024, are now charging £2 a visit as "a temporary deterrent" and have installed barriers on its dam face.

It is concerned about people swimming, paddleboarding, littering and damaging structures around the site.

Although the reservoir can be accessed via public footpaths, the barriers were installed to stop people from walking on the dam face - but these have since been removed by trespassers.

The owners said the £2 levy was introduced in an effort to manage unauthorised visits and help fund clean-up operations, as part of its efforts to discourage public access because of "inherent safety risks".

A spokesperson for the company said: "We have strictly banned [people] from going there and walking on the face of the dam.

"Our long-term vision has always been to build a sustainable public-private framework so the community can safely enjoy this asset.

"However, managing a critical piece of infrastructure presents immense structural, environmental, and financial challenges that cannot be indefinitely sustained by a private entity alone."

The reservoir is a flooded 19th Century colliery that was repurposed to supply water to Port Talbot Docks, and is now famous for its striking turquoise colour.

It plays a vital role in flood protection, helping shield downstream residential areas, and has a "unique aquatic ecosystem" that has faced "severe environmental degradation caused by fly-tipping and littering", Brombil Reservoir Ltd said.

After the landmark went viral on a TikTok video with more than one million views, nearby residents claimed they had been "suffering" because of the traffic and litter problems.

To reach the 30m-deep (100ft) reservoir, visitors must walk up a steep 900m (2,953ft) public footpath, which is also the only way down.

In an effort to combat vandalism, including the destruction of iron security gates on deep-water chambers and persistent littering, the company introduced the £2 charge.

It said it was to "manage unauthorised access and fund clean-up operations. It is not a commercial ticket".

The company added its goal was to safely open the site for public use, saying it recognised the benefits of "blue spaces" for health and well-being.

Since taking ownership in 2024, Brombil Reservoir Ltd said it had invested in structural surveys, engineering assessments, landscaping and waste clearance.

It added that compliance requirements from Natural Resources Wales (NRW) for high-risk dams had increased significantly, requiring tens of thousands of pounds in ongoing safety investment.

Matthew O'Brien of NRW's reservoir safety group said the Reservoirs Act 1975, meant owners were responsible "for ensuring their reservoirs are properly maintained and managed".

He added that these rules were designed "to ensure that reservoirs are managed safely and help reduce the risk of flooding to people and property downstream".

Owners of regulated reservoirs pay an annual fee of £276 towards NRW's regulatory costs.

The company said it had repeatedly sought support from Neath Port Talbot council and local politicians to help fund and preserve the reservoir, but had received no response.

It added: "We genuinely want to work constructively with Neath Port Talbot council, NRW, and our political representatives to deliver a safe, biodiverse, and secure site."

Brombil Reservoir Ltd warned that without public sector support or a partnership agreement, it could be forced to "decommission the reservoir".

It added: "This would unfortunately eliminate the area's primary flood defence and destroy a vital ecological habitat.

"We sincerely hope local authorities will join us at the table to find a sustainable, shared way forward."

The council said it had"offered advice where appropriate" to the reservoir owners.

"As the site is privately owned, decisions regarding its operation and investment are a matter for the owner," it added.

"Any future arrangements should ensure that visitor activity is managed responsibly and does not place undue pressure on local communities.

"We remain open to constructive dialogue with the owner."

Your tips on getting a fussy child to eat, and six recipes they'll love

BBC News Tue, 21 Jul 2026 00:16:08 GMT

It's the start of the summer holidays and you've already had five battles with your child to get them to eat a bit of broccoli.

For many parents, these few weeks can be a stressful time of the year at the dinner table. So how should we deal with our picky eaters?

The BBC asked you for your tips on making mealtimes a more enjoyable experience.

Mum-of-four Natalia, from south-west London, makes veggie nuggets for her children.

"They like green beans but not by themselves, so we just fry them in a little bit of butter and dip in breadcrumbs. The same with cauliflower and lots of other vegetables," she says.

Teacher Kieron Fisher, who lives in Newbury, Berkshire, includes vegetables in meals his six-year-old twins Kit and Ollie already enjoy, such as curries and spaghetti Bolognese.

"It helps increase their vegetable intake without causing a battle."

Emma Robins, from Reading, says broccoli hidden in pesto pasta is a favourite for her three-year-old son Alfred, as well as veg pulsed into pasta sauces. She also recommends making your own burgers with vegetables.

A lack of routine in the holidays can be particularly challenging for some children, so Kieron suggests using visual boards showing the healthy snack they are about to have and another showing the activity they are going to do next.

Children with special educational needs can sometimes experience sensory difficulties when it comes to food - and are not classified as fussy eaters. Some of these suggestions may not be suitable for them.

"If they're hungry, they'll eat. I don't force them to because I think that can instil pressure," says Doone, from London.

She says her daughter Cora, two, used to be the "best eater" but seeing others at nursery turn their noses up at certain foods made her do the same.

"I'm trying not to make a big deal of it. Even though they don't eat it, I always put the broccoli on the plate so that they're seeing it."

Emma suggests giving lots of options, so that kids think they are getting to choose. In Alfred's lunchbox, she always adds two or three healthy options.

And she says to praise them when they take an interest. "If they say one day they want carrots, run and get the carrots and give big praise when they eat them," Emma says.

It may take up to 15 attempts before kids learn to like new foods, research suggests.

"Keep going," says one mum outside Barnes Primary School, in south-west London. "Keep offering it and they will pick it up and try it. We try to make everyone try everything in our house, even the tiniest bit."

Sometimes it can be the colour or texture of a certain food that puts them off, another parent says, until they actually try it.

Children refusing to eat new foods or rejecting ones they've always liked is not unusual. More than half will show fussy eating habits at some point, the NHS says.

Vegetables, in particular, can taste quite bitter to young palates. Most habits will improve over time.

But if your kids start to avoid certain foods and limit how much they eat in an unhealthy way, it's worth seeking medical advice.

"I always eat with my girls and I eat what they're eating," says Doone, who has two "quite fussy eaters".

The British Nutrition Foundation agrees that food should be a family affair - allowing children to learn from what their parents do. When a bit older, they can help with preparation too.

Emma adds to the fun by taking her kids fruit picking and also by letting them choose at the supermarket, then having tasty picnics in the garden.

But first thing's first, says Kieron: think about the portion size.

"I make sure their plates aren't too full or overcrowded, as too much food at once can feel overwhelming," he says.

Doone says: "I am making a conscious effort not to give many snacks because then they're more hungry at dinner time."

Natalia leaves out healthy finger food, like chopped peppers and apples, for her children to pick at.

Don't completely ban them, says Kieron - just serve snacks alongside healthier options, like berries or other fruit, replicate snack times at school and don't stress about the odd treat.

"Six weeks [of summer holidays] is a long time, so it's about focusing on the overall balance of their diet rather than aiming for perfection every day," he says.

'I made £100,000 of TikTok sales in one day': The business of live shopping

BBC News Mon, 20 Jul 2026 23:06:04 GMT

Daisy Kelly's business was inspired by a personal problem - for years she'd been pulling out her eyelashes.

She hid her habit with lash extensions, but when beauty salons closed during Covid Daisy decided to create a serum to help her eyelashes grow back.

She started Glow For It from her mother's kitchen table in 2020 while she was a student and now her business generates £6m a year in sales.

More than 40% of Daisy's sales come from TikTok Shop UK and increasingly from livestreams.

"I think live shopping gives people that connection and interaction that we're all craving... We actually generated over £100,000 revenue in one 12 hour TikTok live," says Daisy, 27.

"It's categorically changed the trajectory of my business."

Daisy's business goes live from a studio for a minimum of six hours a day with different presenters interacting with shoppers, from showing off products to answering their questions.

"It's like having 500 people in your shop," she says.

There are a host of platforms and marketplaces now offering livestreams connecting sellers and customers, from Instagram Live, YouTube Shopping, to eBay and Amazon Live. They're all different.

Live shopping, it seems, is becoming part of everyday consumer behaviour for many.

According to new research from retail agency Savvy Marketing, 30% of shoppers surveyed said they'd bought something from a live shopping event.

"The big retailers have got to grab hold of this," says Catherine Shuttleworth, CEO of Savvy. "It's grown from nothing to a huge thing really quickly. If you haven't got a strategy for live selling, you're going to miss out."

TikTok Shop says its UK sales grew by more than 30% year-on-year in June, with live shopping the fastest-growing format.

It says it now has more than 6,000 livestreams taking place every day.

At an event in the centuries old Covent Garden market, it hosted 20 small businesses with stalls who were also selling live to customers all over the UK.

With nothing more than a smartphone, a lighting kit and a fridge full of fresh meat, halal butcher Manny Malik from Wolverhampton had around two hundred people tuning into his session.

"Last week we did a TikTok live for three hours and we sold £8,000 worth of meat," he says.

It would normally take him three to four days to sell this amount in his family shop, Malik Butchers.

They're now opening a second store in Stoke. TikTok, he says, is helping to drive his expansion.

But there are fees.

TikTok Shop UK keeps up to 9p from every £1 sold on the platform, as its standard commission.

As a comparison, eBay's marketplace business sellers typically pay between 6.9p and 14.9p depending on the category. Businesses selling on the dedicated live selling format, eBay Live, pay a combined fee of up to 8.42p including payment processing.

"It's a lot," says Manny.

"For us in the meat game, there aren't huge margins. However, it's opened up a new platform. We didn't have these sales prior to TikTok. We're not losing money, we've got enough profitability in there," he adds.

Buket Sevik, 34, founded her jewellery brand Adorina in February after quitting her 9-5 job as a business manager. Her new business went from 50 orders a month to 500 orders a week since she started live selling on TikTok UK shop in May.

She's gone from working from her dining table to live streaming from a small unit, where orders are now being packed.

"It's crazy," she laughs.

Demand is so high, she's trying to hire someone to help.

But for Buket, the best thing about livestreaming is the flexibility.

"I can go live whenever I want... which means it works absolutely perfectly for me as a mum. I can put my daughter to sleep and I can just hit go live and do some sales."

Savvy's latest survey of shoppers also found that 66% of Gen Y and Gen Z shoppers said seeing products sell out or go viral made them more likely to buy.

That's something that worries the free debt advice service, Money Wellness, which warns live shopping events are "a recipe for overspending", says external relations manager Rebecca Lamb.

"Every time you snap up a bargain before it sells out, your brain gets a dopamine hit - the same rush you get from gambling," she says.

"And because a lot offer one tap payment, there's no card, no basket and no total. Often you've spent money before your brain has caught up," she says.

The ancient Silk Road city that has a lesson for Silicon Valley

New Scientist July 21, 2026

I stood on the outskirts of ancient Samarkand in Uzbekistan, trying to figure out a path to the citadel. Back in the 7th century AD, this was one of the greatest trade cities on what is now known as the Silk Road, a grand network of trade routes connecting Asia to Europe. I would have entered through an opulent gate, flanked by guards and surrounded by a thronging mass of visitors and traders from all across Asia. The air would have rung with voices and smelled like smoke and spices. But when I visited, it was quiet.

Hunter-gatherers introduced fish to a mountain lake 7000 years ago

From my vantage point at the top of a hill, I could see a landscape of ridges and valleys covered in a thick layer of bright green grass and studded with rocky outcrops. Kids played soccer in a dell nearby, and a small herd of brown sheep wandered downslope as it began to drizzle. The place looked like an oddly lumpy park surrounded by the bustling, modern city of Samarkand. At last, I spotted a faint trail leading to the distant outline of a flat-topped mound – the citadel – that once held the city’s palace complex. I was there to research my next book, and found myself thinking about why cities of nomads were hotbeds of technological innovation. What could Silicon Valley learn from Samarkand?

Historian Valerie Hansen at Yale University, author of The Silk Road: A new history, explains that people who traveled the Silk Road over a millennium ago called it “the road to Samarkand”. At that time, the ridges where sheep wandered would have been ramparts, the dells would have been mansions and temples, and the Siab river would have rushed through the centre of the city, flanked by homes and shops. Outside its walls, a vast roadside inn known as a caravanserai would have catered to merchants who traveled here from China, India, Afghanistan, Iran and beyond.

Advertisement

What was truly revolutionary about this city was its culture. For a few centuries, Samarkand was ruled by the Sogdians, a diasporic people who hailed originally from what is now Iran. As they settled in cities across Central Asia, they took on traditions borrowed from China and the West. In a Sogdian city, you might see a Zoroastrian temple next to a Buddhist one, and scientific manuscripts and technology from the Arab world were traded in the same marketplaces where you might find Chinese silks and Turkish spices.

I passed by a deep depression in the ground surrounded by eroded walls. This unremarkable spot was where archaeologists in the 1960s had uncovered a merchant’s parlor where guests partied and made deals. Its walls were covered in opulent frescoes (now on display at a nearby museum), one of which dramatises a meeting between Samarkand’s king and delegations from China, Korea, Turkey, India and more, each bearing gifts from their homelands. Envoys in their culture’s regalia offer silkworms in their cocoons, painted elephants, exotic birds, carved masks, sumptuous necklaces, fine horses and well-crafted weapons. The Sogdians were a diverse society for both practical and aesthetic reasons. Their ethos might have been “the more the merrier”. And the richer, of course.

Though we have these artistic representations, little remains of the Sogdian palace on the citadel mound. It was obliterated over the centuries by multiple regimes who occupied it after the Sogdians fled the Abbasid Caliphate in the 8th century. As I approached its stippled slope, however, it was easy to find bits of masonry and pottery that had been dislodged by rain and erosion and scattered across the grass. There have been only a few modern archaeological excavations in ancient Samarkand, and the place has many secrets left to reveal.

Still, this city of traders has left us with one, clear lesson about how trade enriched people’s lives along the Silk Road. The people of Samarkand certainly welcomed the flood of trade goods that came through their gates, including novel weapons, chemicals and medicines. But historian Jenny Rose, author of Zoroastrianism: An introduction, points out to me that Sogdian cities grew rich because they opened their walls and homes to new people. The greatest asset to Samarkand wouldn’t have been a collection of swords, but instead a trained sword-maker from abroad. One could say the same about jewelers, paper-makers, horse trainers, philosophers and artists.

Free newsletter

Wealth on the Silk Road came from people and their knowledge. The Sogdians became famous for their finely trained artisans, who came to town not only to sell objects, but to set up shops where they made fine knives, gorgeous ceramics and accurate maps, training the next generation in the process. They shared expertise and that made the whole world more prosperous.

As companies replace humans with automation, it is easy to forget that technology advances with humanity, rather than the other way around. But humans have always been more valuable than things. As we come into contact with new groups and ideas, we make incredible discoveries. We build on each other’s wisdom and innovate together. Put somewhat more whimsically, the Silk Road wasn’t ever just about silk. It was about the people we met along the way.

How to unlock unlimited geothermal energy, anywhere we want

New Scientist July 21, 2026

Deep under your feet, Earth is hot. Really hot. Some of that heat is left over from the planet’s violent formation. More is continually created by the splitting of radioactive atoms in the rocks below. In a few places, Earth’s hidden furnace dramatically makes itself known, bursting through the crust as volcanoes, geysers and rivers of magma.

Spectacular stuff, but also extremely useful – if we can get at it. Conventional geothermal power works best wherever geology has done the hard work for us: where fault lines crack the crust and hot water or steam rises close to the surface. That’s why countries like Iceland, New Zealand, Kenya and Indonesia can turn Earth’s heat into warmth for homes and electricity for grids, while much of the rest of the world has barely touched it.

Its appeal is obvious. Unlike solar power, geothermal doesn’t fade when the sun sets, and unlike wind power, it doesn’t stall when the air is still.

Advertisement

World’s first tunnel to a magma chamber could unleash unlimited energy

Over the past decade, advances in drilling have begun to loosen geothermal power from its geological shackles. Some projects aim to improve on nature, creating cracks and pathways where none existed. Others are more ambitious still: they want to drill so deep that geothermal power could work almost anywhere. “Ultimately, the whole world is the goal,” says Matt Houde, co-founder of geothermal energy company Quaise Energy. That would turn it from a niche resource into something far bigger – a way to tap the planet’s hidden heat wherever we happen to need it.

To convert heat from Earth’s interior into usable energy, engineers pump cold water into naturally occurring reservoirs in hot rock. There, it warms up and returns to the surface as hot water or steam, which can be used to drive turbines and generate electricity. The water is then sent back underground to begin the cycle again.

It’s a simple concept, and unlike fossil fuels, geothermal heat sources are practically inexhaustible on human timescales. “If you measure in terms of the energy stored within the Earth’s crust, geothermal heat exceeds by orders of magnitude all hydrocarbons,” says Houde. The trouble is that traditional geothermal requires three ingredients to work: heat, water and rock that is permeable or fractured enough for water to move through it. “Traditional geothermal systems are very constrained to countries and regions within countries where you have this unique combination of conditions,” he says.

Free newsletter

That is why geothermal has flourished in places like Iceland. Sitting astride the mid-Atlantic ridge, the country has those core ingredients in unusual abundance. The global oil crisis in the 1970s pushed Iceland to exploit that advantage, and geothermal now makes up over a quarter of the country’s electricity supply. That may not sound like much, but Iceland’s geothermal plants can keep generating whatever the weather, making them a steady backbone for the grid. “Geothermal is really well placed to be the glue that will make low-carbon electricity systems work,” says Iain Staffell, a sustainable energy expert at Imperial College London.

However, most countries don’t share Iceland’s good fortune. They may have heat or water or fractured rock, but not all three at depths that are easy to reach. Traditional geothermal plants are limited to mining heat from less than 2 kilometres underground. Go much deeper, and the engineering becomes brutal. Drills must chew through hard, hot rock. The vertical shafts that connect the surface to heat reservoirs, known as wells, must survive punishing temperatures and pressures. Even after all that, the rock may still be too tight and unbroken for water to flow through it.

Still, the prize is enormous. The International Energy Agency estimates that geothermal’s technical potential is around 150 times current global electricity demand, assuming we can exploit heat down to about 8 kilometres. Conventional geothermal typically taps pre-existing reservoirs of hot water or steam in permeable, fractured rock less than 2 kilometres underground, leaving much of that potential out of reach. The implication is clear: to expand the resource, engineers must drill deeper – and create the underground plumbing that nature hasn’t provided.

The first of the new geothermal techniques does exactly that. Enhanced geothermal systems target hot but impermeable rock, typically 2 to 10 kilometres underground. Engineers pump in hot water at high pressures to open or widen fractures and create pathways for fluid to circulate. This is known as an enhanced geothermal system (EGS), and it is the most mature technology in geothermal’s new era.

But this approach has a downside. Forcing water into deep rock doesn’t just create useful cracks. According to a 2023 review of the research, it can also disturb older, pre-existing faults that are already under strain. Many faults are held still by friction, like a heavy book resting on a tilted table. Pump water into them, and the pressure in their pores and fractures rises. That partly props the two sides of the fault apart, reducing the force clamping them together. If the fault was already close to slipping, that can be enough to induce an earthquake.

An investigation commissioned by the South Korean government concluded that a nearby EGS project triggered a magnitude-5.5 earthquake in the city of Pohang in 2017. More than 80 people were injured and the earthquake caused an estimated 300 billion Korean won (£148 million) of damage, making it the most destructive in the country’s history.

Scientists are scrambling to understand how climate change may be interfering with the winds that carry our weather, with potentially catastrophic consequences

Bill Ellsworth at Stanford University in California was part of the team that helped establish what role the geothermal plant played in the disaster. “In Pohang, they drilled a couple of wells that were a long way apart,” he says. The hope was that pumping water into one would fracture the rock enough to connect with the other, creating a route for water to pass between them and gather heat. But trying to force that kind of connection through the subsurface is risky, particularly if the drilling intersects faults that are already primed to slip.

That is why newer projects are trying to be more deliberate, says Ellsworth. In Iceland, for instance, engineers try to create EGS reservoirs more gently without blasting them open all at once by pumping cold water slowly and at relatively low pressure. Over months, the cooling rock contracts and cracks, says Lilja Magnúsdóttir, executive vice president of resources at Icelandic energy company HS Orka.

Iceland also has an advantage born of necessity: it is a seismically restless place, so the country has already invested heavily in monitoring. At HS Orka, that now includes using geothermal wells themselves as early-warning sensors. When magma begins to move, it compresses the surrounding rock, creating a telltale signal in the well. “It’s a really cool design,” says Magnúsdóttir.

But even where EGS projects have learned to manage seismic risk, hard rock still makes an unreliable basis for a plumbing system. Fluid can leak away and contaminate groundwater, for instance. And the same fractures that make the system useful can also make it dangerous.

One way around this is to stop asking the rock to carry water at all. Where natural fractures and reservoirs don’t exist, an alternative to EGS is to drill a sealed loop through hot rock. Engineers drill down, then sideways, until the boreholes connect underground, before lining and sealing them with steel and cement. That creates something like a buried radiator where fluid circulates, but never comes into direct contact with the rock itself.

This closed-loop system is known as an advanced geothermal system (AGS), and it has been tested successfully in Germany, where Canadian energy company Eavor has developed a geothermal power plant at Geretsried, which began construction in 2022 and started producing electricity last year.

Because closed-loop systems don’t force fractures open in the rock, they should reduce the risk of induced earthquakes. And because they don’t depend on continually pumping water into and out of those fractures, they should reduce it further still.

There is another possible advantage. If the working fluid stays inside a sealed pipe, it doesn’t have to be water. Companies can, in principle, use fluids that pick up and release heat more efficiently. Eavor’s working fluid is a company secret. The firm China Huaneng Group, meanwhile, has built the first geothermal demonstration plant that uses supercritical carbon dioxide – CO2 that is compressed and heated until it becomes not quite a gas and not quite a liquid. In that state, it is dense and flows easily, and is very good at moving heat. The firm’s test facility began operating in May this year in Zhengzhou, China.

But these systems have their own difficulties. Eavor has had to scale back the number of wells it planned to drill after rock debris clogged parts of the pipe network. Its plant works, but not yet as efficiently as hoped. That points to a broader question: can closed-loop systems circulate enough fluid, and draw heat from the rock fast enough, to be commercially useful? “The jury is still out,” says Ellsworth. “Time will tell whether these ideas of having just a single closed loop will be actually successful.”

And while AGS could be safer and cleaner than inducing fractures deep underground, it is still limited to places where hot rock lies within reach, usually a few kilometres down. To make geothermal truly global, companies will have to drill much, much deeper.

The deeper you go, the hotter Earth gets. Go deep enough and water crosses a strange threshold. At about 374°C (705°F), under sufficient pressure, it transforms into a supercritical fluid – akin to the CO2 in the China Huaneng demonstration plant – and can carry far more heat than ordinary hot water or steam.

“There are a few countries where geothermal does provide a sizable mix of the energy supply. But strictly the heat itself, which is fundamentally what geothermal energy is, is actually available anywhere if you go deep enough,” says Houde.

Supercritical temperatures are usually found at depths of at least 5 to 20 km, and often deeper. The rocks become harder the further you go: basalt or granite rather than the softer sedimentary layers often found closer to the surface. This rock chews through even the hardest tungsten carbide or diamond drill bits. Then there’s the time spent not drilling at all but instead replacing worn-down drill bits or equipment that begins to fail at higher temperatures and greater depths. These delays quickly push up costs, says Houde.

Quaise, which is based in Houston, Texas, wants to get around this by drilling in a different way – without using a drill bit at all. Its plan is to use conventional drilling for the upper part of the well, then switch to high-powered microwave energy once the rock becomes too hard. The hole would be lined with corrugated steel, helping the microwaves travel downwards. When that energy hit the rock, it would heat it until the rock cracked, broke apart or even vaporised. “There’s no drill bit mechanically destroying the rock here, it’s just the interaction of the energy with the rock,” says Houde.

The rock would be reduced into a fine ash that is purged from the well with a nitrogen-rich gas and collected at the surface. Quaise isn’t alone in pursuing non-contact drilling: Slovakia-based GA Drilling is also trialling laser- and plasma-based systems, and carried out its first field tests in 2023.

Once the hole is open, Quaise wants to create a deep, EGS-style reservoir. Water would be sent through fractures in superhot rock, picking up heat before returning to the surface to generate electricity. In principle, it is geothermal freed from geography.

Quaise’s test holes are still just a couple of kilometres deep, but the company sees them as a proof of concept for something much larger. Its first planned superhot geothermal plant, located in Oregon, is intended to come online by 2030, accessing temperatures up to 400°C (752°F) at a depth of 3 to 5 km. A potential future site would push deeper, potentially to 10 km. “By 2035, we want the first superhot well producing energy at a depth greater than 10 kilometres,” says Houde, who thinks his company’s technology could transform any region into geothermal country.

But there are still serious uncertainties. One is whether such deep wells can be kept open under the immense pressures found kilometres below ground. “It’s unclear whether that is possible,” warns Ellsworth. Houde accepts that the hardest engineering lies ahead. “I think it’s very viable for getting to these initial depths to prove superhot geothermal,” he says. “I think it’ll become increasingly more challenging to push the frontier on how deep we can go.”

Iceland offers a glimpse of how these different strands of geothermal might converge. Instead of simply resting on its laurels as one of the world’s great geothermal success stories, the country is fast becoming a test bed for what comes next, says Magnúsdóttir.

Is the COP30 climate summit already in crisis, with six months to go?

Its deepest geothermal well – the second well by the Iceland Deep Drilling Project, a consortium of the country’s leading energy companies and its energy authority – has already brushed against the promise of superhot geothermal. It was completed in 2017 and goes down 4.7 kilometres. “It is the first well in the world where supercritical conditions were confirmed in the geothermal well,” says Magnúsdóttir. Icelandic operators are also using EGS techniques to get more from existing fields, stimulating deeper faults to reach another kilometre or so of heat.

Next year, the Iceland Deep Drilling Project plans to drill its third well. “There, they just have to go down to a little over 2 kilometres to reach supercritical conditions,” says Magnúsdóttir. But even at that relatively shallow depth, the engineering challenges remain fierce. The main problem is well integrity. At such high temperatures, the steel casings that line the well can expand, deform and fail. In Iceland, engineers have been testing fixes, including flexible connectors between sections of casing.

This sort of engineering will be crucial if geothermal is to win over investors. Projects are expensive up front and slow to prove, and often need permits before developers know whether a site will work commercially. But the reward for patience can be unusually durable. “It’s very, very costly,” says Sanjeev Kumar at the European Geothermal Energy Council. “But once you’ve drilled that hole in the ground, that lasts for over 100 years.”

That is the promise and the problem in miniature. “We know that very deep geothermal energy would be fabulous if we could reach it,” says Ellsworth. “We just don’t yet know if it’s possible.”

Effort to solve biggest controversy in mathematics has made no progress

New Scientist July 21, 2026

An attempt to bring unequivocal clarity to one of the most controversial areas of mathematics has so far come to nothing. Mathematicians have been working on using a computer to check an apparent proof of the ABC conjecture, but an interim report says there are still serious barriers to overcome.

In 2012, Shinichi Mochizuki at Kyoto University in Japan surprised the world with his 500-page proof of the ABC conjecture, a deceptively simple conjecture about the equation a + b = c and how the numbers involved can be split up into smaller prime numbers. Mathematicians had struggled to find a proof for decades before Mochizuki came along.

The problem was, few could actually understand and therefore verify his proof, which hinges on an entirely new field of mathematics that Mochizuki created called Inter-universal Teichmüller (IUT) theory. As a result, there is a small group of people who vehemently believe the proof is sound, but others remain unconvinced.

Advertisement

Mathematicians put AI to work on Fermat’s last theorem

However, one thing that both sides agree on is that computer formalisation could solve the issue. This involves using software – in this case a programming language called Lean – to represent mathematical arguments in code. A computer can then check if the entire proof is correct.

Two projects sprung up to do this: one run by Mochizuki himself, and one run by ZEN Mathematics Center in Japan called the Lean and Anabelian geometry (LANA) project.

LANA has now published an interim report on its work that, far from setting out a formalised proof of what Mochizuki has been trying to explain to the world for over a decade, seems to have become bogged down in the problem.

LANA members have had “lively discussions”, according to the report, but have yet to land on a conclusive decision on whether IUT theories stand up or not. “The members were unable to reach complete consensus on this point,” reads the paper.

They reference a problem they call “the wall”, which relates to a flaw in IUT described in 2018 by two prominent mathematicians – Peter Scholze at the University of Bonn and Jakob Stix at Goethe University Frankfurt in Germany. The report sets out how the problem the pair raised still haunts IUT theory and has rendered it – so far – impervious to formalisation.

New Scientist contacted the five core members of the LANA project, as listed in the report, for comment, but has not yet received a response.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Abhishek Saha at Queen Mary University of London says that the majority of mathematicians see IUT as a flawed theory and the report backs that up. “Most people believe that there is a serious gap,” says Saha. “And I think that this particular report is fully consistent with that: it has not managed to formalise it, which is what we would expect if this big theory had some serious gaps.”

A large amount of maths has already been built on top of IUT theory, which would be in jeopardy if it is proved incorrect, but that indeed most mathematicians believe it will be, says Chris Bowman-Scargill at the University of York, UK.

But IUT theory still has its cheerleaders who believe a formalised proof will emerge in time.

“People followed [Scholze’s] opinion, accepting that it should be the utmost truth,” says Ivan Fesenko at Westlake University in China. “[But] his take on IUT is totally wrong.”
