Tick bites are on the rise in the US and UK. Here’s how to protect yourself

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 16:00:50 GMT

Experts share tips to avoid the blood-sucking pests that can transmit Lyme disease and other illnesses on to humans

I won’t go into gory detail about the tick I found latched behind my ear approximately 35 hours after a hike in early June. Suffice it to say, the parasite was well fed, and I was horrified.

I am far from alone in making such a disgusting discovery. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), emergency room visits for tick bites have been unusually high in the US this year. Thirty-one million Americans are bitten by ticks annually – and the number has been trending up for over a decade. In the UK, ticks appear to be rising in number and species variety.

“Tick populations are expanding geographically because we’re changing the climate,” explains Vett Lloyd, a professor of biology at Mount Allison University in New Brunswick who studies ticks and the pathogens they transmit.

Milder winters and warmer summers raise ticks’ survival rates. Additionally, human expansion – especially “mowing down forests and living in suburbs on previously forested land” – has expanded tick habitat dramatically, explains Lloyd.

Experts say that suburbs mean more prime habitat for mice, who thrive eating our garbage and harbor dangerous pathogens in their blood, like Lyme disease. More mice support more ticks, who feast on rodents as well as booming deer populations, lizards, birds and other creatures. Ticks can transmit diseases they pick up to human hosts. US rates of Lyme disease were 69% higher in 2022 compared with the 2017-2019 annual average. In England, cases of Lyme rose over 20% between 2024 and 2025.

“The pathogens are expanding almost exclusively because of human changes in how we live in the environment,” says Lloyd.

Here’s what you need to know to protect yourself from ticks.

“Ticks have a relatively boring life,” says Lloyd. They hang out in moist, dark and shaded areas like leaf litter. When hungry, they crawl up blades of grass, where they wait to brush on to anything tasty that walks past, she says.

If a tick reaches your body, it typically climbs upward, seeking a dark, damp area, like the backs of knees, navel, groin, armpits or behind the ears, says Lloyd. There, they bite, injecting an anesthetic that prevents you from feeling pain or itchiness as they dig in.

The best time to find a tick is before it bites. “It can’t give you a disease if it hasn’t started drinking your blood,” says Lloyd. Showering immediately after spending time outdoors may wash a tick off before it has a chance to latch.

Perform a tick check after being outdoors. This can be done alone with a mirror, and by lightly running your hands all over your body. Unfed ticks will feel like bumps the size of a poppy seed or a sesame seed. A fed tick can swell to the size of a blueberry. If you’re comfortable with it, another person can help with the search.

The longer a tick feeds, the more likely it is to spread disease. Removing a tick before it’s been on you for 24 hours greatly reduces the risk of disease transmission, per the CDC.

“You want to try to get the whole tick out,” says Dr Charlotte Mao, a pediatric infectious disease physician who works with the Bay Area Lyme Foundation. Mao recommends using “fine tip tweezers with firm gentle pressure” to grasp the tick at its head and pull it up. “You want to try to not have the mouth parts break off and stay stuck in the skin.”

Wash the bite site and your hands thoroughly with soap and water or rubbing alcohol, she says.

Trying to remove it is better than leaving it in, even if you don’t get the tick out perfectly. “While the tick is on you, it can be transmitting pathogens,” notes Lloyd. “The mouth parts are organic; they will eventually dissolve, and the part of the tick that contains the pathogens is all in [its] body,” she says. If you accidentally “pop” the tick, wash your hands well and disinfect the bite site, as these fluids can spread disease.

Both Mao and Lloyd suggest saving the tick in a Ziploc bag in your freezer, noting the date and geographic location it was found, if possible.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“It’s not your ideal souvenir,” says Lloyd, but if you begin to exhibit flu-like symptoms, facial drooping, severe headaches or any other worrisome new health issues in the month after your bite, you can get it tested. The Bay Area Lyme Foundation’s website offers a list of laboratories that perform tick testing, some by mail. In the UK, you can mail your tick to the government’s Tick Surveillance Scheme to help researchers map tick habitat, or to international tick test labs.

Consult your primary care provider after a bite, Mao says. They may give you an antibiotic prophylaxis – typically a single dose of doxycycline – to protect against Lyme, as well as other diseases commonly caused by ticks, like anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis and Rocky Mountain spotted fever. However, there are some tick-borne illnesses that cannot be treated with antibiotics, says Lloyd. These include alpha-gal, an allergy to red meat and other animal products, and babesiosis, a parasitic infection that causes flu-like symptoms and jaundice. If you notice any strange symptoms in the weeks after your tick bite, talk to a doctor right away.

If you identify an expanding solid red or bullseye-shaped rash near the site of your bite, this may be a sign of early Lyme disease. Your doctor may give you a longer course of antibiotics: one to two weeks, depending on the advice of your regional health authority.

To reduce your risk of tick bites, the CDC recommends wearing Environmental Protection Agency-approved insect repellants such as Deet or picaridin, long-sleeved shirts, long pants and closed shoes, and tumble-drying clothing on high after returning home to kill any lingering ticks. Stick to the open middle of trails while hiking rather than getting too close to brush or leaf litter.

Ticks aren’t only a threat to hikers and hunters; depending on where you live, you can be bitten by a tick in your own back yard, notes Erika Machtinger, a medical and veterinary entomologist.

Machtinger recommends a few strategies for making your outdoor space safer.

Cutting back vegetation to prevent big shady areas and mowing your lawn frequently to reduce grassy habitat are the simplest interventions, she says. Stone walls are attractive to rodents, and have been shown to harbor high concentrations of ticks, says Machtinger. Seal up any nooks or replace them altogether.

“The single best way to manage ticks is with an acaricide,” a tick-killing pesticide, Machtinger says.

Some homeowners are wary of the effect of acaricide on pollinators and other beneficial insects. A gentler, more targeted option is tick tubes: cardboard rolls stuffed with permethrin-treated cotton that mice discover and transport back to pad their nests, which basically treats them against ticks, Machtinger says.

Pet owners are at higher risk for tick bites, Machtinger says, because “they spend a lot of time with their pets outdoors”. Pets can also transport ticks on their bodies. While Machtinger says cats are pretty good at grooming ticks off their bodies, she recommends checking dogs for ticks and combing their fur out before they come indoors.

‘Pasta windows’: a charming Italian restaurant tradition – or the sign of a terrible tourist trap?

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:51:46 GMT

A woman ostentatiously making her own pasta in an eaterie in Florence or Rome might seem the height of authenticity. But travellers, beware ...

Name: Pasta windows.

Age: Pretty new.

Pasta windows? That’s never going to work; I mean as soon as it rains they’ll go soggy and collapse … Duh! Not actual windows made of pasta.

Oh, so is it a new pasta shape – like alphabetti spaghetti (remember?), but little windows? That’s so cute … Nope, not that either.

I give up then, what is a pasta window? So picture a lovely cobbled Italian square, in Rome or Florence.

Got it, I’m there. Though let’s make that a piazza, in Roma or Firenze, for the genuine Italian vibes. OK, and there’s a restaurant – sorry, trattoria – with tables outside, and stripy parasols.

Perfect. I’ll have an Aperol spritz and imagine I’m in A Room With a View while I study the menu and decide what to eat. Now look up, and sitting in the window of the restaurant is a person, perhaps an old woman, rolling and shaping the dough, then hanging it: strands of linguine, strips of tagliatelle, sheets of lasagne …

Oh my God, a proper authentic Italian nonna, working with the love and knowledge that has been passed down through the generations of the family. I have discovered the real Italy! Except maybe not.

Excuse me? It’s a tourist trap.

Who says? Actual Italians. Such as Sophie Minchilli, who does food tours of Rome and told the Washington Post that this trend for pasta windows is “wrong”. And Neapolitan chef Michele Pascarella, who told Metro that no proper Italian restaurant would display someone making pasta in the window, and one that does “is usually more of a kitschy tourist trap than an authentic restaurant”.

But, look, they’re all over Instagram! Exactly! And that nonna you can see is an Insta-gran.

Hmm, maybe there is something a bit weird about having someone on display, working in the window. Zoo-like even. Imagine a chippy with a fishwife in the window, gutting and skinning haddock.

Ew, no thanks. Any other tips for spotting a tourist trap restaurant? So you’re on the main street, and a smiling but slightly aggressive and annoyingly persistent person is waving a multi-translated and heavily laminated menu – with photos – in your face while attempting to shepherd you into their establishment …

I’m guessing that’s a no? On so many counts. See also huge places with a huge menu and a huge number of tourists in there already, but very few local people.

So where should I go? Take a stroll a few streets back – from the main drag or from the beach. Ask a local resident for their favourites.

Do say, after consulting a language app: “Mi scusi, può consigliarmi un buon ristorante?” [Excuse me, can you recommend a good restaurant?]

Don’t say: “Look, she’s doing pasta shells now. Go on, get in there with her, for a TikTok …”

Ann Widdecombe was hit on head repeatedly with hammer, court told

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:39:35 GMT

Joshua Kerry appears at Westminster magistrates court charged with murder of former MP earlier this month

A man has appeared in court charged with the murder of the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe.

Joshua Kerry, 28, is accused of killing the 78-year-old former Conservative minister at her home in Haytor, Devon, earlier this month, by hitting her on the head with a hammer 21 times.

During a brief hearing at Westminster magistrates court on Tuesday afternoon, Kerry, who was dressed in a grey sweatshirt and tracksuit bottoms, spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address.

The court heard that security camera footage from the property indicated Widdecombe had been fatally attacked on 8 July.

Kerry is alleged to have entered her bungalow through the front door while she was eating her lunch, after driving there from his home in Rotherham, South Yorkshire.

The prosecutor, Kashif Malik, claimed Kerry was in the house for about two minutes before driving off, having allegedly taken Widdecombe’s wallet from her handbag.

Malik said the alarm was raised after Widdecombe failed to attend a pre-arranged online interview for Channel 5’s Matt Allwright show, shortly before 1pm. Producers from the show are said to have tried to contact Widdecombe and her personal assistant several times.

She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards. Malik said a provisional cause of death was given by a pathologist as blunt force trauma to the head.

Kerry was arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July by officers from Devon and Cornwall police after he was linked to a red Vauxhall Corsa car seen outside Widdecombe’s bungalow shortly before her death.

The case was later taken over by counter-terrorism officers and Kerry was rearrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism. The investigation into whether there was an alleged political or terrorism motivation for Widdecombe’s death is continuing.

Later on Tuesday, Kerry appeared at the Old Bailey before Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb, where he was denied bail and remanded in custody. A case management hearing was scheduled for 9 October, with a provisional trial date set for 8 June 2027.

On Tuesday morning, an inquest opened in Exeter into Widdecombe’s death. Philip Spinney, the senior coroner for the county of Devon, Plymouth and Torbay, confirmed the time and date of the former MP’s death and read a short statement before suspending the inquest until the conclusion of the criminal proceedings.

He said: “The circumstances of the death are as follows: concerns were raised that Miss Widdecombe was uncontactable. So, an employee who was due at the home address was asked to conduct a welfare check. Miss Widdecombe was located within her property. She was found to be unresponsive, and with visible injuries.

“The emergency services were called, and she was sadly declared deceased at the scene. A postmortem examination has taken place, and at this stage the precise medical cause of death has yet to be established.”

Spinney paid tribute to Widdecombe, who was the Conservative MP for the seat of Maidstone and the Weald, previously Maidstone, between 1987 and 2010. In 2019, she defected to the Brexit party to serve as an MEP; latterly, she was an immigration and justice spokesperson for its successor party, Reform UK.

“It is plain that Miss Widdecombe was much loved and will be greatly missed, and it’s important that we all understand the impact the loss of life has had on those who mourn,” Spinney said.

“A court could appear a harsh and clinical setting for what is an intensely private matter, the death of a loved one. I would like to offer my deepest condolences to the family of Miss Widdecombe.”

Big, brave Nige appears in public again with aimless speech to a few mega-fans

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:36:55 GMT

Reform leader’s recycled moanathon included digs at Kemi, the media, immigrants and new PM. But no questions, of course

Is it safe? Is it safe? For the past couple of months, Nigel Farage has been like Laurence Olivier in Marathon Man, wondering if he can come out of hiding. Tucked away in one of his five homes, living on handouts from benefactors and hoping the coast is clear. Free from troublesome reporters who insist on asking awkward questions about where his money comes from and what it’s for.

It’s tough to be the Man of the People when some of your money is coming from a posh convicted fraudster. Then again, Nige is a man who seems quick to forgive criminal behaviour. But – slowly, slowly – he is beginning to show his face in public again. And on Tuesday he took the latest steps on his Long Walk to Freedom.

Fed up with posting videos from random fields on social media, Nige was now ready to face a crowd of about 200 mega-fans in the garden of Kimberley Hall, a Norfolk country house often used as a wedding venue. For a speech, mind. Nothing more. There were to be no questions of any description. He might need his lawyers present for that.

This was just baby steps. The first part of a lengthy rehab plan. Getting his story straight about what the £5m was actually for would come later. Especially now sources say he told senior figures in Reform UK he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election. So today was all about finding his feet. Indulging the narcissistic wound that would never heal. Hearing the live applause again, for a dashed-off speech of little consequence. His bid to show he still counted for something, even when all eyes were on the new prime minister.

First, the warm-up act: Colin Sutton, the new Norfolk police and crime commissioner. A man apparently hell bent on proving he was a lot stupider than he looked. All Colin – a former high-ranking police officer – seemed to care about was stopping equality and inclusion training. As if that alone would restore people’s trust in the police. He also managed to confuse the Lib Dems with the Tories before welcoming Nige to the platform. “I don’t know much about policing,” he said. “But I do know he’s an innocent man.” Phew. That’s good to know.

On came Nige, relieved to have been given a pardon. Though he looked a bit bored. As if he couldn’t quite work out why he had agreed to do this. None of the main broadcasters were that interested, and he was just talking to a handful of the converted. The only plus side was that at least there was no sign of Count Binface. That would have been a humiliation too far.

Life has not been kind to Nige recently. Not so long ago, he had been riding high. Leading the polls, being taken seriously as the next prime minister. Now it was turning to dust as details of his financial affairs began to unravel. Nige always seemed to have believed that scrutiny was for other politicians, not him. Worst of all, he had been the architect of his own downfall. He had been the one to resign his seat in Clacton to engineer a showdown with a comedian wearing a dustbin on his head.

Nige began with a requiem for Keir Starmer. It had been Reform wot dun it. Reform that brought down the prime minister. It was also, unwittingly, a requiem for himself. Proof that you sometimes have to be careful what you wish for. Because in Andy Burnham, Reform now has a far tougher opponent. Someone who sounds credible. Someone to whom most of the country will give a decent hearing. You could almost hear the regret in Farage’s voice. Maybe he should have found a way of letting Starmer carry on as a lame duck leader.

“We need a general election now,” he said. But do we? That doesn’t seem to be what most of the country wants. Burnham had become prime minister without a vote. Hmm. Much like Nige appointing himself leader of Reform weeks before the last election. Dicky Tice, everyone’s least favourite beta male, just rolled over when Nige told him he was no longer in charge. “Whatever you say, Nigel,” Dicky may have simpered. The latest in a never-ending stream of humiliations.

The rest of the speech was just a reprise of some of Nige’s greatest hits. The sort of thing you used to be able to pay him £80 for in a personalised Cameo video. Nige didn’t even bother to pretend his heart was in it. This was Nige-by-Numbers. A man who sounded like he couldn’t wait to be somewhere else. He just wasn’t quite sure where. Everywhere he finds himself now seems wrong.

There was a random attack on the Tories. And the rightwing press. Nige can’t forgive the Telegraph and the Daily Mail for talking about the Kemi bounce and for even mentioning his financial difficulties. It was also outrageous that the media kept bringing up George Cottrell’s time in prison on a money-laundering charge. What was wrong with offering to help out a few major drug dealers? Surely it was far worse that Lou Haigh had failed to report she had found her stolen phone. That was the sort of crime for which people deserved to go down.

As the aimless ramble went on, the audience began to get as bored as Nige. Had they really made an effort to come to this? Then we had the “I’m not a racist, but” section. Nige loved immigrants. He really did. No one could love immigrants more. It was just a shame they were all criminals. London was now a no-go zone. No one dared to wear a watch any more, which is presumably why Nige’s own event had started 20 minutes late. Though it didn’t really explain how so many leading rightwing politicians had turned up at a conference in London the week before without being mugged.

Now things became desperate. Because Nige’s final complaint was that Burnham had used his notes 266 times during his half-hour acceptance speech for the Labour leadership. I mean, who cares? Surely what he said was what really counted. But Nige was having none of it. Style was all. Then again, none of us would really need notes to have made the speech he had just given. I’ve heard it so many times, I could have made it for him. Nige’s Mega Recycled Moanathon. He increasingly sounds like a man out of ideas. Whose time has come and gone. By the time he came to an end, half the crowd had beaten him to the exit.

Hunter Biden for president? Stranger things have happened

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:06:41 GMT

Once Republicans’ favourite punchline, Joe Biden’s son is now building an online following by trolling JD Vance, taunting Trump and embracing the absurdity of US politics

What sort of longshot candidate do we reckon is going to run for US president in 2028? The Rock? Kim Kardashian? Kermit the Frog? US politics has become so debased that being rich, famous and a natural-born citizen (sorry, Zohran Mamdani) now seem to be the only qualifications required for a job in the White House.

Which is why you shouldn’t entirely write off murmurings that Hunter Biden might be interested in following in his daddy’s presidential footsteps. When asked by a Fox News reporter about Hunter’s 2028 odds last month, Donald Trump suggested Joe Biden’s prodigal son might “do well”. If other “basket case[s]” in the Democratic party could do well, Trump added, then Hunter probably had a shot. Various analysts appear to agree. “Could Hunter Biden run for office? Don’t rule it out,” a recent Times headline blared. The article quotes a Biden biographer saying: “With a character like Hunter Biden in a populist, social media-driven political environment, you have to never say never.”

You would definitely have said “never” a couple of years ago: Hunter wasn’t exactly the US’s favourite person during his dad’s presidency. His various scandals made him a target for Maga and a headache for Democrats. But in recent months, Hunter has reinvented himself as a social-media star. Since reactivating his X account in May, the former first son has posted an average of 23 times a day – Elon Musk-levels of posting. Except while Elon is tweeting about how “whites are a rapidly dying minority”, Hunter is cracking self-deprecating jokes about drugs and gaining fans across the political spectrum, with some calling him the “Maga whisperer”. Writing on X in June, Biden said he’d gladly take the title. “Left, right, D or R we all want the same things,” Hunter added. “We’re being divided on purpose by the Epstein Elite Oligarch class because as long as we’re at each other’s throats, they get fat and rich off of our misery.”

Amen to that. Still, despite his refreshing political commentary, I’m not sure we should be treating the man as a folk hero or a Maga whisperer quite yet. It seems to me Hunter’s comeback isn’t so much motivated by political ambitions as by his millions of dollars of debt. He’s always been good at capitalising on his last name, and I suspect he’s realised he can parlay being provocative online into monetisable opportunities. To that end, Hunter has been going on every podcast that will have him, including sitting down with the far-right conspiracy theorist Candace Owens and the white nationalist Nick Fuentes. He’s also launched a paid Substack called Where’s Hunter? (a reference to one of Trump’s favourite catchphrases) and joked about starting an OnlyFans.

Look, if you’re going to milk your famous name, at least make sure you’re not boring. (Trump’s spawn have failed spectacularly in this regard.) And Hunter’s new Extremely Online persona may be occasionally unhinged, but it’s not boring. On Saturday, for example, Hunter went on the progressive commentator Jennifer Welch’s podcast and joked that America’s biggest problem wasn’t “oligarchy”, but “closetocracy”, or the angry “closeted gay mafia” of Republicans in DC. This is relevant, Hunter said, because he believes the “internal conflict creates so much vitriol inside a person that they take it out on the rest of the world”. Hunter added that while he didn’t get a “gaydar ping” from Senator Ted Cruz, the man definitely gave him a “really kinky weird” vibe. I don’t know that this particular conversation was big or clever, but I’m sure it annoyed Cruz, so there’s that.

Speaking of things that aren’t big or clever, Hunter’s also been trolling JD Vance following the vice-president’s creepy comments about Biden’s “suggestive” ice-cream licking. (I’ll spare you JD’s thoughts on corn dogs.) On Sunday, which was National Ice Cream Day for those who celebrate, Hunter posted a photo of himself licking an ice-cream with the caption: “Hey @JDVance. I wish I knew how to quit you.” And Hunter hasn’t minced his words when it comes to Vance’s boss. In a recent interview, he said that if he were sitting next to Trump, he’d tell him to “go fuck his fucking self”. He then noted that he’d challenged Donald Trump Jr to a UFC fight “three times” but hadn’t heard back. He added: “That’s how I’m going to pay all my debt.”

Good luck with that, mate. Hunter has zero chance of ever winning a presidential nomination, but I’d bet good money he’d beat Don Jr in a cage fight. The US may be divided, but that’s a Biden-Trump rematch I think everyone in the country could get behind.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Here are 48 reasons to cherish the World Cup (minus the Geopolitics)

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:05:34 GMT

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

The Geopolitics World Cup is already fading from view, replaced by a thin July gruel of pre-season friendlies and transfer tales. But there’s still time to cast another look back over the 48-team, 104-game, 308-goal leviathan that has dominated the last six weeks of our lives. Without further ado, here are 48 reasons to cherish this year’s World Cup (minus the Geopolitics).

The very first game between Mexico and South Africa saw three red cards dished out, ITV showing off their studio’s Manhattan backdrop, and a duck anointed as a national hero. Germany looked ominous, putting seven past Curaçao, whose solitary goal sent Telemundo commentators wild. Vozinha and Cape Verde had us wondering about Spain, and the giant keeper’s heroics helped his mum get over to watch him play.

Another classy veteran, Lionel Messi, banged in six group-stage goals, (briefly) becoming the World Cup’s all-time top scorer. Cristiano Ronaldo was bad, then (briefly) “back”, and then gone again. Scotland fans left a far greater impression on the tournament than their team, making Boston their spiritual home. England put away Croatia with a dazzling display of attacking intent that was not to be repeated, while Anthony Barry expertly channeled a frustrated lower-league manager in his half-time interviews.

It’s probably time for a hydration break, but Mauricio Pochettino just kicked over the Powerade. Poch did a great turn as a middle-aged actor playing a World Cup coach, and the US (briefly) looked like a really good team, before being derailed by something or other, we forget. Fellow co-hosts Canada earned their first-ever World Cup win in style, smashing six past Sunday League’s Qatar, who earned two red cards. Also sent off: discretion’s Miguel Almirón, for covering his mouth while talking – not that it helped Turkey, who crashed out after two games despite taking 1,057 shots on goal.

Group E saw Japan being tidy on and off the field, an inconsistent Sweden winning and losing 5-1, and Herve Rénard showing up for some reason. Ecuador’s “touchline dreamboat” Sebastián Beccacece turned heads, while Marcelo Bielsa could only shake his dome sorrowfully as Uruguay fell apart in real time. Riyad Mahrez confused everyone by putting Algeria 3-2 up against Austria, who immediately equalised and doubled the torment for Iran, already denied a dramatic winner against Egypt by VAR.

Time for another hydro-break, brought to you by the sweet elixir of goals. Cape Verde’s Sidny Lopes Cabral delivered the goal and celebration of the tournament against Argentina, who brought extra-time magic of their own thanks to Julián Alvarez. Haiti’s Wilson Isidor and Uzbekistan striker Eldor Shomurodov joined the pantheon of great forgotten World Cup goals, while Egypt’s brilliant breakaway against Argentina was cruelly disallowed. Their manager, combustible hardman Hossam Hassan, responded accordingly.

The knockouts brought a sharper edge, with Germany bundled out by ‘housery’s Paraguay and the Dutch denied by a Morocco team who lived up to their billing. Portugal v Croatia was absolute psychodrama, and Belgium looked more likely to fight among themselves than find a way back against Senegal. The Battle of the Azteca was a belter. England players threw their heads at everything, Javier Aguirre delivered the GWC’s best touchline moment, and Harry Kane lost his voice. Brazil’s fragile, vibes-based journey was shattered by Erling Haaland’s merciless precision as Norway rowed on in (almost) perfect unison, with Haaland dominating defences and Social Media Disgraces alike. Neymar, meanwhile, won the Mark Corrigan award for winning in the most minor way possible.

On to the quarter-finals, where Kylian Mbappé dictated the play as France (briefly) looked unstoppable, and Spain conceded a goal (Charles De Ketelaere becoming an eternal pub quiz answer). Breel Embolo’s needless dive was exposed in 4K, England got a little help from on high against Norway, Gabriel Clarke stirred the pot, and Danny Murphy continued the sobering tale of Bob the Cat. The semis can be summed up in two key moments – Lamine Yamal turning Lucas Digne’s brain inside-out, and seven defenders failing to close down Enzo Fernández. Oh, England!

The game of the tournament came in the third-place playoff, a ridiculous knockabout affair won 6-4 by England, with Mbappé stat-padding his way to the Golden Boot. The final was not nearly as much fun, with Wayne Rooney neatly summarising the chaotic half-time show, and Fernández’s bone-headed second yellow card summing up Argentina’s reductive efforts. There’s no bigger moment than the one that wins it all, though, so take a bow, Ferran Torres.

Finally, after a tournament of tedious celebrity-spotting, it was nice to see Javier Bardem and Carlos Alcaraz genuinely celebrating Spain’s success, before Keyne Yamal made the pitch his playground. Ominously, Luis de la Fuente’s red-and-gold army are co-hosts next time, when we may have to rattle off 64 memorable moments. We’ll get to work on that, you can start making your predictions and we’ll do it all again in 2030.

Tributes have poured in over the last 24 hours to Kevin Keegan after his death at the age of 75. His playing career was remarkable – he remains (and will surely remain for a long time) the only British player to be twice named European Footballer of the Year, he won the title three times with Liverpool (and the European Cup), the Bundesliga with Hamburg and was an England stalwart for a decade. But through TV appearances, adverts, even a top 40 hit, his impact as one of football’s early celebrity breakout stars can’t be measured by medals alone. And that’s before we get to his wild managerial career, remembered mostly – for good or ill – by his blow-up at Alex Ferguson in 1996. “Kevin carried the love of the game on his sleeve, there’s no question about that, and that carried right on to the fans, to the players,” said Ferguson on Tuesday. “That period at Newcastle was of emotion, it was excitement. They brought these great players to the club too and they added to it, and it gave Newcastle – I think – their best ever team.” Amid a deluge of other tributes, Alan Shearer perhaps summed up his feelings most succinctly: “My hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss.”

For more on Keegan’s remarkable career as a player and manager, here’s Rob Draper’s wonderful tribute, Richard Williams’s obituary, Louise Taylor on his three eras at Newcastle and his life in pictures.

“As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result. For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn’t just about winning; it’s about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up. It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment” – despite their showing in the GWC final, Enzo Fernández hypes up Argentina’s performance without fully grasping the meaning of the words “pride” and “humility” as they return home.

Healey as chancellor? Streeting as defence secretary? This isn’t a cabinet to change the UK like Burnham promised

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 15:00:50 GMT

Putting Ed Miliband in charge of the Treasury would have signalled a genuine new era. Instead, the new PM has played it safe

Andy Burnham has promised to bring “four decades of neoliberalism” to an end. The first serious test of that pledge was always going to be the cabinet he appointed. The red flags are impossible to ignore.

Ending neoliberalism would mean putting privatised services back into public hands, unleashing public investment and using the power of the state to reshape the economy. Yet Burnham’s support for the government’s suffocating fiscal rules – and his preference for the vaguer language of “public control” over public ownership – had already raised doubts about how far he was prepared to go.

Had he truly meant it, Ed Miliband would have been the obvious choice for chancellor. The former Labour leader has been on a political journey since concluding that his defeat in the 2015 general election was partly the consequence of insufficient radicalism. “I felt my analysis was big,” he later said, “but my response was not big enough, not bold enough.”

As energy secretary, Miliband was the one cabinet minister who combined dynamism with a genuine determination to challenge the status quo. His record included the establishment of the publicly owned Great British Energy, the return of energy-system planning to public hands and an interventionist industrial policy.

He would also have been prepared to confront Treasury resistance to transformative economic policies. This is, after all, a government bureaucracy with much to answer for in Britain’s long economic decline. Its record stretches back to the 1970s, when excessively pessimistic projections of the country’s borrowing requirements helped precipitate the notorious International Monetary Fund bailout and the avoidable public sector cuts that followed.

Yet Burnham seems to have folded in the face of a loud and very public campaign against Miliband’s appointment, centred on warnings of an impending backlash from the markets. Some of Burnham’s allies briefed against Miliband on the grounds of his support for net zero policies – an alarming position for a supposedly progressive party amid rolling heatwaves. It is therefore reassuring that Miatta Fahnbulleh has been appointed as his successor. A bright progressive economist, she at least represents continuity with Miliband’s approach.

But instead, the former defence secretary John Healey has been appointed chancellor. There is one potential bright spot: the choice may bode well for Burnham’s promise of a mass council-housebuilding programme. Healey served as Labour’s shadow housing secretary under Jeremy Corbyn, when the party was committed to building 100,000 council homes a year. As defence secretary, he also oversaw the state’s repurchase of more than 36,000 military family homes. Angela Rayner’s appointment as secretary of state for housing, communities and local government offers further reassurance.

But there is no evidence that Healey is committed to the transformative economic programme required to end four decades of neoliberalism. He served as a minister in Gordon Brown’s Treasury when the government remained wedded to an economic model founded on financial deregulation and dependence on the City, falling corporation-tax rates, the private finance initiative and the continued restriction of trade-union power.

His resignation from Keir Starmer’s cabinet in support of still higher defence spending offers further cause for alarm. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) habitually demands funding for projects that end up billions of pounds over budget. The defence review was supposedly fully funded; it then transpired that an £18bn black hole remained. The department has repeatedly frittered away money. Billions were spent on aircraft carriers derided by the former chief of the defence staff David Richards as “unaffordable vulnerable metal cans”, while the Ajax armoured vehicles arrived eight years late after a catalogue of problems.

As one defence analyst puts it: “We already spend 30% more on defence than France for a smaller, less ready, less-capable military.” Britain’s defence market is unusually concentrated in the hands of a few companies: in 2024-25, the 10 largest suppliers received nearly 40% of all MoD spending, while almost half of contracts were awarded without competition. As defence secretary, Healey could have challenged the MoD over its inefficiency, overspending and dysfunctional procurement. Instead, he amplified its demands for yet more money.

That is likely to mean a renewed assault on welfare spending to fund additional weapons. With the veteran rightwinger Pat McFadden remaining at the Department for Work and Pensions, it is difficult to imagine otherwise.

The defence of Healey’s appointment is that No 10 will exercise an unusually tight grip over economic policy. Burnham has his own economic advisers, including the former Goldman Sachs chief economist Jim O’Neill, who favours applying greater flexibility to the fiscal rules that constrain Britain’s ability to invest. Leaving aside the question of whether a former investment banker is the ideal figure to help lead a rupture with neoliberalism, it remains unclear how coherent Burnham’s economic vision really is. Only Miliband’s appointment would have made his promise of fundamental change remotely plausible.

Miliband has instead been appointed foreign secretary. That is at least an improvement on Yvette Cooper, who has now been moved to health secretary. Miliband won the Labour leadership partly by repudiating the Iraq war and later instructed his MPs to vote in favour of recognising a Palestinian state. In 2012, he warned that an Israeli ground invasion of Gaza would be “a disaster”, and condemned Israel’s subsequent onslaught in 2014 as “wrong” and “unjustifiable”.

after newsletter promotion

Alas, Miliband toed the line under Starmer, and did not vote for a ceasefire in November 2023. His first statement as foreign secretary correctly describes Russia’s invasion as “illegal” but refers only to “conflict in the Middle East”. He speaks of “the terrible suffering of the people of Gaza” without naming who has inflicted it. He should note new polling that says 50% of Britons believe Israel has committed genocide – only 17% disagree – with mass public support for ending all arms sales and imposing sanctions.

Notably, Wes Streeting has been appointed defence secretary. The Blairite former health secretary released correspondence with Peter Mandelson in which he wrote that Israel was “committing war crimes before our eyes”. He must now be asked whether he stands by that judgment – and whether he will abide by the legal obligations that logically follow from it.

For progressive voters already angered by the failure of the Starmer project, the retention of Shabana Mahmood as home secretary will be another source of antagonism. Her plans for one of Europe’s harshest immigration and asylum regimes speak to the broader problem in British politics. Migrants and minorities have been scapegoated for injustices caused by a broken economic system.

Burnham’s cabinet is certainly an improvement on what came before. But on the choices that will decide whether his promised break with neoliberalism is real, he has flunked the first test.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

‘Sent the kittens scarpering’: the best cat toys in the UK, tested by cats

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 14:00:48 GMT

From catnip to interactive, scented and all-natural teasers, here are the toys our reviewer’s panel of feline testers fell head over paws for

The best gifts for cats and dogs

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Watch a cat doing as they please in a garden, and you’ll witness a procession of behaviours passed down from their wild ancestors. They may crouch with ears pricked up at the sight or sound of birds in flight; rub against objects to leave their scent; chase buzzing, drowsing insects; or sniff a favourite plant with gusto. Regrettably, some will hunt and catch prey.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

The best cat toys help any cat – indoor or outdoor – live out these behaviours safely, humanely, and often with their owner’s involvement. Having a few within paw’s reach is valuable to a pet cat’s fitness, mood and fundamental felinity.

In my view, the best cat toys are interactive ones that come to life in a human’s hand. It could be a teaser toy, a ball or a bravely proffered scatter toy – what matters is that you and your cat are playing together and growing closer as a result.

Of course, few among us lead lives of constant play, so you may also choose to get some toys that your cat can play with independently through the day. Laser toys with timers, electronic moving prey toys, or puzzle toys with moving parts can all add stimulation to a pet cat’s alone time. When budgeting for cat toys, bear in mind that they tend to be shorter-term or repeat purchases, especially as cats tend to get bored of or enjoy destroying their favourite toys.

Best cat toy overall: Nature’s Goodies colourful long raffia tail teaser sticks

Best budget cat toy: Pets at Home scrunchie ball

Best scented cat toy: Zebedee’s valerian mouse

Best electronic cat toy: PetSafe Peek-A-Bird

Best catnip cat toy: Honeysuckle Cat Toys honeysuckle and catnip pouch

As a lifelong cat lover, I’ve spent untold hours playing with cats. These include my childhood pet, Jack; my current feline family member, Martha; and more than a dozen rescue cats I’ve fostered for Cat Action Trust 1977: a volunteer-run charity that provides help to feral and stray cats. There’s nothing quite like watching a sweet kitty claw, kick or bite a toy into oblivion.

I’m also a journalist, and one of my most enjoyable gigs is reviewing products for the Filter. I treated the task of testing cat toys just as seriously as I took reviewing electric heaters – which are also adored by heat-loving cats.

Spurning the temptation to dress up as a cat and test the toys in solitude, I engaged a panel of feline testers to play with each one. Most of the cats have a connection to Cat Action Trust 1977: a large group of kittens who were in the care of hand-rearing expert Dianne, and an adult cat named Hovis, who lives under the loving long-term care of fosterer Vanda. I also tested some of the toys with my own cat, Martha, because I didn’t want her to feel left out.

Where possible, I tested each type of toy with multiple cats to accommodate differences in taste. As well as observing how the cats played with the toys, I considered the human’s experience – especially how the toys encouraged interaction between pet and owner. After testing, the toys were left at the mercy of their new owners.

All of the kittens and cats who lent a claw with this article are now homed, but Cat Action Trust 1977 often has large numbers of foster cats in need of adoption.

Rare is the cat who will not respond to a well-chosen teaser. I love toys of this type, as they encourage playful interaction between you and your cat. (Top tip: try trailing one around chair legs or behind items of furniture.)

Why we love itThe best teasers I’ve come across are made by Nature’s Goodies, which sent a selection of beautiful, all-natural teaser toys for our feline testers to review. There are various types, but it’s this raffia option that caused my cat, Martha, to fall head over paws. While I happily wielded the wooden handle, she gamely chased its grass-like bunch of natural strands, made from palm leaves. The rustling sound of the teaser moving across the floor dialled up the excitement – especially when I moved it around while it was out of her sight, behind the sofa.

Other teasers from the brand’s range, such as this feathered sisal twizzle model, hit the spot with Dianne’s rescue kittens, and Vanda’s foster cat Hovis. All of these toys seemed well made, and the natural materials make a nice change from the synthetics used in many cat toys.

It’s a shame that … many cats will eventually tire of a teaser toy – even a good one. I’d recommend buying a few different types to maintain interest.

Type: manual (interactive)Motivation: moving preyMaterials: raffia, pine wood

A great thing about cats – one of the many – is that they couldn’t care less how much something costs. Trivially priced toys can be received like manna from heaven, and so it proved when I tossed this simple, shiny, £1 scrunchie ball into the midst of Dianne’s foster kittens.

Why we love itThe kittens hurtled after this toy, chasing and battering it as it tumbled along the floor. They kept playing with it long after I’d thrown it towards them, so while a little human encouragement helps to get the fun started, the scrunchie was evidently engaging enough in its own right.

Cats are often interested in shiny things, which seem to trigger their hunting instincts – and this must enhance the appeal of the scrunchie, as it glints in the light while it rolls about.

I’d recommend having a few different mobile “scatter toys” around the house to keep cats entertained. This one will sit nicely alongside others, such as crumpled-up packaging or bargain-priced ping-pong balls. You’ll have to be careful where you tread, but that’s part of living with a cat.

It’s a shame that … toys of this type are easy to lose, as cats will often knock them behind furniture or into other obscure nooks and crannies.

Type: manual (static or interactive)Motivation: static or moving preyMaterials: synthetic

The evolutionary reasons why cats respond strongly to certain herbal scents are shrouded in mystery, but it’s well established that many felines go wild for particular plants – hence the abundance of scented cat toys.

Why we love itValerian reputedly makes cats playful, relaxed and contented, and this adorable stuffed mouse toy from Zebedee’s seemed to tick these boxes during testing. Dianne’s kittens took a while to warm up to it, but gradually settled to sniffing the pleasingly scented interloper and attacking its tail, with the fabric proving resilient to their sharp, little claws. This wasn’t my first experience with Zebedee’s valerian mouse – my mum’s cat, Bertie, has enjoyed playing with them, too.

The whole Zebedee’s mouse range is handmade and surpassingly cute. If your cat has more classical tastes, they may prefer the original Zebedee’s catnip mouse to the valerian model here.

It’s a shame that … it’s difficult to guess whether your cat will respond best to valerian, silvervine or catnip. Some cats have little or no response to the same scents that send others into raptures, and this is significantly linked to their genetics. Of course, you can find out your cat’s preferences through trial and error.

Type: scatter toy/scentedMotivation: static prey/valerian scentMaterials: cotton, valerian filling

Tantalisingly twiddling a feather through slots in its right or left side, this electronic, bird-shaped toy can keep cats entertained while you’re too busy with work or chores to pick up a teaser.

Why we love itThis toy excelled during testing with Dianne’s foster kittens. It activates with a tweeting sound that instantly caught the kittens’ attention, and after they’d scoped out the moving feather for a respectful period, they began to attack it, one by one. The unpredictable movements seemed to add to the thrill, sending the kittens scarpering from one side to the other in hot pursuit.

There are two modes of operation to choose from: “one time play”, which activates the toy for 10 minutes; and “play all day”, which makes use of a motion sensor to turn on the toy whenever a cat is nearby. The latter is a great option for owners who spend much of the day away from home.

It’s a shame that … Dianne soon found out why a replacement feather is included with this toy: the kittens tore out the original one. With this in mind, the Peek-A-Bird may provide longer-term enjoyment for a less vigorous adult cat than it would for a roomful of rambunctious kittens.

Type: electronic (three AA batteries required)Motivation: moving preyMaterials: plastic, synthetic feather

If your cat responds to catnip toys, then one of their likely behaviours after inhaling the herb’s scent will be rubbing their face on the toy. This sweet-looking pouch from Honeysuckle Cat Toys is perfectly designed for this, with a textured fabric cover that gives the cat plenty of purchase on the item while they demonstrate their adoration.

Why we love itMartha was immediately taken with this pouch, which elicited enthusiastic nuzzling, rolling around, purring and – I’m afraid to say – drooling after she first caught its aroma. Her interest waned within a few hours, but she was still giving the pouch an occasional sniff after several days. I’ve seen her carrying it around in her mouth from time to time, which is surely one of the cutest things a cat can do.

Scented cat products vary in the quality of their fillings. Judging by Martha’s blissed out response to this pouch, the organic catnip and ground honeysuckle wood inside it are pretty high grade. The toy’s maker, Honeysuckle Cat Toys, uses different fabric with every batch, so you can count on receiving a new pattern whenever you buy a fresh one.

It’s a shame that … as is true with most scented cat toys, the fun is over fairly quickly.

Type: scatter toy/scentedMotivation: catnip and honeysuckle scentMaterials: cotton and cotton-canvas fabric, catnip and honeysuckle filling

Best for: a laser cat toy

This proved to be Hovis’s favourite toy during testing, sending a little red dot of cat-safe laser light dancing around Vanda’s home and tempting him to pounce. It took me a while to realise that the toy is supposed to be elevated – for instance, placed on the edge of a table or hung from a door handle – to project its light around a sufficiently wide area. Once the penny dropped and I had the dot moving properly, Hovis began to chase.

Perfect for owners who need to leave their cat home alone for long periods, this toy can be set in “continuous” mode, which reactivates the dancing dot at intervals.

It didn’t make the final cut because … ideally, it would be capable of projecting its light dot around a wider area from floor level.

Type: electronic (three AAA batteries required); motivation: moving light; materials: plastic

Best for: a long teaser toy

In my humbly cat-besotted opinion, the most enjoyable type of cat toy to play with as a human (and I dare say for cats too) is a teaser. This colourful Pets At Home model provided hours of fun for Martha, as she flailed her paws after it through the air, bit into its ample fabric and watched it slowly, temptingly trailing across the living room floor. The jingling rattle at the end of the teaser is a nice touch.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I preferred Nature’s Goodies’ teasers, but this is an excellent budget alternative. Of course, you can save more money by playing with a piece of string or ribbon.

Type: teaser; motivation: moving prey; materials: wood, fabric and plastic

Best for: a puzzle toy

Catit circuit toys have been a firm favourite with several of the felines in my life since I first gave one to my mum’s cat, Bertie, in the mid-2010s. You slot it together like a marble run or a hamster tunnel kit, and place the supplied ball inside the partially enclosed track, where it can be seen and pawed by your cat – but never caught.

This toy can provide hours of fun, especially if you give it a nudge to get the ball rolling. The track sections can be set out in different configurations, which might help keep it interesting in the long run.

Incidentally, I share the Filter writer Alan Martin’s appreciation for Catit’s formidable cat carrier, the Cabrio.

It didn’t make the final cut because ... it takes up more floor or storage space than some people would like.

Type: puzzle; motivation: moving prey; materials: BPA-freeplastic

Our feline focus group had fun with this reasonably priced, leek-shaped kicker toy from Willow’s. It offers a mixture of textures, with string serving as the roots and soft, textured fabric covering the vegetable’s body. Dianne noticed that when a kitten grabbed hold of one part of the toy, other parts would move about, adding to the stimulation.

While this toy contains some catnip, this won’t have done anything for the kittens, as the herb has no effect on cats until they are about six months old. Clearly, the toy was fun enough regardless.

It didn’t make the final cut because … not all cats enjoy playing with this type of toy. If you’ve seen your cat trying to death-kick other toys or items such as the corners of rugs, there’s a good chance they’ll enjoy one.

Type: kicker; motivation: static prey/catnip scent; materials: fabric and catnip filling

As many cat owners know, cats will tend to become uninterested in a toy over time – sometimes within minutes. A University of Southampton study led by John Bradshaw, the author of Cat Sense, found that this disenchantment is typically with specific toys, rather than types of toys or play itself. So, it’s worth replacing your cat’s discarded old favourites with slightly different toys of the same types.

Of course, replacing cat toys frequently can become costly. Another option is using suitable household objects as toys, or making your own. In my experience, cats can have hours of fun with things like a ball of scrunched-up paper, the turned corner of a rug, or fronds of certain ornamental grasses (check the species is cat-safe before playtime).

With strongly scented toys, my fellow contributor Alan Martin has had some luck with putting them back in their bag in between plays to maintain the aromatic potency. A particularly pungent ferret toy was of far more interest to his cats after a spell back in its plastic pouch than when left out and about.

Felines have an instinct to play – or really, to hunt. If you have an indoor cat, playing with toys is their best opportunity to scratch, pummel, claw and kick that primal itch. Outdoor cats can also benefit from the variety and stimulation afforded by tantalising toys, and there’s opportunity for all pet cats to grow closer to their human devotees through play.

Many of the best cat toys look, feel or move like mice, birds or other critters that scamper around on lower links of the food chain. Another interesting finding from John Bradshaw et al is that cats seem to retain interest in a toy for longer if it starts to fall apart during play – they value proof that the hunter is winning the fight with their prey.

All cats are individuals. Closely observing their behaviour may give you clues as to which play activities they’d enjoy – and therefore which toys you should buy. For instance, cats who bite loose threads or plant stems might appreciate a teaser with long strands for them to chase. Watch and play with your cat, and you’ll get to know them.

‘The Kardashian era is over’: TikTok’s ‘povvo king’ takes on the billionaires

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:26:54 GMT

Shabaz Ali stormed to TikTok fame mocking the designer ice cubes of the privileged. Now he’s on the BBC stoking revolt against the superrich

It was ice cubes that tipped Shabaz Ali over the edge. “A woman online spent her entire day making content about ‘designer ice cubes’,” he recalls. “She’d freeze flavoured waters or fruit juices and show the whole process in tedious detail. I was like, ‘There’s no way she’s got a proper job or has ever struggled for money. Only someone wealthy would have the time to do this.’ It vexed me, so on a whim, I made a reaction video saying ‘On today’s episode of I’m Rich, You’re Poor …’ Soon my TikToks were getting 30m views and thousands of comments. It blew my mind.”

Ali, AKA @ShabazSays, has since become a cult celebrity for his sarcastic commentary on how the other half live. His scathing takedowns of the “rich and ridiculous” have won him more than 4 million followers. Now he’s transferring his viral fame to our TV screens.

It all began when former chemistry teacher Ali, 32, took to his bedroom in Blackburn during lockdown and amused himself by mocking the smugly privileged. In his crosshairs were those who humblebrag about their perfect lives and woo-woo habits. Tongue firmly in cheek, he styled himself as “King of the Povvos” and leader of the “#PovvoGang”.

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

“It was reclaiming an insult,” he says. “I grew up working class and heard ‘povvo’ so much. The community we’ve built is warm, honest and self-deprecating. They’re saying, ‘We don’t have much but at least we’re here’. Povvo is a badge of honour now.”

The disconnect between influencers and their audience is increasingly jarring. “They post about bespoke Bentleys and private jets. Who are you making this for? [US socialite] Becca Bloom really bothers me. Millions of people watch her cats eating out of £20,000 bowls. She has a £100k Louis Vuitton trunk full of Hermès bags. Yet her followers genuinely think they’re friends.”

In Ali’s corner of the internet, a backlash was brewing: “People were tagging me in dozens of videos per day, pointing out tone-deaf displays of wealth.” He calls it “a movement” that is helping to move the dial on unrealistic standards. “There’s been a massive shift in the last few years,” says Ali. “The Kardashian era is over. We don’t want airbrushed reality any more. We want it raw, authentic and unfiltered.”

In these days of doomscrolling, aspirational figures fill a void. “As a teacher, I saw how social media warped teenagers’ perception of the world. Wealth influencers, trad wives and Andrew Tate provide something that’s missing from their lives. The illusion of working hard and getting your reward has been shattered. They’re seeing their parents and teachers struggle. Young people dream of opulence but can’t have it. They’d say, ‘I don’t need to study, I’m going into business. Richard Branson didn’t do his GCSEs.’ I was like, ‘He’s one person!’ There are 3,400 billionaires in a global population of 8.3 billion. That’s a lot of disappointed people.”

Amid the cost-of-living crisis, his videos provided a reality check. “I was telling my students, ‘This lavish stuff online isn’t right. It’s not real’. That’s why I started taking the mickey. It snowballed.”

His BBC documentary, Shabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad?, finds Ali investigating extreme wealth and its real-world impact. With his trademark playful wit, he asks whether the mega-rich are a symptom of a broken culture or if they can be a force for good.

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Wealth hoarding gives him “the ick”. “What annoys me most is that the gap is widening,” he says. “We’re getting more billionaires, who are finding more tax loopholes and ways to hoard assets. I genuinely think 90% of them don’t care. You can’t be a billionaire and be a good person.”

In a bid to understand more, he attempts to meet a billionaire in person. Ali approaches the Kardashians, Beckhams, Trumps, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Beyoncé for an interview. “Kim K definitely saw my message. She didn’t reply, though. A couple of people hearted it. That was it.”

Instead he meets a range of people who are both pro and anti-billionaire. These include the Green party’s Zack Polanski. “He’s the only person on the party political spectrum who’s speaking out about billionaires,” says Ali. “Everybody else is too busy trying to protect their donors. Many of his arguments resonated. I’m a lifelong Labour voter but might I vote Green now? Possibly.”

He spends time with Apprentice winner turned “eight-figure entrepreneur” Joseph Valente (“fascinating character but he uses a lot of hairspray”). He flies to the Colorado ski resort of Vail to stay with Phones 4U founder John Caudwell. “I hate billionaires but I liked John, which was hard,” admits Ali. “I just think he’s unaware of his own power and privilege. He told me, ‘You can’t whisper in the ears of governments. I had a meeting with Keir Starmer and he didn’t take my advice.’ The fact that he even said that sentence! You got into that room because of money. The prime minister might not have taken your advice but there’s someone whose advice he did take. I admire John’s philanthropy but fundamentally we still disagree. Your rich friends are still wankers, mate!”

Ali takes the opportunity to poke around inside Caudwell’s kitchen, hoping to find one of the vast “curated” fridges he satirises online. “I genuinely thought I was going to get the internet lifestyle with everything neat and labelled but it was like a normal person’s fridge. It was dirtier than mine!” Did making the film challenge Ali’s views? “It didn’t alter my beliefs, it cemented them. I still think we don’t need billionaires and they should be doing more for the rest of us.”

He’s told that if we make billionaires pay more tax, they will leave the UK and take their wealth with him. “Let them go!” he says. “Let’s look over the hill and see if the grass is greener. It’s just scare tactics. They ain’t going anywhere. They’ve benefited too much from this country and have too much of a stake here to suddenly leave. Tax them, I say. Tax diamonds. Tax yachts.” He laughs. “If they don’t pay up, move them all to the Isle of Wight and turn it into a giant prison for rich people.”

This future star’s debut documentary ends with a shameless appeal for a full series. “We’ve already started talking about the next film,” he says. “Skincare, cosmetics and plastic surgery is the route I’m keen to go down. Shabaz asks: can I turn back time? That’s the question I want to pose. Watch this space.”

In the meantime, he believes society is approaching tipping point. “I think we’re on the brink of something big,” says Ali with a twinkle of zeal in his eyes. “People are so sick of wealth inequality. We’re French Revolution era, ready to overthrow Marie Antoinette.”

Shabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad? airs on BBC Three at 9pm on Tuesday 28 July and will be available on iPlayer

We’ve been desperate for someone to take on Donald Trump. Who knew it would be Coldplay’s Chris Martin?

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:25:56 GMT

The World Cup left us with some surprising heroes. Kudos to pop’s leader of the bland and his very public rebuke to hatred and division

Long before the United States turned the World Cup final into an orgy of pop music and advertising, the signs were already there that this year’s co-hosts should never have been allowed within a thousand miles of the tournament. The garish half-time show curated by Chris Martin of Coldplay seemed to reinforce that – but then came a moment of improbable genius.

I was surprised. The last time America hosted, the problem wasn’t commercial overkill so much as sheer shrugging apathy. I was in New York during USA ’94. Apart from a few flapping banners outside the Nike store, you wouldn’t have known one of the world’s biggest sporting events was taking place. This, in hindsight, was a blessing. Football was allowed to football.

In our rampantly hypercapitalist age, we can only dream of such innocence. In the run-up to its 2026 iteration, co-hosted with Mexico and Canada, the cost to supporters of handing the lion’s share of World Cup games to America’s supersize-everything culture became horribly clear, from obscene ticket prices to price-gouging by local authorities over travel to games, with a $13 train ticket to the MetLife Stadium, venue for the final, hiked to $105. Then came the announcement of so-called “hydration breaks” midway through each half. This was in no way just an excuse for American broadcasters to cram in more advertising. Never again.

On the eve of the tournament, things only got worse. Africa’s top referee, Omar Artan, was refused entry to the States for having the temerity to be Somali. Iraqi striker Aymen Hussein was detained and questioned for seven hours on arrival at O’Hare airport. In a better, saner universe, all 48 competing nations would have boycotted the whole thing in solidarity at this point. But the reaction of the Fifa president Gianni Infantino to any concerns was to tell us to “chill” and “relax”.

Then Fifa announced that this year’s half-time would last 25 minutes – breaking the organisation’s own rules – due to a pop concert along Super Bowl lines. On the day, it began bizarrely: Madonna singing Music on some weird sci-fi Jeep deep in the bowels of the stadium, then emerging from the tunnel flanked, randomly, by Brazil legends Ronaldinho and Ronaldo. The rest of the show was a surreal jumble. Two men exchanging wisecracks, their presence baffling to anyone who doesn’t watch Ted Lasso. The Muppets doing Seven Nation Army. The uncanny valley faces of K-pop megastars BTS looking more like AI creations than flesh and blood. Shakira being Shakira. Wandering minstrel Justin Bieber doing a mournful acoustic ballad called Everything Hallelujah that’s the very antithesis of a bop, planting the crowd’s arses firmly back in their seats.

But then Chris Martin pulled out his Trump card. After footage of Pelé saying the word “love” on the big screens, Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love, with lines including “Be kind to each other / We’re in this together”, surrounded by dozens of children of multiple ethnicities – the sort of kids Trump’s ICE squads would doubtless deport in a heartbeat – wearing T-shirts with slogans such as “all of us a family”, “I am you and you and you”, and “stars that make a galaxy”. They’re sentiments that would feel trite in more privileged times, but feel radical and essential in 2026. Finally, the sky above the stadium exploded in rainbow smoke above the bleak Sopranos hinterland around the MetLife, an unmistakeable statement of LGBTQ+ solidarity. One can only imagine what the president made of it, behind the bulletproof glass. Martin was, effectively, trolling him.

The US isn’t the only ethically questionable host of a World Cup in history: think of Qatar in 2022 and Russia in 2018, and some of us have memories going all the way back to Argentina in 1978 (and we’ve got Saudi Arabia coming up in 2034). But it’s the first to mess with the fabric of the actual sport, and to relegate football to a sideshow, subservient to the gods of commerce and celebrity.

Ultimately, the Super Bowl is theirs. Let them do what they want with that. Football is ours, everyone’s. Here’s hoping, naively, that some future incarnation of Fifa will consign Trump and Infantino’s venal and vulgar innovations to the dustbin. In his own way, Chris Martin has shown us how.

What will Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills mean for you?

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 13:24:58 GMT

New prime minister is implementing immediate tax cut to help ease cost of living pressures for British households

Andy Burnham to cut VAT on electricity bills as first cost of living move

Household electricity bills for people in Great Britain will not attract VAT for six months, under the first of a series of cost of living measures announced by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Normally households pay 5% VAT on their electricity. This is applied once the daily standing charge and cost of the units you have used have been added up, so the actual sum you pay will vary from bill to bill.

From 1 October – the day the regulator Ofgem’s new price cap on energy comes in – there will be no VAT on the electricity you use if you live in Great Britain. This will cover the winter months, which typically bring the highest bills of the year.

Using figures based on a typical household’s energy use, the government says the saving will in effect reduce the annual price cap by £45. Your actual savings will depend on your usage.

In Northern Ireland VAT will remain at 5% because post-Brexit rules mean that EU rates apply. However, the Stormont government will be given money to fund cost of living measures for people living there.

Yes. On a fixed-rate tariff the cost of your standing charge and units are set for a certain period, but your bill still varies according to how much you use, and VAT is still applied at the end. Your provider will treat you as it does customers on a standard tariff.

Not necessarily. If you are not on a fixed-rate tariff then the amount you pay per unit of electricity moves in line with Ofgem’s price cap, and this may rise in October. The latest prediction from the experts at Cornwall Insight is that the cap will increase by 2%, with the war in the Middle East the main reason.

If that is right, you will be paying less than without the VAT cut, but will still end up paying more overall.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) thinktank says that since the start of the Iran war the price of gas has risen much more sharply than the cost of electricity – 24% compared with 5%. “If the goal of today’s policy is to help households that have lost out as a result of the war, it is not well targeted at achieving that aim,” it says.

This is a saving for everyone, but because VAT is charged on how much you use, as well as the standing charge, households with high energy usage will benefit most.

The cut will be good news for people who rely solely on electricity for heating, and those who have other reasons to use a lot of power. It will also be a boost for households who have adopted some green technologies: electric cars will be cheaper to charge and heat pumps cheaper to run.

Adam Scorer, the chief executive of the charity National Energy Action, says: “It will help everyone, but be less useful for the huge majority of low-income households who heat their homes with gas and cannot afford the upfront cost of shifting to solar, batteries and heat pumps. It is not a trivial distinction.”

Camilla Born, the head of the industry-backed campaign group Electrify Britain, said: “By choosing to take VAT off electricity only – rather than gas – it appears that Burnham has finally gotten the memo that the priority is to get Britain using our homegrown clean power. Until we shift to electric heating, driving and manufacturing we will remain exposed to fossil fuel prices.”

The IFS says that relative to household spending, the cut will be most meaningful to the lowest-income households. “On average, the 10% of households with the lowest disposable incomes allocate 5% of their spending to electricity bills, compared with just 2% for the 10% of households with the highest disposable incomes,” it says.

“In cash terms, however, a disproportionate share of the cost of today’s tax cut will go to higher-income households who use more electricity overall despite it making up a smaller share of their spending.”

Charities say that while the VAT cut is helpful, the government should be looking at the problems faced by people who are already behind with their bills. Energy debt is at a record high, according to the industry trade association Energy UK, which says households owe a total of £5.5bn to providers.

National Debtline says energy is the second most common debt its advisers hear about, and that on average people contacting it owe £2,575 to their providers. A debt relief scheme that would allow suppliers to write off some outstanding bills has been proposed and consulted on by Ofgem, but is not in place.

Steve Vaid, the chief executive of the Money Advice Trust, the charity that runs National Debtline, says: “Ministers should move ahead with the scheme now to provide urgent respite for people who’ve built up energy debts through no fault of their own.

“With nearly half (46%) of the people we support at National Debtline not having enough money to even cover their essential bills, it is clear households desperately need support with the cost of living, support to build financial resilience, and increased access to advice to help them find a way forward.”

Andrew Sissons, a director at the thinktank Nesta, which has advised the new government on energy policy, said that while the VAT relief would help during the colder months, November’s budget “would be the right opportunity for the new chancellor to set out a wider and more long-term set of reforms to reduce electricity costs”.

Nesta has put forward a more detailed plan, which would change the way household gas is charged and remove some policy levies from bills – at a cost of £3.2bn a year to the taxpayer – and would shave £130 off average bills.

Industry has warned that businesses will need help, too. The VAT relief will not apply to most businesses, aside from small companies and charities, so will do little to stem the economic contagion of higher energy costs, which has inflated the price of everyday goods.

Tebas believes Infantino should resign, although he admits he finds it hard to envisage such a scenario. “He has the support of the system, of the federations. There is no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. It is a system rotten at its core.”

Football, golf … behold the future of world sport: Donald Trump as referee-in-chief

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 12:15:11 GMT

After his dubious intervention at the World Cup, the president is now an arbiter of high-level fairway disputes. There’s one word for that: SAD!

For so many of us around the world, the final scenes of the World Cup were a chance to switch off the TV with an eye-roll and observe mildly: “Well, I think that’s quite enough America for us all for a while now.” And yet: there can and must always be more. It is simply the way of things. If you thought the World Cup being carried on to the pitch ahead of Sunday’s final in some kind of Louis Vuitton sex trunk was the nadir of hysterical trashiness in sport, then simply recall the lesson of the past few years and expand your mind. It can always get trashier.

To the parched fairways of Royal Birkdale, then, the host of this year’s Open Championship, which – yesssssss! – was won by someone other than Bryson DeChambeau or Scottie Scheffler or any of the other radioactively ghastly US golfers you’d cheerfully head-flush in a Mar-a-Lago loo just as long as you could clear the classified documents out of it first. It has now been revealed that, during his heated row over a two-shot penalty he was handed for improving the area for his backswing, DeChambeau has been accused of threatening to call the US president unless it was all resolved in his favour. To repeat: threatening to call Donald Trump.

If you missed this, DeChambeau picked up the penalty for improving the line of his swing, apparently having trodden down some long grass close to his ball on the fifth hole during the second round last Friday. He publicly lost his mind about it, demanded to be driven back to the scene with officials, then returned to the tournament scoring area and reportedly threatened to call Trump. Has a new portal to the dark side opened in sport? Given Trump’s known intervention in the World Cup (of which more shortly), who among us would bet against it?

At time of writing, I had read everything about this sensational escalation, but I still don’t know nearly enough about it. I need every detail. I need everyone involved to reconstruct the entire conversation. I want to know exactly how quickly you might go from “no way did I do any gardening” to “fuck you – patch in the president”. This is a new era of American pant-wetting and I need to understand absolutely everything about its conventions.

Certainly, all I already thought about Bryson DeChambeau has been magnified. If you’re unfamiliar with his work, as well as being a two-time US Open champion, Bryson is a hardcore Mar-a-Lago steak-gobbler who got a shout-out in Trump’s 2024 election victory address, though that was delivered at the Palm Beach Convention Center and not at the latter’s Floridian golf-club residence. (Even so, every time we see those words, the hilarity should strike us anew. The president of the United States of America lives in a golf club. Honestly: I just CAN’T.) Anyway, in the small hours after his victory over Kamala Harris, Trump was very keen to pluck DeChambeau from the sliders queue or the ormolu urinals or wherever and get him up on stage. “Bryson DeChambeau is up here somewhere,” Trump told the cameras. “What happened to Bryson? Where is he? Bryson! He’s hitting balls. He’s on the way?” Eventually, DeChambeau realised there was nothing for it but to climb awkwardly on to the stage.

And yet, where is your orange god now, Bryson? Where was he on Friday, as you seemingly failed to summon him to a faraway British links course having been observed doing a bit of landscaping?

There seems, at present, to be no evidence that Bryson put the call in, and since he flaked out of all media appearances for the tournament, no one has been able to ask if he contacted the president in any other way. We understand, however, that he asked for Trump to be called. Sad. Perhaps the only thing worse than demanding that the president be called over you dicking around with the grass is not having the president called over you dicking around with the grass. And then realising that, in many ways, you got less off Trump than some guy called Folarin Balogun who plays a sport called … hang on, let me get my lorgnette … “soccer”. That would be a lot of perspective for Bryson to absorb on a Friday lunchtime.

The maddest thing about the entire revelation is what it says about how comically debased and politicised sport has been in such short order. Because the thing is, you can totally see it. You can genuinely imagine that the only situation room Trump wouldn’t lose focus in after about 10 minutes is one where he was required to cheat remotely at golf. You can just picture him assembling Pete Hegseth and Marco Rubio and all the other guys with the too-big shoes in the White House situation room, and them huddling round a feed like the photo of the Obama administration watching the Seal team raid that got Osama bin Laden. Only this one is coming from a grass-level camera at Royal Birkdale.
