Entangled and Woven review – exquisitely spun textiles that cross borders, culture and time

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 12:04:08 GMT

The Whitworth, ManchesterManchester’s past as a centre of textile production forms the starting point of this seamless showcase of skills

How many hands did it take to make this show? That is to say, how many artisans, craftspeople, weavers and artists’ hands did these pieces pass through? For this is a textile exhibition that doesn’t just celebrate a short list of singular artists, but rather the many highly skilled craftspeople and communities repeating the stitches and specialities of their ancestors. Take Entangled Memories, Interwoven Stories by Péro for example: it was made by 50 artisans and took 18,000 hours to complete. And that’s one piece, in an exhibition that spans three galleries.

These many hands and hours make Entangled and Woven an exquisitely beautiful exhibition. Every slip of fabric is layered with delicate detail and texture. Fabrics are airy and ethereal one moment, and weighty and dipped in deep indigo the next. It is hot, the fabrics sway and flicker in the fans, and hands flicker quickly in the video works capturing the creation of the pieces. I am mesmerised.

What elevates this show from “it looks good” to “it’s great” is the fact it is also a true cultural exchange. The authentic type, where the artists have met in person, have visited each other’s countries, and have made brand new works in response to these research trips. The exhibition draws together eight artists and collectives from Korea and India, inviting them to incorporate new techniques into their own practices, creating something new that crosses borders, culture and time.

The Whitworth holds around 20,000 textiles from across the globe, and for this show it presents several historic Indian and Korean works, some dating back to the 18th century. They are carefully placed around the gallery, sometimes mirroring the new works and other times educating us on technique. It is hard for these pieces – primarily flat on the wall in frames – to command presence alongside the impactful contemporary installations, but they serve as a good historical reference point and a link to Manchester’s past as a centre of textile production.

In the middle of the first gallery is Gilded Veil_A Mysterious Curtain Lightly Draped in Gold by Jounghye Yoo. Suspended from a wooden frame in the ceiling is a tunnel of fabric sheets fading from indigo to red, bursting into glorious gold in the centre and back to red and finally indigo again. Inspired by the gate of the Kashi Vishwanath Temple in Varanasi, the shape of the sheer sheets is palatial, and as I wander through them they adjust slightly in the air, cocooning me in a surreal world drenched in colour.

The work was made in collaboration with Dr Ismail Mohammad Khatri, a master of ajrakh block printing from Gujarat, and his son, Juned Ismail. Ajrakh motifs dance with Korean embroidery using gold thread, and Indian cotton sits with Korean silk creating a work that effortlessly blends varied skills and collapses the separation between heritage, culture and artists – even between my body and the gallery space as I disappear into this veiled passage.

Connection abounds between the artists themselves in the next gallery where Somi Ko, Young In Hong and fashion brand and cultural practice Péro play with weight, fragmentation, animals and teeny-tiny mirrors. Somi Ko’s People of One, Moment is a series of figures on Indian cotton made using traditional Indian mirror work. As I draw closer to the dancing bodies, I see shards of my own reflection split and shatter across the gallery, releasing me from my fleshy form.

At the other end of the gallery, Young In Hong integrates this mirror work into Sacred Empires, a series of ornate flags produced in collaboration with Kala Raksha, a grassroots artisan collective in Kutch, home to seven minority craft communities. In Indian folk belief, the small reflective mirrors are seen as ritualistic devices that ward off evil spirits and mediate divine presence.

The divine – or the spiritual realm – is also very present in the third gallery where Kaimurai, Sumakshi Singh and Yeonsoon Chang make the unseen seen. Singh crafts an ethereal, floating bridge to highlight links between Korea, India and the UK. She embroiders on water-soluble fabric so when the base is dissolved, all that is left is a delicate web of threads, glowing against the deep blue walls in the gallery.

Kaimurai makes visible the process of meditation through stepped khadi sheets that reach upwards toward the spiritual realm. A combination of sculpture and painting, Kaimurai’s work is arresting and intriguing. Beginning with a bell hung over a hefty granite sphere, his sheets of khadi rise up in stages, each with a graduating splash of indigo that gets smaller and smaller as if reality were receding.

Meanwhile, Chang ponders on the Buddhist concept of Worincheongang, which means “the moon reflected on a thousand rivers”. Her glowing structural pieces, dyed in indigo and shimmering as if possessing a divine power, enhance this sensation of togetherness both with the spiritual realm and the communities that dream under the self-same moon.

Back in the main gallery, a mythical creature by Boito is made through the mingling of skills from across the Indian state of Odisha. A papier-mache chest comes from Raghurajpur; ringa textile and beads from Malkangiri; cane craft from Talabasta – the list goes on. It is an unusual creature, with a chicken’s head, elephant’s leg, human’s arm and camel’s hump, each boasting a different fabric and way of making. It is also the perfect symbol of what has happened – joyously – in Entangled and Woven: cultures combining to make the most striking works of art.

Hyundai Translocal Series: Entangled and Woven is at the Whitworth, Manchester until 3 January 2027

What the EU wants from Andy Burnham

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 11:31:25 GMT

European leaders have made positive noises about the new UK PM, but he is likely to face the same restrictions as Starmer

UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham is unknown in Brussels, but that will soon change. In his schedule for the autumn is an EU-UK summit that may underscore the same dilemmas that have confronted previous British prime ministers in the relationship with Europe.

EU leaders were quick to offer congratulations to Britain’s prime minister, the seventh since the 2016 Brexit referendum. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to strengthening the EU-UK partnership “for the security of our shared continent” and “the prosperity of people on both sides of the Channel”. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, invited Burnham to visit Berlin “very soon”, noting that the UK and Germany’s “deep connection is particularly evident in these times”.

Georg Riekeles, a former adviser on the commission’s Brexit taskforce, told the Guardian: “People don’t know what to expect. But he also starts with a blank sheet of paper … and that can be an advantage.”

The main concern, said Riekeles, who is now an associate director at the European Policy Centre, was whether Burnham would be “on the same trajectory” in terms of defence and security cooperation, energy and the “very positive agenda” on economic issues.

One EU diplomat observed: “For a British prime minister it is not necessarily a bad thing to be little known. If you are well known it is probably because you were prominent on one side or the other of the Brexit debate.”

Burnham’s most notable statement on the EU was his wish to see Britain rejoin in his lifetime, while speaking to the Guardian at the Labour party conference in September 2025. But during campaigning in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield, he made it clear reversing Brexit was not a priority, because “Britain would be stuck in a permanent rut if we are just constantly arguing”.

Michael Jacobs, who advised the former prime minister Gordon Brown, said Burnham’s statement on rejoining “felt like it was from the heart” but was also politically astute. “It tells pro-Europeans that he is one of them. But it tells leave voters that it’s not his political priority for now, and he is not going to relitigate the Brexit arguments.”

Among the first calls Burnham had after entering No 10 were with von der Leyen, Merz and the French leader, Emmanuel Macron.

He has appointed Hamish Falconer as the Europe minister, replacing Nick Thomas-Symonds. The latter’s departure is a blow to the UK-EU reset talks started by Starmer, but some claimed they had lost momentum and Falconer would bring fresh energy. One of his first calls after being appointed was to the European trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič.

Elected as an MP in 2024, Falconer brings a wealth of international experience, with a decade spent in the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a stint in the National Crime Agency, and a career dealing with international terrorism, hostage recovery and countering human trafficking.

He served as Middle East minister under Starmer.

The return of Johnny Reynolds, as business secretary, will help in talks aimed at protecting European trade from China, and tricky negotiations to scrap an upcoming 10% tariff on exports of British cars to the EU and vice versa.

Under Starmer, the UK and EU signed a security and defence pact and cooperated closely on Ukraine. Despite failing to agree British participation in a €150bn EU defence loans scheme, the two sides moved on. In Starmer’s final week in office the UK signed an agreement to participate in the EU’s €90bn (£77bn) loan for Ukraine, meaning British companies can provide more weapons funded through the scheme.

Now Burnham inherits the reset agenda launched by Starmer. The two sides are due to sign a trio of agreements at the summit: a deal to reduce paperwork and certification for fresh food in an effort to ease trade barriers for British exporters; linking emissions trading systems; and a youth exchange scheme enabling 18- to 30-year-olds to work, study, travel and volunteer in the EU and UK.

Ireland’s Europe minister, Thomas Byrne, told reporters this month that he expected “positive continuity, at the very least”.

Ireland, which holds the EU Council’s rotating presidency until the end of the year, will be involved in the diplomatic preparations for the summit, the date of which is yet to be decided. “There are tricky issues there, and I think we can get them over the line,” Byrne said.

Talks have been deadlocked over the youth mobility agreement. EU member states think the UK’s proposed cap of 50,000 youth visas is too low and they oppose their nationals paying the NHS surcharge and higher rate of tuition fees for foreign students. But Some diplomats see a middle ground whereby EU students get a discount on foreign fees but pay above the domestic rate.

Jacobs suggested Burnham may raise the cap on numbers. “The idea that leave voters regard such a scheme as a form of immigration was always slightly absurd, and I think Burnham will see that as a relatively easy win to offer pro-Europeans.”

But when it comes to the UK-EU economic relationship, Burnham will face the same constraints as Starmer.

Earlier this year the EU rejected an attempt by Starmer to negotiate a single market for goods, minus the free movement of people. EU member states suggested the UK could join the European Economic Area, but that would require accepting the free movement of people and making payments to the EU budget with no voting rights in shaping new EU rules.

Jacobs said: “Given Burnham’s sensitivity to the immigration concerns of his own Makerfield voters, and of many others, the idea that he would seek to re-enter the single market by allowing free movement and making a massive financial payment to the EU budget (which is what the EU would demand) seems implausible.

“On the substantive issues, I think he will do pretty much what Starmer has been trying to do with the so-called ‘reset’, and he will come up against the same barriers in Brussels.”

Only four years to the next men’s World Cup – what can we expect from the 2030 edition?

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 10:23:46 GMT

If you thought the 2026 tournament was sprawling, think again with six host countries over three continents getting involved in four years’ time

If the 2026 World Cup was the tournament’s largest edition yet – featuring 48 teams for the first time in its 96-year history, being played in three different countries – the 2030 World Cup is going to have an even bigger footprint.

Technically three. The tournament is set to be jointly hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain, marking the first time the World Cup will be held in more than one confederation and the first time it will visit north Africa.

In addition, though, and in honour of the World Cup’s 100-year anniversary, a special match is scheduled to be held at Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, Uruguay – the stadium that hosted the 1930 World Cup final. There will also be one match each in Argentina and Paraguay.

The bidding process for the 2030 World Cup began in earnest in 2022, with the host to be officially selected at the 2024 Fifa congress. The governing body’s rules for rotating the tournament between continents meant that football federations from Asia (AFC) and North America (Concacaf) were ineligible to host following the Qatar 2022 and North America 2026 bids respectively.

Uefa federations Spain and Portugal – unsuccessful in 2018 and 2022 and ineligible in 2026 – added Morocco to their joint bid in 2023. That same year, Conmebol federations Uruguay, Argentina, Paraguay and Chile launched their joint bid, with a proposed tournament name of “Centenary World Cup”.

In October 2023, the Fifa council unanimously selected the Morocco-Portugal-Spain bid over the South American bid.

The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, announced that Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay would host one match each to celebrate the centenary of the World Cup “in the most appropriate way”. Uruguay hosted – and won – the tournament’s inaugural edition with Argentina beaten 4-2 in the final. A game will also be played in Paraguay in recognition of the country’s role as the home of Conmebol, the only confederation in existence in 1930.

Fifa has also announced “a unique centenary celebration ceremony”, scheduled to take place in Montevideo the week before the tournament begins on 13 June 2030.

Initially the idea was for it to be 48 teams again, but during this World Cup Infantino raised to prospect of it being expanded with a further 16 nations.

“That’s definitely ​an issue that will be examined and discussed in the relevant committees after this World Cup,” Infantino said. “When organising ⁠a World Cup, it’s important to organise it for the whole world – not just Europe and South America – but effectively the ⁠entire world.

An expansion had already been suggested in 2025 when the Conmebol president, Alejandro Domínguez, put forth an official proposal to expand the number of participating teams to 64 in honour of the tournament’s centennial. “[It] will be unique because 100 years are celebrated only once,” Domínguez said.

after newsletter promotion

Spain last hosted the World Cup in 1982, the final of which involved Italy defeating West Germany in the Bernabéu. Co-hosts Portugal and Morocco have hosted various major sporting events, among them the 2004 Euros and the 2025 Afcon.

The 2030 World Cup will take place across 17 host cities – one more than the 2026 edition – with 11 of the proposed 20 stadiums located in Spain. Among the 17 host cities are Marrakech and Tangier in Morocco, Porto and Lisbon in Portugal and Barcelona, Madrid and San Sebastián in Spain.

Without a doubt the inclusion of the centenary match hosts. By rejecting the South American host bid but declaring that Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay would host one match each Fifa ensured that Conmebol would be ineligible to bid for the 2034 World Cup with Asia and Oceania the only two continents able to host. (The 2034 edition has since been awarded to Saudi Arabia, a decision that has been heavily criticised by human rights groups).

Well, who knows? After the shenanigans of Donald Trump’s intervention and Folarin Balogun’s red card being suspended, could we see the Spanish king, Felipe VI, get involved after an over-zealous Lamine Yamal tackle in the last 64? With these guys in charge, nothing is off the table.

My stepmother compliments everything I do – and my ego is getting out of control

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 10:00:43 GMT

She praises me whether I’m heaving a plant pot into the air or pairing a phone to a Bluetooth speaker. It’s enough to make me start believing I am, in fact, quite magical

After about five minutes of my stepmother’s company, I’m always in a good mood. It’s not because of our beautiful harmony, though please think that too if it makes me sound good. In her 80s, and feeling the ravages of time ever so slightly, she makes a constant litany of benevolently envious remarks. There’s a lot of general observation about the condition of being me, and how fabulous that must be: “Oh to be 50 again”; “It must be wonderful to have an appetite”; “I wish I could still sleep in”. Ordinarily I don’t give much thought to the singular pleasures of human maintenance activities – eating, sleeping, having a shower – and when you really look at it, it isn’t a bad life, to be 52.

Then she’ll move on to admire my particular skills: “Look at that!”; “What?”; “Look how fast you got out of the car.” It’s a fact, I’m incredibly good at this: I don’t grunt while I’m doing it; it doesn’t take 17 minutes. I’m pretty good at all sitting to standing manoeuvres. “That’s nothing,” I think. “You should see me get out of a squat.”

Pairing a phone to a Bluetooth speaker; getting a printer to work; rewinding live radio; for these acts and more, I am basically Clive Sinclair. Strength-based activities, mainly unscrewing lids, picking things up and putting them somewhere else, unleash a torrent of enjoyable plaudits. Sometimes I’ll heave a plant pot into the air and set it down again nicely, just showing off. Today I opened her front door, which is a bit stiff, by kicking it and she simply said: “Marvellous”. I can keep my ego in check for as long as a lunch, but if we spend a couple of days together, I basically think I’m magic.

Sometimes my stepmother will think I can do something that I cannot – read a menu without glasses, remember the name of a person we were just talking about – and because she’s only human and schadenfreude never gets old, that puts her in a good mood. So that makes two of us.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

‘A big job ahead of him’: world leaders congratulate Andy Burnham as he becomes Britain’s PM

Beyond the diplomatic platitudes global media focuses on the ‘immense’ scale of the challenge he faces in the job

UK politics live – latest updates

World leaders have warmly congratulated Andy Burnham on his entry into 10 Downing Street as Britain’s seventh prime minister in a decade, but international media largely focused on the scale of the challenges awaiting him.

Emmanuel Macron, France’s president, said he hoped for a deeper relationship “in the service of our peoples, and by giving new momentum to the partnership between the UK and the EU” rekindled by Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who spoke with Burnham on Monday evening including about continued support for Ukraine, said Germany and the UK were close partners and he looked forward to working together.

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to “strengthening the EU-UK partnership”. A “very good first discussion” had revealed a common commitment to “bringing the EU and UK closer and closer”, she later added.

Beyond the diplomatic platitudes, however, media coverage focused on Burnham’s regional persona – and the huge task awaiting him. France’s Public Sénat said the new prime minister came from “the working class of the north of England”.

He had managed to “build an image as an ‘everyman’, appearing without a tie, very often in a T-shirt”, the political TV channel said on its website, standing out as “a politician on the ground, close to everyday concerns”.

Italy’s Corriere della Sera said the UK was experiencing “profound unease, instability and social resentment” and “needs a push” forward, but Burnham’s nationalisation, state intervention and reindustrialisation plans suggested he saw the past as a model.

The UK “appears incapable of imagining and planning for the future and prefers to take refuge in a backward-looking Eden”, it argued, even though the pre-Thatcher years were marked by “energy rationing, rubbish in the streets and IMF bailouts”.

The Irish Times noted that Burnham may be “a breath of fresh air” but the challenges that brought down Starmer – “a budget unable to meet desperately needed demand in defence, housing, welfare, care for the aged, and training for the young” – remained.

The new prime minister, the paper said, would be “hamstrung by a commitment to abide by strict fiscal rules. His instinct may be to tack to the left, but he is already trying to prove that … he will govern from the centre” and the job was “immense”.

In an New York Times essay titled The King of the North Won’t Save Britain, Tom Hazeldine said that with his “northern accent, casual attire and everyman persona”, Burnham “trades on his outsider status, a precious commodity in antipolitical times”.

But, Hazeldine added, a UK that had wanted “a bounce” after Starmer had actually ended up with – in the absence of anything better – “a career Blairite with a northern soul and a Whitehall brain. For the country, it looks a lot like more of the same.”

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, wished Burnham “a successful tenure”, adding that Italy and the UK were “bound by a deep friendship and a collaboration that, over the years, has grown ever stronger” and she was sure would continue.

Outside the EU, Donald Trump, who had previously described Burnham as “the mayor of a town” and “extremely liberal”, said on Monday night the two had had a “very good conversation” on topics including North Sea oil.

“The Prime Minister has got a big job ahead of him, but he will be able to do it and, of course, the U. S. A. will be there to help!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “The call was interesting, and went very well. I wished Prime Minister Burnham, GOOD LUCK AND GODSPEED!”

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, described the UK as “one of the global leaders”, adding that the two countries’ relationship was “stronger than ever and Kyiv stood “ready to work together in all possible formats”.

Anthony Albanese, the Australian prime minister, said Australia and the UK were “longstanding friends” bound by “deep ties”. He looked forward to strengthening the partnership and promoting “security, resilience and prosperity in the years ahead”.

Andy Burnham promised urgent action on the cost of living – the heat is now on chancellor John Healey to deliver it

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 09:04:20 GMT

The PM and the new boss at the Treasury face an even trickier task than their predecessors. They need a good plan, and we have one

Alfie Stirling is an economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation

As Keir Starmer found, it takes more than words alone to warm a tepid bath. Voters reserve the greatest punishment for the politicians they think acted too little, or too late, to prevent them getting poorer. For Andy Burnham, much will now depend on whether he has got the right ideas, and in John Healey the right chancellor, to address Britain’s growing affordability crisis: not least as the new prime minister sets out new measures today to give people “some breathing space”.

Before Rachel Reeves took office, the average family was set to be worse off in 2029 than they had been in 2019. That’s not supposed to happen. The norm is for household incomes to rise by about £5,000 (2026 prices) every five years. Never before on modern record have they fallen across an entire decade.

Given the scale of the challenge, the last chancellor ultimately failed to move the dial either far enough or fast enough. That means Healey will inherit essentially the same outlook for living standards as Reeves did. Only this time, there is next to no time to prepare, and he will have barely half as much time to act – before having to defend his record at the ballot box.

To make matters worse, the economic situation is even more complicated now too. Household and business spending is drying up, and crying out for replenishment through interest rate cuts or government support. But at the same time, inflation and borrowing costs are already elevated, just as fresh price pressures from the conflict in Iran start to penetrate supply chains.

So if anything, the Bank of England is more likely to raise interest rates higher – and reduce economy-wide spending further – than it is to cut them. Any government that intervenes too clumsily in support of living standards now risks even higher borrowing costs for itself, families and firms.

It’s hard to overstate the seriousness of this triple bind faced by the new chancellor: a politically non-survivable outlook for household incomes, little time to respond and a “natural” macroeconomic trap, where a wrong move could only make things worse.

The key problem to solve is how to provide the right support for families now, without provoking higher interest rates. The answer: lower inflation directly by pushing down on essential prices, especially for low- and middle-income families; and pay for it with slightly higher tax contributions, or a small amount of foregone profit from investment income such as capital gains, dividends and rents.

Take two examples: energy and renting a home. On the first, today’s temporary VAT cut on electricity is a good signal of intent, but the government will need to upgrade again soon. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation has recommended an “affordable energy guarantee” that reforms the Ofgem pricing system to provide a basic portion of cheaper energy for everyone – with larger portions for those with lower incomes or greater energy needs.

Energy support of this kind could replace the less well-targeted VAT cut in future years, but retain a focus on electricity to support net zero transition. It can be designed to fit a range of price tags for government, and the revenue could be raised by closing the gap in tax treatment between capital gains (and other forms of investment income) and earnings from work – thus ending the current unfairness whereby a quarter of people with incomes above £10m year pay a lower effective rate of tax than the average employee.

On the second – renting a home – government should intervene to slow the growth in rents nationally, while allowing mayors to opt out or go further so measures can be tailored for local housing markets. This should be accompanied by a rebalancing of landlord taxation that allows mortgaged landlords to fully tax-deduct their interest costs, paid for by charging national insurance on any remaining income instead.

Because mortgaged landlords typically have far lower profits than those who own outright, the latest evidence shows that the combination of rent controls and tax reform of this kind could actually reduce the number of landlords in financial distress overall. This is important for maintaining house prices and the supply of new development into the market, which has been the traditional concern with rent controls.

New modelling shows how a package built around proposals such as those above (on energy, rents and tax) could return real incomes to growth for a majority of households – more than making up for both the fall in incomes from the last parliament and the anticipated effects from conflict in the Middle East as well. These measures could also reduce inflation by half a percentage point, easing pressure for higher interest rates.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

There is also good – albeit often overlooked – evidence that improving household economic security in this way helps to drive longer-term economic growth as well. When people are more financially secure, they are both more productive at work today and more likely to risk the move to a better job tomorrow.

Of course, considerable challenges remain. Healey will need to sort the wheat from the chaff from a plethora of competing demands, and the noise from those losing out from tax reform will need to be managed too. Ultimately Burnham is right to make “breathing space” from the cost of living his early priority. The question is whether, and by when, Healey can deliver it. Voters were promised a “change” chancellor once already – both they, and the new prime minister, really need one now.

Alfie Stirling is an economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation

The Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilers

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 09:00:07 GMT

Inside all the blink-and-you-miss-it moments, subtle easter eggs and poignant takeaways from Christopher Nolan’s ancient epic

This article contains spoilers for The Odyssey

The Odyssey looks set to be the blockbuster hit of the summer, with global opening weekend grosses of $264m, critical rave reviews including five stars from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, and reports of fans traversing continents to experience Christopher Nolan’s epic tale of gods and monsters in one of the few dozen screens worldwide with the capability to screen Imax in 70mm. It also has the potential to rule the box office for the coming weeks, with few other true blockbusters to be released this summer, with the exception of Spider-Man: Brand New Day (hence the cast’s humiliation ritual of a press tour). Read on for a spoiler-packed breakdown of the epic battles, narrative twists and out-of-nowhere cameos that bring richness to Nolan’s idiosyncratic vision of ancient life.

After Oppenheimer won best picture at the 2024 Oscars, Nolan knew he had a once-in-a-lifetime chance to realize a decades-long dream of bringing Homer to the big screen. “OK, I’ve now got an opportunity to make a film I wouldn’t be able to make otherwise,” he recently told the Guardian. You can see every penny of The Odyssey’s reported $250m budget on screen. The landscapes of Ithaca are breathtakingly beautiful, and there’s a creepy pall to our hero’s journey to the underworld that Nolan achieved by shooting on the black sands of Iceland’s beaches under the hazy light of the midnight sun. (Fun fact: Nolan also used Icelandic glaciers as the backdrop for the alien planet of Interstellar.)

Nolan filmed in six countries to achieve the range of landscapes in the film, which also included Scotland, Greece, Italy and Malta, and, more controversially, Western Sahara. Controlled by Morocco, the region is often referred to as Africa’s last colony, with the UN classifying it as a non-decolonized territory. “Audiences coming to see The Odyssey deserve better,” the artist and writer Mohamed Sleiman Labat wrote in an essay for the Guardian. “Those cinematic shots sold to them as the places and moments where historical epics took place were captured at the expense of the Sahrawi people’s suffering.”

The film’s epic scenes in the Mediterranean were filmed in the ocean, with Nolan eschewing CGI in favor of real roiling seas and Odysseus and his crew aboard the only functional Viking ship in the world (the delightfully named Draken Harald Hårfagre). A replica of the boat was built for scenes shot in a colossal water tank on the Universal lot. “There were these two jet engines, like 737 engines, blowing water on us,” Damon has said. “It was definitely about as hard as you can make water work in a controlled environment.”

Nolan has been a champion of Imax for two decades: in 2008, The Dark Knight was the first major Hollywood film to use the cameras for its action sequences. The camera set-up has been used increasingly prominently in his films since then. Nolan used half a dozen Imax cameras to shoot the film, all enclosed in soundproof “blimp” casing to mask their loud operational whirr.

The team also worked with an LED company to create lighting rigs they called “pyrohedrons” (fire pyramids) to give the illusion that warm firelight was casting a glow over interior and night-time scenes. “I wanted the camera to see what the human eye would see,” Nolan told the New York Times.

In Homer’s epic poem, gods are “self-interested beings, whose interventions in human lives are motivated primarily by their own desires, whims, and preferences”, as classicist Emily Wilson put it in her translation. Yet Nolan’s vision of how gods, demi-gods and mortals interact is somewhat earthier than in Homer, with Zendaya’s Athena less of a fearsome divine force than a pal and a confidante to Odysseus.

Charlize Theron is always a treat (even in her ropey Netflix fare), but Nolan’s interpretation of nymph Calypso may not feel strong enough for some viewers to work as a framing device for the bulk of the film. In Homer, the nymph is a cruel enslaver who holds Odysseus captive on her island; Nolan sees the character as lonely and somewhat pitiable. It’s worth wondering what Theron would have done with a spikier version of the role – she excels as a cartoon villain.

Like classicist Emily Hauser, who recently wrote for the Guardian about Nolan’s omissions, some viewers may also miss the Homeric princess Nausicaa. While interacting with Odysseus, she sniffily pooh-poohs him as “an unpromising man” – her barbs would have added a little light relief to the picture.

When Lupita Nyong’o was announced as Helen of Troy – the face that launched a thousand ships – rightwing commentators denounced the casting choice for predictably small-minded reasons. It is ironic that the character is afforded little screen time: when Tom Holland’s Telemachus goes to visit Helen and her husband, Menelaus (Jon Bernthal) in Sparta midway through the film, the famed beauty is near mute, with a grisly scar covering the left side of her face. It’s a bold choice from Nolan, but a little odd that we never find out the cause of her injury.

Odysseus’s loyal wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) is a steely and cunning presence despite the suitors’ invasion of her palace. “We wanted to make sure that she did not look like she was mourning her husband,” said costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, who dressed Hathaway in the red and blue colors of Ithaca. “She was always viewed as the queen.” The actor has likened her character to a slowly simmering volcano that eventually erupts in scenes where she curses the suitors and pushes her double-crossing servant Melantho (Mia Goth) to certain death while the palace is at war.

One of the film’s most memorable scenes sees Odysseus and his men face the sirens, whose alluring song can lure sailors to their death. As their boat approaches their island, Odysseus is tethered to a mast to hear their beautiful yet terrible song while it is muffled to the audience’s ears, as if we, like Odysseus’s first mate Eurylochus (Himesh Patel), have our ears plugged with wax. The sound is “all the things you want it to be, then all the things you wish you never wished for”, says Odysseus, as Nolan powerfully leaves it to the audience’s imagination to fill in the blank.

Some of the film’s most touching moments come from John Leguizamo, barely recognisable with white hair and a dirty smock in the role of Eumaeus, the nearly-blind swineherd that remains loyal to Odysseus to the very end. As Greek military leader Agamemnon, Benny Safdie strikes a fearsome presence in a smart bit of against-type casting from Nolan. Meanwhile, not all cameos were planned: a pod of dolphins who made a surprise appearance on a day of shooting ended up making the film’s final cut.

Yet perhaps most surprising of all is the casting of rapper Travis Scott as a bard storyteller who opens the movie with a story of Odysseus’s heroic exploits at Troy. As he orates, the character pounds his staff on the floor in the tempo of dactylic hexameter (which as every good classicist knows, is the original meter of Homer’s poem). “I cast him because I wanted to nod towards the idea that this story has been handed down as oral poetry, which is analogous to rap,” Nolan said in an interview with Time.

It’s likely far too early to make many accurate predictions about next year’s Oscars, given that many of the awardsiest-seeming films won’t premiere until fall film festivals. But Nolan is one of the Academy’s favorite directors, winning seven out of Oppenheimer’s 13 nominations in 2024 and a respectable three out of eight for Dunkirk a few years prior. The Odyssey seems like a lock for nominations in best picture, best director and most of the craft categories, leaving the acting categories as a toss-up.

There’s no debate about who the male lead of the film is, but there’s all to play for in the supporting categories, with Holland and Robert Pattinson eligible for supporting actor and Zendaya, Nyong’o and Theron potential competitors in the supporting actress category – and Hathaway, if Universal decides not to run her in lead. But I’d personally lean towards Leguizamo for his turn as Eumaeus, and Samantha Morton’s staggering, scene-stealing role as Circe, a witch who turns Odysseus’s men into pigs.

Being something of an outsider to the Hollywood star system hasn’t stopped Morton getting two Oscar nominations to date (for Sweet and Lowdown and In America). With the weight of Nolan’s film behind her, I’ll be gunning for her to go all the way this time.

There’s a good case to be made that The Odyssey’s best sequence is its final 30 minutes, where Odysseus finally makes it back home with the help of Athena and sneaks into his Ithaca palace disguised as a beggar man. After Penelope challenges the men to string his bow – and Odysseus is the only one able to – he throws off his rags and reveals his true identity.

His face-off with the suitors isn’t the merciless slaughter that Homer described – it’s a fair fight with both sides armed – but the suitors, led by Pattinson’s slimy Antinous, are no match for the master of the house. His recapturing of Ithaca is bittersweet, interspersed with flashbacks to the “fires of anarchy and pain” that blazed through Troy as the Greeks sacked the city. There’s no glory in war for Nolan, echoing the sentiments of Dunkirk and Oppenheimer. As Odysseus puts it: “We have broken the fragile bond between men.”

There may be few true winners here, but Nolan’s cap to the story is somewhat more uplifting than Homer’s. Whereas the great poet ended The Odyssey with Odysseus planning “raids” to recoup his lost wealth, Nolan sees a rosier and less grimly mercenary future for Odysseus and Penelope. In a beautiful coast-side scene, the reunited couple embark on a journey west to honor the souls of his fallen men while Telemachus – who may be anywhere between 16 and 22 at this point; Holland certainly doesn’t seem to know – stays to rule over Ithaca.

I was struggling after eight rounds of IVF – then a midwife became my surrogate

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 09:00:05 GMT

Narzny McKinney and her surrogate, Sarah, discuss their experience – and the misconceptions that surround the practice

UK surrogacy law ‘creaking at seams’ as demand rises sharply

After struggling with infertility and eight unsuccessful rounds of IVF, Narzny McKinney had two precious embryos left – her last chance to have biological children. After considering her options, she made the decision to find a surrogate to carry her child for her.

“We were eight years down the line at this point and I just didn’t want to risk anything going wrong,” she said. “It was a tough decision but it was absolutely the right thing to do.”

She and her husband, Roy, signed up to two UK surrogacy agencies, and began attending social events, where prospective parents get the chance to meet potential surrogates.

But soaring demand – due to a rise in infertility as well as older people and gay couples seeking to be parents – meant McKinney and her partner had little luck meeting anyone other than parents in the same position as themselves.

“It’s quite emotionally draining, because obviously you go with high hopes each time. You can probably go to a social most weekends; it takes up a big part of your life,” she said. They also considered going abroad – as a growing number of people in the UK are doing, with agencies reporting bumper demand – but knew it would be logistically difficult.

After two years of waiting, they got a call from the agency, Nappy Endings, to say a surrogate had come up – Sarah Turner, a mother of three and midwife in London, who had always wanted to be a surrogate.

Turner said: “I’d always felt very lucky that I was able to have low-risk pregnancies and have babies without any issue. So I thought I would always really like to help somebody that couldn’t do it as easily as I could. I was very up for it. I did a lot of research. I know myself and I was quite relaxed about it.”

The two couples hit it off instantly, and a short while later, Turner, then aged 41, became pregnant with one of the last two embryos.

From the beginning, Turner tried hard to ensure that McKinney was as involved in the pregnancy as she could be – she bought her a bracelet that would vibrate every time the baby kicked.

“Having had three of my own babies, I can’t even imagine how difficult it must have been for Narzny, trusting another woman to carry her baby for her and not being able to do it herself,” Turner said. “That really got me in the guts, and I just used to sit and think, how must she feel? She has to trust me to do everything right for her.

“So I thought it would be so nice if she could feel the baby move and have that reassurance.”

McKinney said the strong relationship between mother and surrogate was crucial in ensuring the process went well and was comfortable for everyone involved: “We went to all the appointments together. I was really connected.”

After meticulous planning for the birth itself, their best-laid plans went out the window when Sarah gave birth at home so quickly that McKinney and her husband – who lived a 40-minute drive away – weren’t able to make it in time.

“People would say, ‘Oh my God, how do you feel about missing it?’ But I imagine we would have been so stressed and anxious, so it was nice turning up and being told, ‘it’s all done, he’s safe and he’s perfect’,” she said.

Turner admitted the immediate aftermath of the birth was the most difficult part of the whole process for her. “The hormones come into play and you can’t do anything about that. So it was challenging,” she said.

“Your mind knows there shouldn’t be a baby but your body doesn’t. But Narzny McKinney and Roy were perfect; they didn’t just abandon me as soon as they had their baby. They checked in, they sent photos, we visited them. They were really mindful of how I was feeling.”

Now McKinney is enjoying motherhood with one-year-old Zak, and is still regularly meeting up with Turner and her family for catch-ups.

They both agree that some legal reform – along with better education and awareness around how surrogacy works – would have helped their experience run more smoothly. Under current UK laws, the surrogate and their spouse must be listed as the baby’s legal parents until a parental order is completed after birth.

McKinney said she had to visit three different courts to get the parental order to transfer legal parenthood to her and Roy, something which campaigners say should be the case from birth. They also said it took months to get Zak a passport.

“It’s a shame because he’s obviously been ours since day one, but the legal documentation to show that is quite far behind,” she said.

McKinney also said she had come across people who assumed she had deliberately chosen surrogacy due to a reluctance to give birth, or questioned whether she would have the “same bond” with her child.

“You don’t say that to fathers, do you? You wouldn’t say that if we’d adopted our child. You would not find that an acceptable thing to say,” she said.

Turner agreed that more education and acceptance was needed. “Because then people wouldn’t feel like it has to be done behind closed doors or that it’s something to be ashamed of,” she said. “Families can be made in all different ways, and actually it’s lovely that we can all help each other.”

The pair said they didn’t face any negativity about the surrogacy, but they’re aware of some people’s preconceptions and criticisms of the practice.

“I know there are a lot more celebrities doing it now, but for us, it was down to her fertility. It wasn’t just like, ‘Oh I can’t be bothered to carry a pregnancy, I’m going to get someone else to do it’. It was a purely medical thing,” said Sarah. “So nobody had anything negative to say to us about it.”

Turner added that while people have hailed her decision to be a surrogate as an incredible selfless act, she doesn’t think of it in such grandiose terms.

“I’m quite chill about it,” she said. “Everyone says it’s this amazing thing you’ve done. I don’t necessarily even think like that. I’m glad I did it, I’m glad they’ve got their baby and I’m glad they’re a happy family – it’s really lovely to watch them grow.”

‘A guy did a runner in a Jaguar’: the petrol theft scandal – and the garage owner struggling to stop it

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 04:00:10 GMT

Since the start of the Iran war in February, there has been a 23% rise in fuel theft, with more than £1.2m stolen from British forecourts each week. Why aren’t the police doing more to apprehend the culprits?

A petrol station tucked away in the suburbs of Birmingham seems an unlikely place for a crime spree. But this garage has become a prime target for thieves. Some fuel runners are easy to spot, approaching the petrol pumps in face masks, but after a recent spate of fill-and-dashes by less conspicuous drivers, no motorist is beyond suspicion. “It could be anyone,” says Shailesh Parekh, who is on high alert, as always.

The 62-year-old owns six forecourts across Birmingham, and today I’m visiting his station in Erdington, a residential area about five miles from the city centre. Parekh remembers a time when a motorist speeding off with an unpaid-for tank was rare. So much so, it would be the talk of the station for months. Those days are long gone. Now, it’s a weekly and sometimes daily occurrence. “In the last three years, it’s been very bad,” Parekh tells me from the back office, where a monitor beams CCTV images from every inch of the forecourt.

Thefts have grown worse since the start of the war in Iran in February. In the first week of July, the station saw three fuel runners, and in June, 12 people drove off without paying. Across his six garages, says Parekh, fuel theft cost him more than £40,000 last year, and predicting who will drive off is becoming impossible.

In his experience, fuel theft used to be carried out by organised thieves or criminals on the lam, who might have stolen a car. Not now. “I had a guy all suited and booted do a runner in a Jaguar,” he says. Sometimes, thieves will wear hi-vis jackets to impersonate workmen. The day before my visit, at another of his forecourts, a man who “looked like a farmer” filled up his tank with £140 worth of petrol and “buggered off”. Parekh says thieves are becoming casually audacious. “They come right in front of you, because they have no fear.”

The issue isn’t confined to Parekh’s garages. Petrol stations have seen a 23% rise in fuel theft since the start of the Iran war, with incidents soaring from 9,089 in January and February to 11,170 in March and April, according to Forecourt Eye, a company that collects payments on behalf of about 1,000 garages around the UK. The Times estimates that more than £1.2m of fuel is being stolen from forecourts each week. Gordon Balmer, executive director of the Petrol Retailers Association, a trade body representing forecourts, says “first-time offenders” are becoming more common, with many “trying it on” due to a “combination of rising household costs and a bit of opportunism”.

The soaring levels of theft come amid rising fuel prices, which have shot up after the successive crises of Covid-19, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war. According to the RAC, prices reached a high of 199.09p for a litre of diesel in 2022, before subsiding again. From mid-February to June 2026, the cost of petrol rose from 131p to 155p per litre, while the cost of diesel rose from 141p to 176p per litre. This means that filling a 60L tank with petrol went from £79 to £93, while filling it with diesel rose from £85 to £106.

Parekh’s forecourts are fitted with “more CCTV cameras than Birmingham airport,” he jokes, but pursuing a fuel thief is usually pointless. “Half of the runners, we don’t even report them. It’s such a mission,” he says.

With CCTV footage and a licence plate number, catching the thieves should be easy, but in reality failing to pay for fuel ends up in a legal grey zone. While intentionally driving off without paying for fuel is a criminal offence, convictions are rare, especially for one-off offenders. If a motorist drives off by mistake or discovers after filling up that they cannot pay, the unpaid amount is generally treated as a civil debt rather than a criminal offence. Unless it’s pretty blatant, it’s difficult to prove that a motorist didn’t drive off in error. And if a driver has filled up and then can’t make the payment, it’s up to the forecourt owner to do what they can to recover the amount. Still, bilkers who are caught and prosecuted face up to two years in prison and a fine. One prolific fuel thief in Kent was jailed for 16 months after pleading guilty to stealing fuel from nine forecourts in 2024.

Not all the thieves Parekh encounters dash off after filling their tanks. Some use the pump, then come in and declare themselves penniless, leaving him with few options, because “we can’t retrieve our fuel from their tank”. Balmer says a lot of first-time offenders are doing this, because many “see it like a payday loan”. Regardless of how unpaid fuel is taken from his forecourt, Parekh says when he has reported incidents to the police, they often tell him “it’s a civil thing”. This is something Balmer has encountered too. Another station he is in contact with reported an intentional drive-off to police, who incorrectly told them it was a civil offence and there was nothing they could do.

In November 2024, Supt Fran Harrod, a senior Lincolnshire police officer, told the BBC that somebody who has driven off without paying for fuel might not be “having a great day” and the incidents don’t always constitute a crime. She recommended that forecourt owners try to recover money through a civil route instead of “using huge amounts of officer hours to go round and ask people to pay up, because the police’s time isn’t free either”. Parekh says this approach adds insult to injury: “You can’t go into Asda and say, ‘I’m leaving with this trolley full of items but I’ve got no money to pay for it.’”

In March this year, the Times reported freedom of information data first revealed by the Forecourt Trader website. It found that in 2024, five police forces across the UK closed a fuel theft investigation without identifying a suspect in nine out of 10 cases.

West Midlands police, the force Parekh deals with, did not respond to the Times, but a 2022 freedom of information request revealed that, of the 1,150 reports of “people driving off without paying for fuel” between January and March 2022, 1,126 (98%) had a recorded outcome indicating that no further action was taken. Of these, 1,106 involved no identified suspect and 20 involved an identified suspect; the outcomes of the remaining 24 reports were left “blank”. Parekh says officers “take the view that this is a totally preventable crime”, telling him he should install prepaid pumps to stop thefts. This, he says, is a non-starter because “the whole trade has to move to that system, otherwise people will get annoyed and go elsewhere”.

West Midlands police say it investigates reports of “bilking, and people need to be clear that driving off without paying for fuel is theft and the consequences are very serious”, adding it would “encourage businesses to take steps to minimise the likelihood of them becoming a victim – such as operating a prepay policy and installing good-quality CCTV”.

Balmer says he has also faced police indifference. He recalls one incident in which “two guys broke into a forecourt, filled up with fuel and filmed it all for TikTok”. Despite this incident being raised with the relevant police force, the culprits weren’t brought to court because police “didn’t think it was something that they should criminalise them for”, says Balmer. “Even though they had committed a crime.”

Parekh has faced similar challenges with getting police to take this crime seriously, including an instance on his forecourt that turned violent. One of his cashiers approached a van driver who he suspected of stealing fuel and stood in front of the vehicle to stop it driving off. The van began advancing towards the cashier, and a tyre went over his foot; luckily he managed to escape with only bruises. A customer helped track down the perpetrator, and the incident was reported to the police. There was also CCTV footage of the vehicular assault. “I pursued the police for 14 months,” says Parekh. “They didn’t go and arrest that man – they didn’t do anything. In the end, I left it.” The West Midlands force says it “won’t tolerate any type of theft” and will “always seek to identify, detain and pursue prosecution against anybody involved in theft offences”.

Parekh recalls one time when police did act. Officers were grabbing a coffee from the garage shop and telling Parekh about a notorious fuel thief they were after. On the forecourt, a van parked next to a pump caught their attention. Officers went to inspect it. Inside the van, they found a man surrounded by containers, in the process of filling them with Parekh’s fuel. After being caught in the act, the thief was arrested.

Can-fillers such as this, who sell containers filled with stolen fuel, are becoming more common. Christmas and Easter used to be the worst seasons for fuel theft, but recently it has become a year-round phenomenon, especially since fuel has “become a more sellable item,” says Parekh.

The losses to Parekh are having an even greater impact given rising national insurance contributions and business rates, the latter of which, he says, rose from £16,000 to £43,000 last year. And it isn’t just fuel theft he is contending with: he says his forecourt shop is often ransacked by thieves. It’s so bad that at one point there were 20 pictures of shoplifters in the window. He blames this, in part, on people with addiction issues and prison leavers being placed in houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) in the area.

Parekh says this has led to a number of violent encounters at the station. Garry Backhouse was manning the till when a regular customer “snapped” and “flashed a massive blade” at him, before being apprehended by a police officer who was in the shop at the same time. On another occasion, the 51-year-old cashier was attacked on the forecourt, while off duty, when trying to stop a shoplifter. Backhouse, who started working at the forecourt 11 years ago, quit after the first incident, but returned after a stint in a tile shop. Now, as a protective measure, none of Parekh’s staff work alone, which further adds to costs, and the door to the shop is kept locked after 8pm.

Another tool for the garage is VARS Technology, an automatic number plate recognition system and debt recovery service, used at one in eight petrol stations around the UK. It flags up “blacklisted vehicles” that have previously driven off without paying for fuel at a member forecourt. “If the registration flashes up, we don’t start the pump,” says Backhouse. But this technology, and other similar products, have been accused of issuing “false” fuel debts. In one case, this meant that a family who had been accused of driving out of a petrol station in Manchester without paying for £20 of fuel was effectively banned from more than 1,300 forecourts. Any visit they made set off an alarm.

Some fuel thieves steal or clone licence plates to hide their tracks, which can pose further difficulties for those falsely accused of fuel theft. Balmer says he has heard of cases where “perpetrators get a stolen vehicle, go online and look up a similar car in make, model and colour” and print out plates before stealing fuel, leaving the innocent original owners to receive letters falsely accusing them of stealing petrol. For forecourts, this means no chance of recovering their money. “They’ll just have to write it off,” he says.

While a petrol station forecourt might not be the first place that comes to mind as a community asset, Parekh says they are important. “Petrol stations are no longer just purveyors of fuel. We have everything,” he says. They are one of the few businesses that remain open into the early hours. “You can come at midnight and put £10 on the gas – we keep things going for people.”

But after decades in the trade, Parekh is doubtful about the future. “I’m 62 years old,” he says. “I’m beginning to think: why am I doing this?”
