‘She was almost a Batman figure’: Mexico’s avenging Mother Courage

The Guardian Tue, 21 Jul 2026 04:00:08 GMT

After her son disappeared, Isabel Miranda de Wallace swore she would bring the culprits to justice. She became a national hero. But did she go too far?

When her son, Hugo, failed to answer his phone on the morning of 12 July 2005, Isabel Miranda de Wallace did not waste a moment. Everyone knew that kidnappings were rife in Mexico City, and Wallace immediately enlisted her brother and nephew to help with the search. They walked the streets near Hugo’s last known location until they came across his SUV. A passerby told them they’d seen someone being forced out of his car and into a nearby apartment, Wallace later said. She also described speaking to a boy who had heard gunshots and seen an injured man being led out of the apartment around 4am. “Within 24 hours, we found his car, then the building where they took my son. We had the case practically solved,” Wallace later said. “But the police didn’t believe us.”

At that time, many kidnapping cases went unreported, as families feared that the police couldn’t be trusted. Those who did go to the police often struggled to get them to take their complaints seriously. But Wallace was different. She was a successful businesswoman, who had set up an advertising agency that owned and operated billboards across Mexico City. “She didn’t beg or say please,” said Federico Döring, a politician and an early ally of Wallace. “She would point her finger at public officials not doing their job – and this was unheard of,” Döring told me. “In Mexico, a lot of people are often afraid to speak up because you don’t know if a politician is in bed with the cartels. That intimidates them, but it didn’t intimidate her.”

At 35, Hugo was a fast-living rich kid with a passion for motorbikes, American football and chasing women. He was Wallace’s first son and he was used to getting his way, his ex-girlfriend Vanessa Bárcenas told police. In the years before his disappearance, he had distanced himself from old friends and appeared to be using drugs, Claudia Muñoz, another of Hugo’s former girlfriends, told me. Hugo had other problems too. He had told Bárcenas that some of the suppliers for a clothing business he owned had ties to “something like drug trafficking”, which had created problems for him with the police and made him a target for kidnappers. According to Bárcenas and Muñoz, after a run-in with gang members, Hugo started driving an armoured SUV and installed cameras at his home in a gated complex.

When the police investigation into Hugo’s disappearance stalled, Wallace took up the case herself. With remarkable speed, she obtained Hugo’s phone records and the names of people he spoke to in the hours before his disappearance. It is not uncommon for families to conduct their own investigations in Mexico, but Wallace’s family took this to new levels, hiring private detectives and surveilling targets round the clock. Yet no breakthrough arrived. None of the occupants of the apartment block where Hugo was allegedly taken reported hearing any disturbance. The witnesses Wallace and her family cited in their testimony were never found.

From the start, Wallace insisted that the case be investigated as a kidnapping linked to organised crime. Yet without hard evidence, it seemed that Hugo’s disappearance would be relegated from a federal crime to a state-level inquiry, which Wallace feared would go nowhere. In interviews, she portrayed herself as a simple mother navigating an impenetrable system. The pain of a woman searching for her missing son resonated with the public, and Wallace was able to use her popularity to gain institutional support.

Through her contacts, she pushed for the case to stay open. Marta Sahagún, the wife of President Vicente Fox, wrote to prosecutors asking them to support the investigation. Döring arranged meetings with the head of the federal police and later the senior prosecutor responsible for kidnapping investigations. “I was really struck by how she just entered the prosecutor’s office like it was her own home and started giving orders,” her ex-husband, Carlos León, later said.

Wallace became a hero to a nation angered by rising crime, police incompetence and pervasive corruption. She channelled that rage, publicising her fearless hunt for the suspects who, she said, represented the moral decay of Mexican society. “She was almost like a Batman figure,” said Ricardo Raphael, a journalist who interviewed Wallace and has written extensively about the case. Wallace’s message was clear: she would stop at nothing to bring her son’s kidnappers to justice.

On 10 January 2006, police made their first arrest in connection with Hugo’s disappearance – and Wallace was right by their side. The suspect, Juana Hilda González, was a 30-year-old professional dancer who lived in the apartment where Wallace believed her son had been kidnapped. Although González denied any involvement, and offered an alibi, police were able to hold her in custody for up to 40 days without charge, thanks to arraigo, an emergency legal measure that gives police expanded powers in organised crime cases (though in practice this limit is often exceeded). “If you are indicted for organised crime, you lose all of your procedural rights,” the defence lawyer Salvador Leyva told me.

For Hugo’s kidnapping to be treated as a federal case, investigators had to ascertain that the suspects were part of an organised crime group that had committed multiple offences. In the weeks and months after González’s arrest, Wallace placed billboards across the city, featuring photos and full names of suspects and offering rewards of up to 250,000 pesos (£12,000 at the time) – more than double the then annual average Mexican salary – for information on their whereabouts. One billboard showed a photo of González’s boyfriend, Cesar Freyre, over the words: “Kidnapper. If you were the victim of this criminal, report him!” In a documentary later made about the case, Wallace herself said: “No one had ever dared to accuse a kidnapper publicly before – much less using their full name. Neither the Mexican public nor the press could have imagined it.”

It wasn’t long before Freyre was caught. In late January 2006, news cameras arrived on a dark street in Mexico City where police had apparently just arrested him. Wallace told reporters that she and her brother had located, followed and subdued Freyre, managing to get a passing police patrol to arrest him just before he was able to draw his gun and shoot them. Leading national papers dubbed Wallace “Madre Coraje”, Mother Courage. One veteran TV host called her a “lioness”. Mexico City’s then secretary for public security declared that she should receive a prize for her bravery. Wallace retold the story of Freyre’s capture on countless talkshows.

Just like González, Freyre denied all charges. Then, on 8 February 2006, came an unexpected development. González confessed, and named five others, including Freyre and a woman called Brenda Quevedo, as part of the plot. It was a kidnapping that had gone wrong, she said. She had lured Hugo to her apartment under the pretence of a date, but a struggle ensued in which he had died. The would-be kidnappers had photographed his body in the hope of claiming a ransom. Then they dismembered the corpse with an electric saw in her bathroom sometime after 3am, and disposed of the remains.

After the confession, the case moved quickly. Police returned to González’s apartment, seven months after the first search had turned up nothing. This time they found evidence that seemed to confirm the prosecution case: an expired driving licence belonging to Hugo and a single drop of blood which matched samples given by Wallace and her husband.

Although they had not found his body, investigators concluded Hugo had died in the apartment. Wallace placed new billboards across the city displaying the faces of the suspects, publicly branding them kidnappers and murderers. Within a few weeks, two more suspects were in custody. Several relatives of the suspects were also arrested and held under the arraigo system and later accused of forming part of the alleged kidnapping gang. Some of them remained in custody for years.

Wallace had achieved something most relatives of victims could only dream of. She cared little for niceties: she bragged about slipping cash to anyone who might have information, including police officers. As for the billboards, they were almost certainly illegal, being defamatory and violating the presumption of innocence. But few seemed to care. “The press saw this as incredible bravery on [Wallace’s] part, to accuse kidnappers in such a public forum,” said Ambar Treviño, the defence lawyer for several of the accused. In a flattering profile in Reforma, an influential Mexican daily newspaper, Wallace cast herself as an avenging vigilante: “If I have to become a killer to find my son,” she said, “I’ll do it.”

At the time of Hugo’s disappearance, Brenda Quevedo had been visiting her family in Mexico City. She was in her early 20s and home for what was meant to be just a few months before she returned to London, where she had lined up a job as a PR manager at a consulting company. During those months, she met Jacobo Tagle, a handsome car dealer, who happened to be friends with Hugo. She and Tagle soon became an item.

In 2005, just a few weeks after they met, Quevedo joined Tagle and a group of friends, including González and Freyre, as well as two brothers, Tony and Albert Castillo, for a day trip. They drove a few hours out of the capital to Chalma, a popular Catholic shrine, to pay tribute to Freyre’s brother, who had died the previous year. They posed for a photo in front of the church, smiling, with their arms around each other. Prosecutors came to believe that almost everyone in the photo was involved in Hugo’s disappearance. (The only one who was not a suspect was a young child.)

A year after the photo was taken, on 26 February 2006, Quevedo was visiting family with Tagle a short drive from Mexico City when her aunt called, sounding upset. “Come quickly, and come alone. Don’t bring Jacobo,” her aunt told her. Quevedo was shaken to learn that her mother and teenage brother had returned home to find dozens of armed federal police turning over every inch of the family home and asking where she was.

Hugo’s case was becoming a public story, but Quevedo had heard nothing about her boyfriend’s friends being arrested, she said. Upon learning that police were looking for them, her first thought was that Tagle was mixed up in something bad. She called him, demanding answers. It was possible one of the cars he had sold may have been stolen, he said. Quevedo wanted to go to the police station together to clear things up, but he refused. Quevedo left town immediately, and went to stay with an aunt in Guadalajara, a six-hour drive away.

Through a lawyer, she learned more about the investigation. She barely knew Tagle’s friends. Now they were implicated in the disappearance of his friend Hugo, and so was she. Some of the group – including González and Freyre – were already in custody. Soon Albert Castillo would be arrested, and allegedly beaten and tortured to force a confession. His brother Tony was next and alleged similar abuse. By April 2006, the only suspects who had not yet been arrested were Tagle and Quevedo herself.

From her aunt’s house, she watched, horrified, as Wallace appeared on the news, day after day, accusing Tagle and others of killing Hugo. When Quevedo saw on the news her own face on a giant billboard, with the words “kidnapper” and “killer”, she crawled under the bed and sobbed, she told me.

With so much publicity, Quevedo realised she wasn’t safe in Mexico. She took scissors to her waist-length hair and began cutting. With each snip she felt as if she was leaving a part of herself behind. She got a fake ID, and took a new name: Nadia, from “nadie”, or no one. With $200 cash, some baggy clothes, a Bible and a phone with only one number saved – that of distant relatives in Kentucky – she travelled north. From a cramped safe house on the US border, she and a dozen others were herded across the rushing waters of the Rio Grande by people smugglers. From there, they crossed the desert on foot and in pickup trucks.

After a month, Quevedo reached the suburban sprawl of Louisville, Kentucky. It was too risky to speak directly to her parents or brother, but Quevedo received news through her extended family. When no one was around, she would go online to read about the Wallace case, as it was known. In her absence, she had become an object of morbid fascination for the press. In an error-riddled book about the case, for which Wallace wrote the foreword, a journalist described Quevedo’s physical appearance in vivid, lingering detail, portraying her as a femme fatale. Later coverage used a photo of Quevedo attending a Halloween party to suggest, implausibly, that she dressed as a bunny rabbit to sell drugs. “They claimed I was someone who made it her business to seduce men and lure them into a trap,” Quevedo said.

In Louisville, Quevedo found work as a waitress in a Cuban restaurant. She told no one about what she was running from. One day, at work, she met a customer named Fernando López, who was in the US military. He later returned to the restaurant with flowers, and soon after they began dating. A year later, López took her on a hot air balloon trip. As they rose above the clouds, López reached into his pocket for the ring which he placed on the finger of the woman he knew as Nadia.

For a brief moment, it seemed Quevedo might be able to start again. “I checked the news, waiting for the day when they would announce that the real culprits had been caught. I thought it would all be over,” Quevedo said. “But it never happened.”

In the years after Hugo’s disappearance, Wallace became a fixture on the nightly news. For the media, the story of a humble mother turned dogged investigator was irresistible. In 2006, the New York Times ran a piece about her under the headline “A Mexican mother turns detective, driven by devotion to her kidnapped son”. In Mexico, where she was known as La Señora Wallace, people would stop her in the street for autographs or to wish her luck. By 2007, she had signed a deal with Ricky Martin’s publicist, and there was talk of making a film about her life.

Hugo’s body had never been found, and homicide charges were never filed, but after González’s confession was made public, mainstream media largely accepted the prosecution’s case, despite the fact that all the defendants, including González – who had retracted her confession, claiming she had been tortured – insisted they were innocent. In April 2006, criminal proceedings began against Freyre, González and the Castillo brothers, who were all charged with kidnapping and belonging to an organised crime group. (Freyre and González were also charged with possessing weapons reserved for security forces.)

To most lawyers, it seemed that representing the four defendants would be a losing battle. But when Ámbar Treviño, then a thirtysomething criminal lawyer with a short bob of curly hair and a wry sense of humour, looked into the prosecution’s evidence, she felt compelled to take up the case. She quickly learned that the press wasn’t interested in the defendants’ version of events. “Individual liberty and due process isn’t exactly a narrative that captures the public’s attention, especially at a time when people are angry and beset by crime,” she told me.

Treviño argued there were glaring weaknesses in the prosecution story. In the early months of the investigation, Wallace had emphasised the accounts of eyewitnesses who allegedly heard gunshots and saw Hugo leaving the apartment injured. Following González’s confession in February 2006, the story shifted. Now the prosecution claimed that Hugo had died in the apartment of a heart attack, and the assailants had disposed of the body. The eyewitness accounts were no longer mentioned. Meanwhile, the suspects, as well as their family members, reported being pressured by prosecutors to change statements. Key witnesses changed their evidence, many later alleging that they, too, had been pressured by prosecutors.

At the time, Mexico’s justice system afforded prosecutors near-exclusive control over evidence and its framing. It was not uncommon for judges to issue a verdict based almost entirely on the prosecution case, while many of the accused claimed they never had a chance to be heard. After defence and prosecution had submitted evidence and witness statements were taken, the judge would move to written deliberation. And while, by law, criminal proceedings should last no longer than one year, in practice they often went on much longer.

In the case of González, Freyre and the Castillo brothers, it would take almost four years before the judge handed down his verdict. “If Mexico did not exist,” Treviño said, “Kafka would have had to invent it.”

In January 2007, a few weeks after a new government had taken power, Wallace, trailed by TV cameras, led a group of relatives of the disappeared – victims of forced disappearances in the conflict between warring drug cartels and the state – to the gates of the presidential palace to demand an audience with the president. A few days later, President Felipe Calderón met with Wallace. The meeting lasted more than an hour and the president took notes while she spoke, Wallace later boasted. Calderón ordered his attorney general to give her any assistance she needed in tracking down Brenda Quevedo and Jacobo Tagle, the two suspects who were still on the run. Their faces were soon plastered on police cars across Mexico City and international warrants were issued for their arrest.

From the US, Quevedo was following news of the case while attempting to build a new life for herself. In late 2007, she was still working as a waitress in Kentucky when she noticed two men in suits sitting at a table. There was something off about them, she thought. They had been there for half an hour and had yet to order food. As she started to panic, Quevedo’s manager called her over, his face drained of colour. The FBI were looking for her, he said. She was arrested in front of her colleagues, and led away in handcuffs. Quevedo didn’t know it at the time, but Wallace was nearby. She had travelled to Kentucky for the arrest.

Quevedo’s fiance, López, was at home when he got a call from the FBI saying she was in their custody. He could speak to “Nadia”, but only in English, they warned him, otherwise the agents would assume they were conspiring. López knew right then this was not simply an immigration issue, he told me.

Nadia began by telling him her real name. Then came everything else – the allegations, the billboards, the manhunt. López’s head was spinning. Afterwards, he spoke with Enriqueta Cruz, Quevedo’s mother, who shared with him the evidence she had amassed about inconsistencies in the official narrative. “I didn’t feel betrayed because once I understood everything, I saw that she was in real danger, and that she feared for her life,” López told me. Soon López and Cruz met in person, and together formed a support group for Quevedo. López was struck by Cruz’s courage and resilience, despite the toll it took on her health and finances. “If she could have sold her skin for her daughter, she would have done it,” López said. (After getting married while she was in prison, Quevedo and López divorced in 2009.)

For the next two years, Quevedo was moved between jails across the US as she fought extradition. She was the only defendant in the Wallace case with a university education and a clear understanding of her own rights, and she argued she would face torture if she returned to Mexico. In 2009, she was finally extradited, after the US court received assurances from the Mexican federal prosecutor’s office that her rights would be guaranteed.

When the plane door opened at Mexico City airport on 25 September 2009, the first thing Quevedo saw was the flash of cameras. Handcuffed, in an orange jumpsuit, she was led across the tarmac flanked by armed police in tactical gear. “It was like I was Chapo Guzmán,” she told me, referring to the infamous drug lord.

After processing, Quevedo was taken not to jail but to a room where she found herself face to face with Wallace for the first time. According to Quevedo, Wallace gestured to a seat near her and told her that they were going to make a deal. Wallace – who was recognised as a victim of Hugo’s kidnapping but held no official judicial role – offered Quevedo a reduced sentence if she testified against the other defendants and helped them find Tagle. Quevedo refused.

By this point, Wallace had become one of Mexico’s most prominent anti-crime and victims’ rights activists, a powerful position in a society in which violence had exploded since the start of the “war on drugs” in 2006. The murder rate surged by 260% between 2007 and 2010. Cartel executions, beheadings and the discovery of mass graves were increasingly common. Through her NGO Alto al Secuestro (Stop Kidnapping), Wallace published her own statistics for kidnapping and murder rates in Mexico, which often exceeded official figures and embarrassed governors. “They were scared of her. And they hated her for it,” said Samuel González Ruiz, a former head of the prosecutor’s specialist unit against organised crime and later personal adviser to Wallace for more than 15 years. Wallace was “hard-nosed, ruthless”, González Ruiz said. She advocated directly for families of victims, among them members of the business elite. “And when Isabel spoke to the anti-kidnapping unit, you can believe they listened,” González Ruiz said.

The day after being returned to Mexico, Quevedo was taken to Santiaguito, a state prison 90 minutes outside the capital. She says that, on 27 November 2009, she was taken to a room where two men waited, wearing balaclavas. They blindfolded her and tied her to a chair, then began to strike her head, asking her where Hugo’s body was. According to Quevedo’s account, they suffocated her with a plastic bag. After they were disturbed by guards, the men left.

A year later, in October 2010, Quevedo was transferred to Islas Marías, a remote prison island in the Pacific usually reserved for convicted detainees. Shortly after arriving, she was driven to an isolated building facing the sea. The following day, according to her account, around five masked men appeared. For hours, Quevedo said, they used electrocution, waterboarding and sexual abuse to make her confess and incriminate her co-defendants. They threatened her family. They knew about her mother’s recent surgery, her brother in Canada, everything. (Both federal prosecutors and the CNDH, Mexico’s national human rights body, initially dismissed Quevedo’s claims, citing insufficient evidence. But a later review revealed that the CNDH had disregarded its own internal psychiatric evaluation from 2011, which had already documented indicators of torture against Quevedo. Her allegations were also corroborated by a medical report issued in 2022 and by consistent testimony from three family members. In a report by a UN working group, the Mexican government did not contest the allegations of torture against Quevedo.)

Quevedo was held in isolation, unable to contact her family, and deprived of medical treatment. After a week, she managed to pass a note and a phone number to an inmate. Hundreds of miles away in Mexico City, Brenda’s parents received the news that their daughter was in an island prison where she had been tortured.

In the years since federal agents had raided her home, Cruz had reorganised her life to support her daughter and help her son get asylum status outside Mexico. Softly spoken, the years of struggle etched on her face, Cruz had sold the family apartment and moved in with relatives in 2008 to pay mounting legal fees in her daughter’s fight against extradition. (Cruz and Brenda’s father are separated.) Brenda’s brother had fled to Canada, after being assaulted by men who said they had been hired to look for his sister. “We were pariahs. Even being related to those accused condemned you,” Cruz told me.

When she received the news from her daughter, Cruz was inconsolable. It came not long after a court hearing in which Cruz had questioned the story around Hugo’s disappearance and pointed to evidence that he himself had been in trouble with police. Cruz was convinced the torture was meant as a punishment. “It was clearly revenge,” she told me.

Still, Cruz kept filing complaints to the prosecutor’s office and the CNDH – which was tasked with investigating torture claims – most of which were dismissed. At the same time, she started looking further afield, to international human rights organisations outside Mexico, beyond Wallace’s influence.

“I cried every time I saw a complaint dismissed,” Cruz said. “Then, when I was done, I said to myself: What can I try next? What haven’t I done yet?”

On 24 December 2009, the verdict in the trial of González, Freyre and the Castillo brothers was finally delivered. All four were convicted of aggravated kidnapping and organised crime offences. Their sentences ranged from 28 to 47 years. In Wallace’s view, this was too lenient. Over the next few months, she met with members of the supreme court and held an event calling for the death penalty for kidnappers. The sentences were finally set by a federal appellate court at 78 years for González, 131 years for Freyre and 93 years for the Castillo brothers.

In late 2010, the final suspect, Jacobo Tagle, was arrested in a satellite city on the outskirts of Mexico City. He had been living under a false identity for years, disguising himself with false teeth and wigs. After his arrest, Wallace called a press conference in which rifle-wielding police paraded Tagle before the media. “Now I’d like to invite the press, who have always been so supportive, to take note that Jacobo has not been beaten. Because it is so common for people, once they are in front of a judge, to later claim to have been tortured,” said Wallace, directing the police to lift his shirt for the cameras. Then she addressed the suspect directly. “Jacobo, I’m now going to ask you to confirm what you said yesterday about the role of all of the accused – Brenda Quevedo Cruz, Cesar Freyre Morales, the Castillo brothers, Juana Hilda [González] and you, in the kidnapping of my son.” Tagle, his hair greasy, gaze vacant and voice barely audible, assented.

Less than a fortnight later, President Calderón awarded Wallace Mexico’s top human rights prize. “Her story is one of pride, courage and dignity, and serves as an example to all of us,” he declared.

Wallace was now firmly at the centre of national security policy. She met with supreme court judges, attended meetings usually reserved for top officials and helped allies get elected to oversee the CNDH. Wallace also weighed in on legislation. She became an increasingly useful voice of support for the government. In 2011, when protesters demanded the resignation of Calderón’s security chief, Genaro García Luna, Wallace publicly defended his record. The following year, Calderón’s party picked Wallace to be its candidate for governor of the Mexico City region, one of the most important jobs in the country.

Her entrance into electoral politics brought Wallace her first real taste of press scrutiny. During the campaign, it was revealed that she had been arrested in July 1998 after a violent dispute with officials who were trying to remove three of her company’s billboards, which had been deemed unsafe. Wallace, assisted by a man matching Hugo’s description, had reportedly cut the cables of a hydraulic crane that was removing the billboards, before trying to flee the scene. (Wallace had spent several days in jail for resisting arrest, though she was eventually acquitted.) After a bumpy campaign, she finished in third place with 13% of the vote, a historic low for the party.

Although she had failed to win office, Wallace retained access to allies within the highest levels of government. In 2016, at an event about miscarriages of justice, she presented Calderón’s successor, Enrique Peña Nieto, with a birthday cake, and led the crowd in a rendition of Mexico’s happy birthday song, Las Mañanitas.

In 2010, five years after Hugo’s disappearance, the Wallace case was still working its way through the courts. González, Freyre and the Castillo brothers were appealing against their conviction, while the case against Tagle and Quevedo was still in the investigation phase. There seemed little hope for the defendants. The few journalists, lawyers and activists to publicly defend the accused had faced a vicious backlash.

Soon after the first sentence was handed down, the defence lawyer Treviño had, after years of dogged work, reluctantly withdrawn from the case. It began with death threats, she said. Then a group of masked men with assault rifles broke into her home. Shortly after, authorities detained her. The allegations were almost comically trivial: Treviño had submitted a medical note excusing her from a hearing because of back pain, but contrary to requirements, the note came from a doctor who had not examined her in person. At Treviño’s first hearing before a judge, the charges were dismissed.

Treviño had never been naive, but she still found herself shocked by what she saw as the power of Wallace and her allies in the prosecutor’s office to go after anyone who stood in their way. She had spent a total of two months in custody for not having obtained the proper paperwork relating to a minor medical condition. “I’m the smallest grain of sand in the desert in this whole story, and this is what they did to me,” she said. “You genuinely fear what the state is capable of.”

This was exactly the kind of cause that animated David Bertet, head of a tiny Canadian NGO working on wrongful convictions. He came across the case in 2010, when he met with Wallace in a downtown Mexico City restaurant to discuss a separate case. She was forthright, though not unpleasant. But Bertet left the meeting troubled by what he saw as Wallace’s belief in her ability to determine guilt by gut reaction. Soon after, he began hearing stories about people who had been detained or threatened after criticising her.

Bertet decided to look at Hugo’s case himself and, almost immediately, he found inconsistencies. Bertet’s day job was teaching college philosophy, but he spent his spare time chugging energy drinks and reading the case file. “It amazed me how easy it was to find things that clearly did not add up,” he recalled. Yet the Mexican authorities seemed uninterested in re-examining the Wallace case. “There was one version, and that could not be undermined,” Bertet said.

For several years progress was slow. Then, in 2014, as Bertet and a colleague scanned through Hugo’s documents, they realised the missing man had multiple identities and several birth certificates, issued years apart and listing different fathers. Bertet was aware that DNA from a drop of blood found in the flat had been key to the investigation. It had placed Hugo at the flat on the night of his disappearance. But if Hugo’s parentage was in question, Bertet realised, so was the DNA evidence that underpinned the prosecution’s case. “It was exciting,” Bertet recalled. “And at the same time it was like, fuck, it’s actually true.” Now he had to decide how to use it – and anticipate Wallace’s response.

As a child, Quevedo’s hero was her father. A strong-willed lawyer who loves to debate, he would push her to express herself precisely and know her rights. He encouraged her to be independent and adventurous. Her mother, who worked as an administrative assistant at a bank, was a quieter presence. With his legal background, Quevedo’s father, Roberto, initially led efforts to organise his daughter’s defence. But, particularly after his health deteriorated, it was Enriqueta Cruz who would become her daughter’s most implacable champion.

In June 2019, Cruz arrived at the public defender’s office in Mexico City, which had just opened a new unit to tackle the widespread use of torture in criminal investigations. There she met Salvador Leyva, a 28-year-old public defender. He was a teenager when Hugo had disappeared, and like many of his peers he had grown up seeing Wallace as a national hero. But when he met Cruz, he was struck by her humility and the obvious toll the case had taken on her. “She wasn’t asking for anything; she just wanted someone to listen,” recalled Leyva. In the weeks that followed, he travelled the country’s prisons, interviewing the four people convicted, as well as Tagle and Quevedo. He pored over hundreds of thousands of pages of evidence. Later, he spoke to Bertet, who pointed him to the doubts around Hugo’s paternity.

To Leyva, one of the things about the prosecution case that did not add up was the discovery of Hugo’s DNA in the apartment where he had supposedly been murdered. In a combative 2018 television interview, Wallace had insisted that her second husband, José Enrique del Socorro Wallace, was Hugo’s father. Watching from his home, Wallace’s first husband, Carlos León, was galled. He contacted journalists to insist that Hugo was his son, throwing into doubt the central forensic evidence of the case: a single drop of blood found at the scene of the crime, which matched both Wallace and José Enrique.

In October 2019, DNA tests confirmed that Wallace’s first husband was telling the truth. Hugo really was his son. But in that case, why had a blood sample found at the scene of the crime been shown to match her second husband, rather than her first? In the early days of the investigation, León told a judge in May 2021, Wallace convinced him to give a DNA sample, but when she handed the DNA sample to prosecutors, she told them it came not from León but from José Enrique. By doing so, Wallace ensured that any tests of Hugo’s DNA would match her and the man she claimed was his father, her second husband. For Bertet, this small, unnecessary lie was an act of hubris on Wallace’s part, and one that would ultimately undermine the whole case. “She was too self-confident and she believed that it wouldn’t ever come to light,” he suggested. “Or that if it did, no one would care.”

Then, in April 2021, Leyva found that the apartment where Hugo had purportedly been killed had not been secured by police for the seven months between the first and second search. Not only that: it had been rented in the interim to a new tenant – a man who happened to work for Wallace, and later married into her extended family.

Since the case’s inception, the accused and their families had maintained their innocence. A few dogged journalists such as Anabel Hernández and Guadalupe Lizárraga had argued the case against defendants was fabricated. But now there was compelling witness testimony from Wallace’s ex-husband saying that she had tampered with evidence, and strong circumstantial evidence that the key physical evidence could have been planted.

In July 2021, Leyva filed a criminal complaint against Wallace, accusing her of lying under oath and fabricating evidence by allegedly renting the apartment to plant the blood sample and later falsifying the DNA submission to ensure it matched. It followed an earlier complaint lodged by his office naming those it said were responsible for torturing Quevedo: more than a dozen officials – and Wallace, for allegedly ordering it. Now, for the first time, Wallace’s role in the case was being investigated.

Wallace still wielded considerable power. And she was far from the only person whose reputation was intertwined with the theory of Hugo’s kidnapping. A whole cast of career prosecutors and politicians had supported her cause for years. This began to change in 2020, after a UN group that works on cases of arbitrary detention called for Quevedo’s immediate release, citing allegations of coercion and failure to investigate claims of torture. “That completely changed how the media treated the case,” Leyva said. “Media that had never spoken about this case from the victim’s perspective started doing so.”

In 2022, Mexico’s supreme court took up an appeal against the conviction of González, who was now 16 years into her 78-year sentence. Her lawyers argued that her confession had been obtained through torture. Wallace struck back by accusing the then president of Mexico’s supreme court, Arturo Zaldívar, of accepting bribes to review González’s case. Zaldívar told reporters: “If she is capable of falsifying evidence and making complaints against the president of a court, what wouldn’t she have done to defenceless people when she had total power and enjoyed the protection of [former presidents] Fox, Calderón and [former security chief] García Luna?” (Neither Calderón nor Fox responded to requests for comment for this article.)

Wallace’s political influence was fading. After the election of leftwing populist Andrés Manuel López Obrador in 2018, she no longer had the same close ties to the presidency. Meanwhile, the powerful figures Wallace had allied herself with were now in trouble. In 2023, García Luna was convicted by a US court of working with the Sinaloa cartel. García Luna had overseen the federal police force that began the investigation into Hugo’s kidnapping, then later the prosecutors who developed the case, and the federal prison system in which Quevedo and her co-accused were allegedly tortured.

Amid the slow drip of revelations, many Mexicans were coming to see Wallace not as a critic of a corrupt system but as an example of its worst excesses. In October 2022, on Wallace’s instructions, billboards appeared across Mexico City plastered with confessions made by some of the accused, even though there was strong evidence that the statements had been made under torture. (A judge quickly ruled the billboards illegal, and ordered them to be taken down.)

A few weeks later, in another attempt to control the narrative, Wallace opened a pop-up “Wallace case” museum in Mexico City. Using mannequins and stage sets, the exhibit recreated key scenes from the prosecution’s case, including Hugo’s death itself. In one room, a video of Tagle taken during a police reconstruction played in the background. Onscreen, in a confession he had retracted soon after, Tagle explained how they dismembered the body. Nearby, a blindfolded and bound mannequin representing Hugo in his final moments lay on a mattress. “You will see for yourselves how the narrative told by those responsible for this crime is false,” Wallace said of the exhibit. “They were never tortured or coerced in any way, nor were any of their rights violated. And in fact they confessed spontaneously.”

Some 16 years after first being hailed a hero by the media, Wallace’s promotional efforts were largely ignored. At the exhibition, a text message from Hugo to his mother on the night of his disappearance was displayed on a wall. “I’m going into the cinema, Mum,” it said. “I’ll call you when I get out.” The message was followed by a string of emojis. No such message had ever been filed in evidence, and even more strikingly, the emojis in question had not been introduced in 2005, when the message was supposedly sent.

When the judgment from the supreme court finally came, it was damning. On 11 June 2025, it ordered Juana Hilda González’s immediate release after nearly 20 years in prison, ruling that her confession was obtained through torture, and that “there is not a single piece of evidence directly linking Juana Hilda to [Hugo’s] disappearance”. The court added that because González had been characterised as a bad mother and an ambitious woman, she had received a heavier sentence, and that this gender stereotyping constituted an additional violation of her rights. The court also threw out all the evidence that derived from her coerced confession, including the controversial second search of the apartment, which found the blood sample and Hugo’s expired driving licence.

Yet the supreme court decision did not lead to the immediate release of the five other people implicated in Hugo’s disappearance, even though they were partly convicted on the basis of González’s coerced confession. The decision merely opened the door to review of their cases. In the meantime, they remain in detention.

Wallace did not live to see the collapse of the case she had built. Three months before the judgment, she died after suffering complications following surgery. Her funeral was private, and little is known about the circumstances of her death.

Many of Wallace’s former allies and advocates see her as the victim of a politically motivated witch-hunt. After her death, one of the country’s leading broadcasters condemned what he said was the left’s “perverse vilification” of Wallace. Calderón and a host of senators and political heavyweights offered their condolences. Samuel González Ruiz, her former adviser, claimed Wallace was targeted in retaliation for exposing corruption and her aggressive, sometimes misguided campaigning in several complex, politicised cases. “Those cases enraged them and that’s the reason they fabricated these accusations against Isabel Wallace,” he told me.

While most of Wallace’s supporters reject claims that she fabricated evidence, some concede that she sometimes acted outside the law. “Isabel did things that, to be honest, don’t align with human rights – because in her desperation, she had to do what the government wasn’t doing,” the conservative politician and ally Döring said. “She lost her faith in government, she lost her faith in justice. And she carried out justice herself.”

Wallace always categorically denied the allegations against her. She refused to answer questions about Hugo’s parentage, saying it was a personal matter. The organisation she founded, Alto al Secuestro, now headed up by her family’s lawyer, declined my requests to answer questions about Wallace or her work. “Neither the family, her former employees or anyone from the NGO [is] interested in giving interviews,” it said. Mexico’s prosecutor’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Even from beyond the grave, Wallace continued to push her story. In a letter published posthumously, she predicted the supreme court decision would go against her, saying it was part of a plot. “I know that sooner or later those trying to free my son’s kidnappers will get their way,” she warned.

More than 20 years after Hugo disappeared, his body has still not been found. But from the early days of the investigation, Treviño had insisted there were signs that the story Wallace was telling about Hugo didn’t add up. Nine days after he disappeared, his bank card was used several times: to pay for a seafood meal, for a purchase in a department store and for a paintballing game. A few months later, a payment was made on another of his cards, this time to a dating site. In May 2006, one of his friends and her partner went to the police to report being contacted multiple times by Hugo and later meeting him in person after his disappearance. They later claimed their statements were ignored by prosecutors.

Police efforts to track calls made from Hugo’s multiple phones after his death also turned up intriguing results. After being contacted by investigators, one recipient of these calls pointed police to a strange answerphone message they had received from an unknown number at around 3am three months after Hugo’s disappearance. The caller, whom multiple listeners identified as Hugo, said: “I’m sick of this shit, man. Yeah, I know I messed up, but honestly? I don’t give a damn. I’m out here drinking, man – look at me. Whatever. You know what? You know who screwed me over?” But these oddities were brushed over by the media and the legal system.

Last year, on the request of some defendants, Claudia Muñoz, one of Hugo’s former partners and the mother of his child, gave a deposition at a consulate in the US. She spoke about a phone call she received almost two years after Hugo is presumed to have died. “When he called, I couldn’t believe it was him. But then I recognised his voice,” Muñoz told me.

She said Hugo called asking about their daughter. “He told me he was going through something very serious. But he wanted to see our girl,” Muñoz said. Muñoz told him he needed to resolve his problems first. The call ended abruptly. After they spoke, Muñoz said she contacted Wallace. “As soon as I said I had spoken to Hugo, she became angry and told me it couldn’t be true,” she recalled. Muñoz said Mexican prosecutors ignored her requests to give evidence at the trial of the accused.

What happened to Hugo remains a mystery. Hugo’s security concerns and a 2001 conviction for smuggling suggest he may have been involved in criminal activity. It is plausible, as the journalist Ricardo Raphael has suggested, that Hugo owed money to some dangerous figures and his mother helped him to “disappear”. To cover up one crime, this theory goes, Wallace invented a second crime out of thin air. For now, however, this remains speculation.

The point, for Leyva, is that this is a story about much more than Wallace herself. “She wouldn’t have been able to do anything if there wasn’t someone in the government, in the judiciary or in the prosecutor’s office or in politics allowing it,” he said. Mexico’s human rights commission has now concluded that there was evidence to corroborate claims all six defendants were tortured with the intention of forcing them to incriminate themselves and their co-accused.

After 19 years in prison, González is now free, trying to rebuild her life. (She declined to speak for this article.) Yet her three co-defendants remain in prison pending their own separate appeals. Meanwhile, Tagle and Quevedo are still awaiting trial for their alleged role in Hugo’s kidnapping. Tagle and Quevedo’s cases are exceptional in their duration, but they are not uncommon in their outline. This year, almost half of all detainees in Mexican prisons had no sentence and were being held under a system of mandatory pre-trial detention. Two international court rulings have declared this system incompatible with human rights law.

Theirs are not the only lives affected. Many of the accused’s family members were targeted by prosecutors based on scant evidence, as were their lawyers. Leyva himself was a frequent target of Wallace, who made multiple procedural complaints against him, and in 2020 implied he was involved in an alleged kidnapping attempt against her lawyer. In 2022, the UN criticised the use of “criminal investigations and acts of intimidation” against Leyva and several colleagues after their work on Quevedo’s case. Leyva now lives in Ireland and does not plan to return to Mexico. “I would have definitely been better without this case,” he told me. “Still, I don’t regret it.”

In 2024, after almost 18 years in jail, thanks to a petition lodged by her defence years earlier, Quevedo was released and placed under house arrest. She lives in a small house with her mother on the hilly outskirts of Mexico City. Her case remains stuck in the investigation phase, bogged down by technical legal disputes. “How can it be possible for the system to be this slow?” Quevedo said when we spoke recently. “Almost 20 years waiting for a resolution. It’s unbelievable.”

Quevedo returned to a world that felt alien – technology that she couldn’t understand, cousins she had last seen as children now with their own families. She was 25 when she was first branded a murderer on a billboard. She is now 45, and worries she may never have the chance to get married, have children or pursue a career.

Outside her house, the endless urban sprawl stretches out like a muddy blur beyond the horizon, but Quevedo is bound to a few dozen square metres. Just out of sight, a police car sits on the street. “It’s another incarceration, just a more comfortable one,” Quevedo told me. She must wear an ankle tag at all times.

Last month, a new group of lawyers took on Quevedo’s case, calling for the judge to finally rule on her case and acquit Quevedo. She is grateful for the growing support after so many years of struggle. “Nobody believed us, nobody helped us, nobody wanted to know or even talk about the case. Whoever tried – it went terribly for them.” But for more than 20 years, her mother never stopped trying to advocate for her daughter. “The one who was most out there fighting,” Quevedo said, “was my mum.”

Meet Jimothy, the ‘Silly and Round’ Creature Taking Over Instagram Feeds

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The stout raccoon, which has a spinal condition, is “an example to all of us that you don’t have to be perfect to be loved,” a Seattle City Council member said.

By Madison Malone Kircher

The thing about Jimothy is that when you see Jimothy, you immediately understand that the bizarre creature, both cute and just a little bit freaky looking, could not be called anything else.

“Ah, yes,” you say to yourself, nodding. “That is a Jimothy.”

Jimothy, a raccoon with a spinal condition in Seattle, has gone from being a local legend to a national celebrity after several videos of the critter circulated on social media this month.

In the most popular of the videos, Kiana Hall, a 33-year-old marketing specialist, spots the raccoon while walking through her neighborhood of Ballard, in northwestern Seattle, in July.

“He was under a car, and I thought he was a cat,” she said. “I just love cats and wanted to take a closer look.”

When she pointed her phone at the animal, it was something else. “What am I looking at?” Hall exclaims in the widely shared video, as Jimothy scampers across a sidewalk looking like a 5-year-old’s crayon rendering of a raccoon, or a lesser character from a horror film.

In her Instagram caption, Hall dubbed the creature Jimothy. “He just looked like a Jimothy to me,” she explained, describing him as “just a silly and round little guy.”

The animal is likely to have short spine syndrome, an extremely rare congenital deformity that results in a significantly shortened spinal column and a rounder appearance, said Dr. Marcie Logsdon, a veterinarian who teaches at Washington State University College of Veterinary Medicine.

“Everything is kind of cramped up next to itself instead of being long and spread out like it should be,” Dr. Logsdon said, adding that the condition can affect how other body parts develop, too. “One of the things that you might notice first on Jimothy is how his legs are all a little bit disproportionate to the rest of his body, probably because as he was growing and those legs were developing, his spine wasn’t normal,” she added. (Short of performing a physical exam, Dr. Logsdon said it was not possible to discern Jimothy’s sex.)

Dr. Logsdon said it was “surprising” to see an animal with this condition appearing to thrive in the wild. It “seems to be in reasonable body condition and he seems to be moving very well and seems to have adapted quite well to what’s going on,” she said.

Jimothy has captured quite a few hearts around Seattle. Rebecca Sorensen, the owner of Ballard Clay, a pottery studio, commissioned a local artist to paint a mural of the raccoon outside her business.

“We thought behind the garbage can would be most appropriate,” Andrew Miller, the artist, said.

Sorensen, 45, said she first spotted Jimothy about six months ago. “We live at the dead end of an alley, and something caught in my headlights as I turned in and scurried away,” she said. The creature startled her so much that she asked her neighbors to check their home security camera footage. She told her neighbors, half-jokingly, that she had seen a chupacabra, a creature from folklore known for sucking the blood of livestock.

The small mural outside her studio has already begun drawing fans, Sorensen said.

Jessica Hinnenkamp, 38, stopped by Sorensen’s studio on Monday for a quick visit while in town from Virginia for work. “My husband and I are, like, the world’s biggest raccoon fans,” said Hinnenkamp, who is in the Navy. “We call each other our trash pandas. We have matching raccoon tattoos.”

Laura Exley, a Seattle-based tattoo artist, recently began offering a few Jimothy tattoo designs on her Instagram page. One customer had already taken her up on it, she said. “Every time that there’s a little internet thing that captures people’s hearts, there is an influx of tattoos of that thing,” Exley, 47, explained. She has over a dozen more appointments booked with people looking for raccoon ink.

In recent days, Dmitriy Ishimskiy, 36, posted videos he had filmed over a year ago of what appeared to be Jimothy as a baby, climbing on a fence in Ishimskiy’s backyard.

“They were the cutest little raccoon family, wandering around our neighborhood and visiting everyone’s backyards,” Ishimskiy wrote, adding that he had not seen the round-backed raccoon in many months and was happy to see Jimothy was doing well.

Jimothy’s fame has begun to spread beyond his small neighborhood in Seattle, too.

The city’s baseball team briefly changed its social media profile picture to one of the raccoon wearing a Mariners hat, and a person dressed as a raccoon participated in a mascot race during a recent game. (Jimothy took home the “win-othy,” a spectator reported on X.) During the World Cup final, the official Budweiser Instagram account posted a picture of Jimothy, and on Monday an official NASA account on X posted a photo of Seattle taken from the International Space Station, stating, “Jimothy runs this city.”

Alexis Mercedes Rinck, a member of the Seattle City Council, announced that she would soon present a proclamation to “celebrate the majestic Jimothy” and “commemorate Jimothy Summer.”

“I think he’s an example to all of us that you don’t have to be perfect to be loved, and it’s what makes us different that makes us sensational,” she said. Jimothy’s viral moment felt like the Seattle equivalent of New York City’s “Pizza Rat” episode, she added, when a persistent rodent was captured dragging a slice of pizza down some subway stairs.

“It is a dream of mine to encounter Jimothy in real life and then keep my measured distance from him so he can live his good little life,” Rinck added.

Dr. Logsdon echoed the need to keep a safe distance from Jimothy — and all raccoons — and advised any fans against feeding the animal, adding that attempts to “help” it were likely to do more harm than good.

“His best life is going to be just out in the wild, essentially being left alone,” she said.

Still, even from a distance, Jimothy’s tale has become somewhat allegorical. For Sorensen, the clay studio owner, the raccoon is a symbol of resilience.

“I think worldwide right now, in a lot of ways, with everything that we’re experiencing and seeing,” she said, “he’s a story of surviving when things maybe aren’t quite right.”

Madison Malone Kircher is a Times reporter covering internet culture.

Error Led to 400 Noncitizens Voting, New Jersey Governor Says

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A 2023 software glitch at the state’s Motor Vehicle Commission led to roughly 6,600 noncitizens being registered to vote during the Murphy administration, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced.

By Tracey Tully

Roughly 400 noncitizens cast ballots in New Jersey after about 6,600 residents were improperly registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024 because of a software error at the Motor Vehicle Commission, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced on Tuesday.

All the people affected had disclosed that they were not citizens when seeking either a driver’s license or ID, but were nonetheless placed on the voter rolls in error.

Those people will be removed from the voter rolls. The governor said she feared that they might now be at risk of federal prosecution or unexpected hurdles — “through no fault of their own” — as they worked toward becoming citizens.

“We are working very hard to protect them,” Ms. Sherrill, a Democrat who took office in January, said at a news conference.

The New York Times could not independently verify the figures disclosed on Tuesday.

The software vendor that Ms. Sherrill said was responsible for the error, Idemia, was being phased out of use in New Jersey, the governor said.

The state had “no evidence, at this time, that any elections were swayed,” she noted, including the 2024 presidential contest.

Officials with Idemia, a technology company based in Virginia with offices around the world, did not respond to calls or emails requesting comment.

Officials within the Sherrill administration became aware of the “serious software error” last week, the governor said, and began an immediate investigation. The error was discovered and corrected in 2024, while Philip D. Murphy was governor, but never publicly disclosed, Ms. Sherrill said.

A spokesman for Mr. Murphy, a Democrat who served for two terms, did not reply to emails, calls or a text message.

Ms. Sherrill was unstinting in her criticism of the way the Murphy administration handled the problem, citing “reckless failures.”

“It’s unacceptable that the vendor released software with such a glaring error. It’s unacceptable that the M. V. C. took a year to get this issue fixed. And it’s unacceptable that no one in the previous administration brought this to light, demanded accountability or took action when it happened years ago,” Ms. Sherrill said.

The finding that roughly 400 noncitizens had cast ballots in New Jersey is one of the larger confirmed instances of noncitizens voting in American elections. But it remains an exceptionally small percentage of the overall vote total.

If those 400 noncitizens had all voted in the state’s local elections in 2023, they would constitute just 0.02 percent of the electorate. If they voted in the 2024 presidential election, those 400 noncitizens would make up about 0.009 percent of the state’s overall vote totals.

Kamala Harris, the former vice president who ran against President Trump in 2024, won New Jersey by more than 252,000 votes.

The findings may nonetheless add fuel to claims by Mr. Trump and his allies that noncitizens are illegally on voter rolls nationwide and are casting ballots in elections in wide numbers, as the president makes a final pitch to Congress to pass the SAVE America Act. The act would limit mail voting and add a documentary proof of citizenship requirement to voting.

“Democrats and their media allies have repeatedly said it is impossible for noncitizens to register to vote, let alone cast a ballot,” a White House spokeswoman, Abigail Jackson, said Tuesday in an email.

“American voters deserve to have confidence that our elections are safe and secure,” she added.

David Becker, the executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan group, said that administrative errors such as the one that took place in New Jersey were rare, but “do infrequently occur.”

He said that state officials, not the federal government, were best positioned to address problems when they happen.

“They have access to substantially better data than the federal government,” Mr. Becker said in a statement, adding that “noncitizen registration remains extremely rare, and noncitizen voting is infinitesimally rare.”

Joe Gruters, the chairman of the Republican National Committee, said that the disclosure confirmed information the party had also learned through a public records request. Mr. Gruters, a state senator in Florida, said that it was further evidence of a need for Congress to pass the SAVE America Act.

“Democrats keep claiming this never happens,” Mr. Gruters said in a statement, “yet every new discovery tells the same old story. Enough excuses.”

Ms. Sherrill contrasted her decision to publicly disclose the error with what she called Mr. Trump’s efforts to “weaponize elections for political gain.”

“For the past 10 years, he’s cried wolf and peddled bizarre conspiracy theories about fraud with no evidence,” Ms. Sherrill said.

“Trump could care less about the actual integrity of the process,” she added. “His only concern is himself.”

It is unclear how long Idemia had provided software in New Jersey. The company says on its website that it works with more than 600 government agencies and state and federal organizations.

Idemia is being replaced in New Jersey by Talus Software, according to Rosalie Johnson, who leads the Motor Vehicle Commission. “I know that M. V. C. has work to do to rebuild trust,” Ms. Johnson said on Tuesday.

To protect migrants who might have been unwittingly registered to vote, Ms. Sherrill said the state would hold firm to its practice of not releasing “personally identifying information to the federal government.” She also said that the New Jersey Innovation Authority, which she created this year, was working to ensure that electronic pin pads used at motor vehicle sites displayed voting regisrules in five languages, to safeguard against misunderstanding. (The rules now appear only in English, she said.)

“We will be looking at different possibilities of making our elections more secure going forward,” Ms. Sherrill said.

In 2019, New Jersey adopted a law that allows undocumented immigrants to obtain driver’s licenses. Those eligible to vote may also register at a motor vehicle agency when applying for, or renewing, licenses or nondriver identification cards.

The New Jersey attorney general’s office notified Ms. Sherrill of the software error last Wednesday, state officials said, but offered no additional details about how the failure was detected. The state has since hired a private law firm to lead an independent investigation of the error. Ms. Sherrill said that she would publicize the final analysis.

“We will be holding — I will be holding — people accountable,” she said.

Nicholas Corasaniti contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article and its headline misstated the name of New Jersey’s motor vehicle agency. It is the Motor Vehicle Commission, not the Department of Motor Vehicles.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Tracey Tully is a reporter for The Times who covers New Jersey, where she has lived for more than 20 years.

Millions Across the Northeast Face Heavy Rain and Powerful Winds on Tuesday

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Storms

Advertisement

Supported by

Forecasters zeroed in on an area from Kentucky to New York as being the most at risk for dangerous weather.

Some

Moderate

High

Severe storms risk

Notes: This map indicates risk in up to three tiers: Some, there is at least some chance of extreme weather in the area; Moderate, it is likely that damaging weather will happen in the area; and High, extreme, dangerous weather is expected in the area. Data is as of 4:01 p. m. Eastern on July 21 and is not available for Alaska and Hawaii. Times are Eastern. Source: National Weather Service The New York Times

By Erin McCannJudson Jones and Nazaneen Ghaffar

Weather team

The good news for people across the Northeast is that the plume of wildfire smoke that made the air so difficult to breathe in the last week has largely dispersed, for now.

The bad news is that in its place on Tuesday will be yet another run of severe storms that could bring torrential downpours of rain, flash flooding, powerful winds, large hail and even a possible tornado to areas that are still reeling from similar storms over the weekend.

Precipitation intensity

Note: Times are Eastern. Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration via Iowa State University William B. Davis, Joel Eastwood and Bea Malsky/The New York Times

The Storm Prediction Center, an arm of the National Weather Service, warned that tens of millions of people from Kentucky to New York were facing a risk of severe thunderstorms on Tuesday. In many places, forecasters said, the greatest threat is likely to come from damaging wind gusts — some potentially as strong as a hurricane’s.

Philadelphia, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Washington are all in the bull’s-eye of an area that is likely to experience the most severe weather on Tuesday. New York, Cleveland and Nashville are in the next ring out, where the forecast still has meteorologists concerned, but the risk is slightly lower.

Though some storms are expected early in the day, forecasters across the Northeast warned that the most severe weather was likely to arrive in the afternoon and evening.

In Pennsylvania, the State College office of the Weather Service warned that Tuesday’s storms could reach a level of intensity to which only one or two systems rise each year. In Washington, forecasters warned late Monday that the ingredients were building for a “significant” severe weather situation to unfold on Tuesday.

Heavy rainfall is also expected to become a significant concern on Tuesday. Although the storms are forecast to move through the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast relatively quickly, forecasters said that repeated rounds of storms could pass over the same areas, producing high rainfall amounts that could lead to flash flooding.

In New York City, the storms are expected in two rounds: one between 9 a. m. and 2 p. m., and another, more severe, from 6 p. m. to 11 p. m. The Weather Service office in New York warned that up to two inches of rain per hour could fall — easily enough to lead to flash flooding in urban areas. A flood watch was in effect for New York City and southeast Pennsylvania through to northern New Jersey through late Tuesday night. Flood watches were also in effect for areas of Kentucky, southern Ohio, western Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

“While no two events are the same, the setup tomorrow is similar to what we saw last Saturday,” forecasters at the New York office of the Weather Service wrote late Monday night. In the New York area on Saturday, potent storms dropped huge amounts of rain over just a few hours, leading to flash flooding across the region. More than three inches of rain was recorded in Jersey City and Manhattan, and one weather station near Newark recorded four and a half inches of rain.

Videos shared on social media showed people caught driving in floodwaters, including a box truck that became partially submerged under a Brooklyn-Queens Expressway overpass.

Troy Jackson Tightens Hold on Democratic Senate Nomination in Maine

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

State Democrats released a ballot for their nominating convention on Saturday that includes Mr. Jackson and two long-shot candidates with little public support from delegates.

By Bayliss Wagner

Bayliss Wagner reported from Portland and Topsham, Maine.

Troy Jackson has further tightened his grip on Maine’s Democratic nomination for Senate.

Mr. Jackson, a logger and former state lawmaker, is set to appear on the ballot at Democrats’ nominating convention on Saturday in Bangor alongside just two other candidates who have won almost no public support from delegates: David Costello and Saundra Pelletier.

Hundreds of delegates aligned with Mr. Jackson were elected last weekend, giving him a seemingly insurmountable advantage that forced his leading primary rivals to suspend their campaigns.

The lack of well-known opponents appears to set up the convention as a celebration of Mr. Jackson’s nomination. His campaign announced on Monday that it was turning its effort toward defeating Senator Susan Collins, a five-term Republican, in a race widely seen as crucial to control of the Senate.

While the other top contenders had announced that they were withdrawing from the race, there had been indications that at least one of them hoped to appear on the ballot at the convention.

But when the state party announced on Tuesday which candidates had made the ballot, the other leading candidates were not included — meaning that they had not turned in the 500 verified signatures required for a spot.

They included Dr. Nirav Shah, a former public health official who came in second in the primary for governor in June; Shenna Bellows, the Maine secretary of state, who came in fourth in that race; and Jordan Wood, a progressive activist who placed third in the Democratic primary for Maine’s Second Congressional District. Dr. Shah had previously announced that he had gathered more than 800 signatures.

Dan Kleban, a brewery owner, qualified for the ballot but filed paperwork to withdraw, a representative of the Maine Democratic Party confirmed to The New York Times.

“I’m proud to throw my support behind @TroyJackson207 to beat Susan Collins and fight for working Mainers,” Mr. Kleban said in an X post on Tuesday announcing his withdrawal. He ran for the same Senate seat last fall, but dropped his bid.

Each candidate needed to collect 50 signatures per county in at least eight counties, a requirement that had some contenders bouncing among county meetings last weekend to find signatories. All of the signatures had to come from registered Democratic primary voters.

The wave of campaign suspensions prompted CNN to call off a debate on Thursday that was set to feature Mr. Jackson, Dr. Shah, Ms. Bellows and Mr. Wood.

While delegates still have until Saturday to change their minds, the likelihood that large numbers would abandon Mr. Jackson continues to diminish as the week goes on.

Mr. Costello, an environmental policy consultant, placed third in the Democratic primary for Senate in June. Ms. Pelletier, the chief executive of a pharmaceutical company focused on women’s health, is a first-time candidate.

The party remains on edge after Graham Platner, who won 72 percent of the vote in the Democratic primary for Senate in June, relinquished the nomination following an allegation of rape and a string of other scandals. The upheaval left Democrats rushing to find a new nominee to face Ms. Collins.

Just over 600 delegates will vote at the convention in Bangor on Saturday, including 500 who were elected over the weekend and 101 from the state Democratic Party committee. More than 17,000 Maine Democrats voted or otherwise participated in county meetings to elect delegates over the weekend, the party said, including nearly 3,700 delegate hopefuls. Voters overwhelmingly favored delegates who were committed to Mr. Jackson.

“Today’s certification marks another important milestone in this open, transparent, and inclusive nominating process,” Devon Murphy-Anderson, the executive director of the Maine Democratic Party, said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “We look forward to hearing directly from these candidates and bringing Democrats from every corner of Maine together on Saturday to choose the strongest nominee to defeat Susan Collins.”

Any candidate has the option to withdraw from the race before Saturday, according to the party.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Zelensky Dismisses Ukraine’s Top General After Protests

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

The move followed the firing of a popular defense minister, who had clashed with the general over how to fight the war.

By Marc Santora

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine removed his top general on Tuesday night amid swelling public protests and growing concerns that the national unity that had helped the country survive nearly five years of war was in danger of fracturing.

The dismissal of the general, Oleksandr Syrskyi, was a major reversal for Mr. Zelensky, who just days earlier sided with him and fired Ukraine’s defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.

Mr. Zelensky said he was replacing General Syrskyi with Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi, the commander of the Joint Forces. The choice was likely to please the protesters, after Mr. Drapatyi had publicly sided with Mr. Fedorov in his clash with General Syrskyi over warfighting strategy.

Thousands of people had joined mass demonstrations to pressure Mr. Zelensky to change course and reaffirm Mr. Fedorov’s vision of warfare as increasingly dominated by drones and robots. As he championed a military overhaul that leaned into high-tech innovation, Mr. Fedorov, 35, emerged as a symbol of hope to many Ukrainians, particularly young people.

General Drapatyi, 43, is part of a younger generation of Ukrainian officers. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, he built a reputation as a frontline commander focused on tactical innovation, drone integration and direct accountability. He is generally highly regarded by rank-and-file soldiers and military reformers alike.

In a statement, Mr. Fedorov called General Drapatyi’s appointment “a breath of fresh air and a new source of hope,” adding that “the voice of change” could “no longer be ignored.”

Mr. Fedorov’s dismissal last week after only six months as defense minister came as Ukraine seemed to finally have regained the initiative in the war, in large part through the increasingly effective use of long- and medium-range drones to strike targets in Russia and Crimea.

Mr. Zelensky said that he had been forced to choose between Mr. Fedorov and General Syrskyi as the differences between their camps had become impossible to resolve.

Ultimately, as the protests grew, it became clear that the rift extended far beyond a clash of personalities. For many Ukrainians, Mr. Fedorov embodied a tech-driven path to victory that might spare lives, while General Syrskyi had come to represent the darkest, most punishing realities of a war fought through sheer attrition.

General Syrskyi, 60, played a crucial role in the defense of Kyiv early in the war and in a counteroffensive in Kharkiv in September 2022. He was appointed commander in chief of the armed forces in February 2024.

In a statement on Tuesday night, Mr. Zelensky praised the general for his service, saying that he had “delivered results” and that “every warrior deserves to be treated with dignity.”

Like many senior Ukrainian commanders, General Syrskyi was trained in the Soviet military system, where personal loyalty was frequently valued over tactical innovation. Critics described him as rigid and out of touch, and he never won widespread public admiration.

During the prolonged and bloody 2023 battle of Bakhmut, General Syrskyi earned the nickname “the Butcher” for his perceived tolerance of high casualties for limited tactical gains. It was a narrative he disputed, saying that preserving soldiers’ lives was his top priority.

Criticism of General Syrskyi erupted almost immediately after Mr. Fedorov was fired. Veterans, analysts and active-duty soldiers accused General Syrskyi of blocking initiatives to adapt to a rapidly changing battlefield. Protesters took to the streets with signs bearing variations of “Fedorov is innovation, old grandpas are degeneration.”

Mr. Fedorov said that the military establishment had resisted procurement reforms that he championed to promote competition and to sever informal ties between the General Staff and politically connected arms manufacturers.

He accused General Syrskyi of maneuvering behind the scenes to preserve his own power and said that instead of defeating Russia, the general had “figured out how to split the country.”

The situation reached a breaking point as dissent within the military spilled into the open.

Last week, General Drapatyi issued a rare public statement supporting Mr. Fedorov, writing, “Silence does not protect the army; it only allows mistakes to accumulate.”

Col. Pavlo Yelizarov, a deputy commander of the air force, submitted his resignation, calling Mr. Fedorov’s removal “a great blow to the country’s defense.”

Faced with this deepening turmoil, Mr. Zelensky met with brigade commanders to hear their concerns. His office urged patience at home while seeking to reassure allies abroad.

“The situation is being resolved professionally, constructively and in the interests of our state,” Kyrylo Budanov, the former intelligence chief who is now the head of the president’s office, said in a statement. “I ask everyone to remain calm.”

“The enemy is closely watching every one of our internal disagreements and is waiting for us to start fighting among ourselves,” he said. “To our enemies, I say this directly: You will not live to see it.”

Mr. Zelensky spent days huddled with senior military leaders from across the ranks and sought to bring Mr. Fedorov back into the fold.

After meeting with the president, Mr. Fedorov said a constructive dialogue to address his concerns had begun. “There will definitely be changes,” he said in a statement.

Since Ukrainians have largely accepted that there can be no elections while the war rages, mass demonstrations have become a pressure release valve and a check on power.

Last year, tens of thousands of Ukrainians staged protests across the country after an effort by Mr. Zelensky to neuter the nation’s anti-corruption agencies. The government quickly changed course in response to the protests.

The demonstrations that followed Mr. Fedorov’s firing exposed long-simmering tensions within the military. The infighting was profoundly dangerous, soldiers said, because it could undermine combat cohesion and worsen the military’s personnel crisis by driving disillusioned troops toward desertion.

General Syrskyi remained largely silent as the controversy swirled, posting only videos of himself meeting with commanders on the front. But on Monday, he published a column in the Militarnyi news outlet to respond to what he called a “mythology about conflicts” and to defend his tenure.

He wrote that he was surprised to learn of any conflict with Mr. Fedorov and apologized if any offense had been taken.

“Ukraine is bigger than Fedorov, Syrskyi and any of us,” he wrote. “Ukraine will stand not because it has irreplaceable people, but because it has an army, institutions and millions of people who do their job. Reducing this war to a confrontation between two people is the greatest service we can do to the enemy.”

Ultimately, Mr. Zelensky concluded that removing the general was the only way to restore unity.

Cassandra Vinograd contributed reporting.

Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

By Sarah Kliff

The Trump administration announced Tuesday it was withholding more than $1 billion in Medicaid funds from California and Minnesota, the second time it has targeted the two states with Democrat governors for suspected fraud in their public health insurance programs.

The federal government will hold more than $867 million in payments from California and over $200 million from Minnesota until they can provide proof that certain claims were legitimate, officials said.
