“If Gov. Gavin Newsom or Gov. Tim Walz wants this funding released, all they have to do is provide basic documentation showing that these services are legitimate and not fraudulent,” Robert F. Kennedy, the heath and human services secretary, said at a news conference. “That’s common sense.”

The Trump administration was already withholding $243 million from Minnesota since February and $1.3 billion from California since May. Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid for the Trump administration, said the government had not released any of that money.

“We hope to return funds as soon as they submit and figure out all the documentation,” he said at the news conference.

OpenAI Says Its A. I. Models Went Rogue and Attacked a Digital Library

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The incident, which targeted the computer systems of another company called Hugging Face, happened while OpenAI was testing the systems.

By Kate Conger

Reporting from San Francisco

OpenAI said on Tuesday that two of its artificial intelligence models went rogue and successfully hacked into Hugging Face, a digital library of A. I. technology that is popular among developers.

The incident, which happened last week while OpenAI was testing the cybersecurity capabilities of its systems, displayed the kind of science-fiction potential that A. I. companies have warned would soon become a reality.

A. I. labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have over the past year released A. I. models that are customized to expose cybersecurity problems, while warning that their technology could pose new risks by finding holes in corporate computer networks faster than defenders could fix them.

OpenAI’s revelations on Tuesday are an indication that those security incidents are already starting to happen, and even savvy A. I. companies may not be entirely ready for them.

The intrusion into Hugging Face began when OpenAI tested a combination of two of its models, GPT‑5.6 Sol and a more powerful, unreleased model, to see how well it could chain together online vulnerabilities into a successful cyberattack, OpenAI said in a blog post about the incident.

The test was designed to keep the models in a safe testing environment, known as a sandbox, OpenAI said. But the models found a vulnerability that allowed them to escape the sandbox and connect to the internet. Then they targeted Hugging Face because they inferred that the library, which contains millions of A. I. models, could hold clues about how to successfully pass the evaluation.

OpenAI said it was working with Hugging Face to fix the issues that led to the attack.

“We consider this to be an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities, and are responding accordingly,” OpenAI said in its blog post. “We are implementing strict controls in infrastructure configuration at the cost of research velocity while the vulnerabilities are patched.”

Hugging Face said last week that it had detected the intrusion and knew it had been caused by an autonomous system, but did not say at the time that OpenAI was responsible.

Clem Delangue, the chief executive of Hugging Face, said in a statement that he was “grateful for the collaboration” with OpenAI in the wake of the hack. “This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: A. I. safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret,” Mr. Delangue said.

A. I. models have proved to be adept at programming, and that has made them useful to both hackers and people in charge of protecting computer networks.

In April, Anthropic released a cybersecurity-focused model called Mythos, and made it available to only a small group of organizations so they could defend against cyberattacks. OpenAI soon introduced its own cybersecurity model and made it available to a limited group of organizations to prepare their defenses, before rolling it out more broadly. And on Tuesday, Google said it had also developed a model focused on cybersecurity and released it to a small group of testing partners.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Kate Conger is a technology reporter based in San Francisco. She can be reached at kate. conger@nytimes. com.

Mamdani’s Version of DOGE Tries to Put a New Spin on Efficiency

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Mamdani Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The mayor’s version has sought to include public input as it formulates changes to the New York City Charter aimed at streamlining the government.

By Emma Goldberg

When President Trump took a swing at government efficiency, it involved an Elon Musk-led campaign called the Department of Government Efficiency, which slashed essential contracts and pushed out veteran civil servants.

In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is trying to put a new face on the fraught term.

Roughly two months ago, Mr. Mamdani announced the creation of a Charter Revision Commission designed to make city government work better for New Yorkers. To make his intent clear, he gave the commission a cheeky name, the Commission on Government Efficiency, drawing a comparison to DOGE, which never met its promise of finding $1 trillion in savings.

Mr. Mamdani has pledged to do better, and his commission on Monday released its five proposed changes to the City Charter. These would speed up approvals for outdoor dining and create new bus and bike lanes, among other ideas. The commission is supposed to operate independently, but the mayor is typically influential in proposals.

Other potential changes would reform the procurement process, simplify building permitting and set goals for the city’s rainy day fund. If the commission approves the five proposals at its final hearing on Thursday, they will appear on the November ballot for voters to consider.

Proponents of the commission argue that government efficiency is personal — experienced in delays for families who need housing vouchers, and in 311 reports of jagged sidewalks that go unanswered for weeks. Patrick Gaspard, who chaired the commission, recalled being moved by testimony from a homeless woman and her child, who talked about how forms had to be refiled and information got lost when agencies didn’t communicate with one another.

“We have turned the use of the word bureaucracy into the pejorative,” Mr. Gaspard said. “More than a few times, the folks who testified in front of us noted the rhyme with DOGE and were pleased that the approach was quite different.”

Even for some critics of Mr. Mamdani, the commission is an encouraging sign of his approach to democratic socialist governance, which has tended to emphasize making the public sector run more smoothly and effectively, and more like the private sector. Mr. Mamdani has made the theme central to recent public appearances, from a news conference where he shredded papers that listed cumbersome small business regulations to another on Coney Island where he entered on a Go-Kart to announce plans to make the city’s technology run faster.

Mr. Mamdani campaigned with the notion that his spin on democratic socialism would look like “sewer socialism,” meaning a focus on small-bore public sector improvements. In his first 100 days in office, his Department of Transportation filled nearly 4,000 potholes in March and held a “Municipal Madness” bracket-style competition for New Yorkers to pick a problem for him to address. COGE is in many ways an effort to make that work longer lasting, by proposing changes to the City Charter.

Mr. Mamdani also had political motivation to create this commission. His predecessor, Eric Adams, created his own charter review commission just before he left office on Dec. 31. Mr. Adams’s commission was to be devoted to creating an open primary system, which many feel would undermine the new mayor’s leftist coalition.

Mr. Mamdani disbanded that commission by using a new provision in the state budget, though the old commission is still fighting in court. By convening COGE, Mr. Mamdani has tried to put the attention on his own agenda.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

“This commission has been focused on the wonky, nitty-gritty government reform stuff that is really sexy to people like me,” said Caitlin Lewis, an alumna of the de Blasio administration who runs Work for America, a nonprofit focused on government staffing reform. “It isn’t necessarily what you hear mayors prioritizing all the time.”

Kathryn Wylde, a COGE commissioner who was the longtime head of the business advocacy group, Partnership for New York City, said the group was focused “not on dramatic things like solving the housing crisis, but it was much more on the brass tacks of helping government work better.”

Leaders of some civic groups say the commission has put a necessary spotlight on dysfunction in city permitting and procurement. The COGE report proposes reforms that could cut qualified nonprofit procurement time in half, to six months from 13 months.

“There are few things more embarrassing than knowing that when someone gets a city contract to provide essential human services, the city employees tell them, ‘You should call and get an advanced loan,’” said Ruth Messinger, a former Manhattan borough president.

The efficiency commission largely punted on trying to fix New York’s civil service rules, given how much the state has authority over this system. Lags in city hiring and struggles to hire high-tech talent came up repeatedly during public testimony to the commission, according to Ms. Wylde.

Various agencies, including the Department of Housing Preservation and Development and the Department of Social Services, have 12 percent vacancy rates. Even the agency responsible for administering civil service exams has a 16 percent vacancy rate, which slows hiring across the city.

Civic groups say there are plenty of steps the mayor could take to speed up hiring, including removing civil service exams for licensed roles or broadening which roles are exempt from the exams. The exams started in the 1880s, as an effort to reduce Tammany Hall patronage, but has now made city hiring in some cases torturously slow. Recently, Mr. Mamdani and the Department of Citywide Administrative Services commissioner, Yume Kitasei, announced the city would waive exam fees for city high schools students and first-time test takers.

Emma Goldberg is a Times reporter who writes about New York City and the Mamdani administration.

Call the Veep, Agent Mulder!

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bret Stephens

By Bret Stephens

Opinion Columnist

Somewhere around the two-hour mark in JD Vance’s nearly three-hour podcast interview last week with Joe Rogan, the pair got into a serious conversation about supernatural and extraterrestrial phenomena. By serious, I mean it in the sense that Rogan seemed to take the subject seriously while Vance cynically, or cretinously, or cravenly, or credulously or conspiratorially — or perhaps it’s all of the above — played along with him.

It contained the following insights from the vice president of the United States:

“If we’re talking about an extraterrestrial being that is humanlike, but not human, that contains effectively infinite powers and is torturing human beings, you can call it an alien if you want, but I think there’s a lot of historical precedent to call that a demon.”

And:

“If you’re looking for me to concede the point that there is something different or could be something different between an angel, a demon, a space alien, a supernatural but non-any-of-those-other-things beings, yes, I concede that.”

And:

“I got two-and-a-half more years as V. P., and I swear to you, if there are little green men, like body remains, I’m not going to text you. I’m going to try to smuggle a camera in and get a photo of these things.”

Call the veep, Agent Mulder!

By this point, the two men had already propounded one conspiracy theory — that the Los Angeles mayoral election had been rigged (a claim previously debunked by a Trump-appointed federal prosecutor); followed by Vance’s accusation that Joe Biden’s staff got him to eat ice cream “in the most ridiculous, suggestive way imaginable” (a remarkable way of turning naked mendacity into adolescent prurience into another conspiracy theory); followed by an exchange about eating corn dogs in public (because, you know); followed by an argument about whether the Ten Commandments should be mandated in Texas public schools, in which neither man appeared to be aware that the commandments are not originally Christian.

Then — sandwiched between the Bible in the classroom and the alien remains that may or may not be in Area 51 — is a discussion that begins with Vance defending his diplomatic work to resolve the war with Iran and devolves into a long foray on Jeffrey Epstein, the sex offender whose death in 2019 Vance — in the most bizarre twist of the podcast — manages to connect with the decline of wokeness in academia. Really.

None of these connections are incidental. Vance describes himself as one of the “O. G. Epstein conspiracy theorists.” Rogan seems keen to push the idea that Israel blackmailed Trump into going to war. Epstein is the prime demonic force in U. S. politics today, a figure of beyond-the-grave powers, who may be as responsible for the current war in the Middle East as he is for the vogue in land-acknowledgment statements by universities. And while Vance dutifully defends his boss against the charge of blackmail, he’s quick to play into Rogan’s suggestion that Epstein “was Mossad.”

Now how did he make that connection — and are the “space Jews” far behind?

“Yeah, Mossad or C. I. A. or some other deep state,” the vice president replies. “Or both. You know, look, was he — he clearly had connections to the upper — the highest levels of American intelligence. He clearly had connections to the highest levels of Israeli intelligence.” In fact, there is no credible evidence whatsoever that Epstein had any ties to either spy agency, a point Vance conveniently covers up by telling Rogan that if evidence did exist, “it wouldn’t exist in 2026.”

So, as Agent Mulder said on “The X Files,” “The truth is out there.” Or maybe the truth is staring us in the face.

The truth — that the most influential media figure in America today, with tens of millions of followers on social media, is a jocular bro with an Everyman affect who seems never to have encountered an idiotic or despicable conspiracy theory he isn’t willing to promote (moon-landing denial) or platform (Hitler revisionism). We are a nation that has moved at speed from the realm of fact colored by opinions to a kingdom of delusion infested with fear.

The truth — that the current vice president is by far the worst person ever to hold the office (move over, Aaron Burr, John C. Calhoun and Spiro T. Agnew); that he thinks, probably correctly, that there’s no political downside in today’s Republican Party to talking like a guy who thinks Dan Brown novels are works of nonfiction; and that it’s equally OK for a person who, by his own admission, has access to all U. S. intelligence to tease the possibility of deep-state conspiracies of the sort his political base is likely to believe. The prospect of this callow and sinister opportunist taking the place of the erratic buffoon now governing us may be the single scariest thought in world politics today.

The truth — that Vance’s interview with Rogan (as close as politics gives us to a national cancer diagnosis) was a blip in the news cycle, because crazy today is every day, and our capacity to feel shocked diminishes with every asinine utterance coming from the vice president’s mouth, to say nothing of that of his boss.

The truth is that the demons are here. We elected them.

What the Cyclospora Outbreak Reveals

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Cyclospora Outbreak

Advertisement

Newsletter

Warming is expected to fuel the spread of food-borne pathogens. We might not be prepared.

By Claire Brown

The United States is going through the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak on record. Thousands of people, mostly in the Midwest, have fallen sick with stomach cramps and severe diarrhea. The authorities have linked the food-borne illnesses to lettuce grown in Mexico and served at some Taco Bell locations.

My colleagues on the Well team have been covering the race to trace the source of the outbreak, and it took a twist this week.

On Saturday, the Food and Drug Administration announced that lab tests had confirmed cyclospora contamination in iceberg lettuce from Mexico. The company that runs the operation, Taylor Farms, issued a recall based on other epidemiological evidence and then expanded it after the lab test came in. But then, on Sunday, the F. D. A. said the test had been a false positive. Taylor Farms is still a focus of the investigation, and the recall remains in effect.

It’s still not clear whether climate change played a role in the current outbreak. Cyclospora is a parasite that spreads through human feces, and it’s rare for investigators to pinpoint a precise source of contamination.

But experts say it’s plausible that warming could contribute to an increase in cyclospora illnesses. Don Schaffner, a food microbiologist at Rutgers University, told me that cyclospora tends to grow in the spring and summer, so higher temperatures could extend its season. In previous cyclospora outbreaks, investigators have theorized that heavy rainfall might have somehow caused human waste to seep into irrigation water, contaminating crops.

Whether or not this outbreak was directly linked to climate change, we know that warming is expected to fuel the spread of a wide variety of food-borne pathogens. And the current episode has exposed potential vulnerabilities in public health detection systems at a time when the need for accurate monitoring of the food supply is only growing more important.

According to the World Health Organization, some 600 million people get sick each year from eating food that has been contaminated with bacteria, parasites or viruses. Scientists have predicted that climate change will drive caseloads higher in many parts of the world.

Higher temperatures and more rain tend to correlate with increases in illnesses from pathogens like salmonella and campylobacter. That’s the case in part because germs can multiply faster in hotter weather. Salmonella, for example, is happiest when the temperature is in the 90s Fahrenheit, when it can grow quickly in animals or on food. A 2014 study found that, in Mississippi, a temperature increase of 1 degree Fahrenheit was associated with an increase in salmonella cases.

Warming oceans pose an emerging food safety risk, too. A 2024 paper found that climate change is “undeniably” contributing to the spread and prevalence of a family of bacteria known as Vibrio, the most infamous of which is the flesh-eating bacteria Vibrio vulnificus. People can get Vibrio infections from eating raw seafood or swimming in contaminated water.

Dry summers and heavy rainfall can each also increase pathogen spread. During droughts, more dust can float through the air, spreading bacteria across farms. On the other hand, torrential rain can distribute germs by spreading human and animal waste from one place to another. Tropical storms, which can be intensified by climate change, are associated with big spikes in E. coli infections.

It’s exceedingly uncommon for the F. D. A. to retract an announcement of a positive lab test. Dr. Schaffner said the agency may have made the statement too early, before it completed confirmation testing.

“Now they’ve got egg on their face, and nobody’s happy,” he said.

In a statement, an F. D. A. spokeswoman, Emily Hilliard, said the Trump Administration has mounted a robust response to the outbreak and has provided Americans with the information they need to protect themselves.

But the back-and-forth has been confusing for people trying to understand which foods to avoid. The retraction didn’t mean the focus of the investigation had shifted away from Taylor Farms or lettuce, but the company issued a statement saying “F. D. A. apologized to us.” The agency said it had not apologized, according to news reports.

“The big concern I have about the flip-flop is also the impact it has on trust,” Dr. Susan Mayne of the Yale School of Public Health told my colleagues. “Changing such an important determination certainly raises questions,” she added.

Federal cuts to health funding may be playing a role in hampering the response to this outbreak. State and local health departments, which rely on federal support to monitor and respond to food-borne illnesses, received less than half the money they requested this year.

Until recently, several states were required to track and report cyclospora cases to a national database. But last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made this voluntary. Incomplete data may have made it harder for officials monitoring the database to identify the outbreak.

“It certainly doesn’t strengthen our ability to do anything about cyclospora,” Dr. Schaffner said.

This fall, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, we’ll be hosting our annual Climate Forward event, bringing together world leaders, policymakers, executives and activists for a full day of live journalism.

We’ve got another exceptional lineup this year, including Gerard Barron, chief executive of The Metals Company; Katharine Hayhoe, chief scientist at The Nature Conservancy; the comedian and writer Nicole Conlan; and the Indigenous chef Pyet DeSpain.

We’re still adding guests, but you can check out full the lineup so far. Tickets are on sale now. If you can’t attend in person, we’ll have a free livestream.

The Old Ladies Against Underwater Garbage was started in 2018 by a retired psychologist who lives on Cape Cod, Mass. The group cleans about 20 ponds a year on the Cape. To date, the women estimate they’ve hauled out about 6,000 pounds of trash.

Members have to be at least 64, and they say the group has reshaped their lives. They’ve grown stronger, because they’ve had to, in order to haul up heavy refuse from the bottom and heave it onto kayaks. And they’ve forged new friendships after relocating or retiring, after becoming widowed or divorced, after losing cancer-ridden breasts.

We joined them for a recent outing on Lovells Pond in Barnstable. The trash never stood a chance. — Cara Buckley

Officials in Boston and the Army Corps of Engineers have a $10 billion plan to defend the city from rising seas, the Commonwealth Beacon reports.

With Another Storm On the Way, Businesses Brace for More Flooding

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Some businesses in low-lying areas of New York City have developed routines to keep their goods and customers dry.

By Hilary Howard

When severe storms hit New York City, workers at Empire Luggage Center in SoHo make sure the suitcases and other merchandise stored in the basement, which regularly floods, are elevated.

At nearby Flipper’s, a restaurant known for its soufflé pancakes, garbage bags are kept handy to distribute to customers to wear over their shoes when they are leaving.

But at the longstanding French bistro Felix, the owner has learned to wait out the storm and clean up after it passes. “We’ve been here for 35 years,” said Alain Denneulin, the owner. “Here, there’s nothing you can do but pray.”

Mr. Denneulin said flooding in SoHo used to be worse until “the city fixed the streets” about 10 years ago. But now that storms are stronger and more frequent because of climate change, the sewers are backing up again, he said. And businesses are on their own to deal with it, he said.

On Tuesday, business owners and residents in low-lying areas around the city were bracing for another evening of flooding, after being pummeled by downpours on Saturday. Videos of waterfalls in subway stations and of narrow city streets turning into gushing streams went viral over the weekend. Severe storms are expected to strike the area in the late afternoon and evening on Tuesday, according to the National Weather Service, which said parts of the Lower Hudson Valley, Connecticut and New Jersey had already been inundated earlier in the day. There are flash flood warnings for all of New York City, except for Staten Island, the National Weather Service said.

“Please exercise caution,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted on social media on Monday night. “City agencies are prepared to respond, but we need everyone to be careful out there.”

Mr. Denneulin and other business owners said they often couldn’t count on the city for help. “We call 311 but often no one shows up,” he said.

Over the weekend, his staff cleaned the sidewalks and streets with bleach and a water-pressure hose to get rid of the stench from the sewer water. Other SoHo business owners said they called the city last weekend to complain as well and got no response.

Once a flood watch has been announced, representatives from the city’s environmental protection, sanitation and transportation departments work to clear major thoroughfares and check and clean about 1,000 of the city’s highest priority catch basins, said Beth DeFalco, a spokeswoman for the city’s Department of Environmental Protection. Catch basins have a chamber to capture debris that comes in with storm water before it moves into the city’s sewer system.

“Topography matters,” Ms. DeFalco said. Most of the priority storm drains are in low-lying areas, she explained. Even when those catch basins are clear, if storm drains on higher ground are clogged, the water will still flow downhill, and more trash along with it, which can reclog catch basins below, she said.

It’s also difficult for city officials to predict where the heavy rain will occur because of “the scattered nature and the intense pockets we are seeing,” she said.

Ms. DeFalco, who lives in Red Hook, a low-lying coastal neighborhood in central Brooklyn, said it did not flood last weekend, but nearby Greenpoint, another coastal area at the northern tip of Brooklyn, “got walloped.”

In March, Mr. Mamdani announced that the city would invest $108 million to upgrade some of the city’s catch basins, but Lisa Garcia, who leads the Department of Environmental Protection, said in a Spectrum News NY1 interview on Tuesday that New Yorkers needed to be vigilant about cleaning catch basins in their neighborhoods. “We now need to change our culture around raining and storms,” she said.

Kissena Park, near Flushing, Queens, floods regularly, since it dips down, like a bowl. One resident said that his neighbors regularly cleaned their storm drains, but the area still floods. And last weekend was no exception.

For his own home, he has added a check valve, a device that makes liquid flow in only one direction, to stop the sewer from backing up in his home. He has also installed a new sump pump in his basement and he surrounds his basement entrance with sandbags before every storm.

The man, who did not want his name used for safety reasons, said it’s terrible to live in fear every time a storm passes, and expressed hope that the city would speed up its planned work in the area to stop the flooding.

Ms. DeFalco said that major infrastructure projects can take years to design and complete. Last weekend, a member of the City Council sent her a video of a business — one of many — that was flooding along Knickerbocker Avenue in Bushwick, in northern Brooklyn. “We’re doing a $390 million project to upsize the sewers there, but those large projects take time,” Ms. DeFalco said. But construction on it is not scheduled to begin until 2029. “It won’t help us in time for this storm.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Hilary Howard is a Times reporter covering how the New York City region is adapting to climate change and other environmental challenges.

The Quick-Fix Fantasies of the World’s Strongmen

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Thomas L. Friedman

By Thomas L. Friedman

Opinion Columnist

Donald Trump, Benjamin Netanyahu and Vladimir Putin are drastically different men, but they do have one important thing in common: Each thinks he is the smartest person in any room he enters. Alas, though, because they have all done the dumbest thing you can do as a leader — surround yourself with sycophants — they have all blundered into dead-end wars from which they can extricate themselves today only by eating a banquet of crow.

Watch out. There is nothing more dangerous than a reckless leader faced with a plate of crow: Sometimes his instinct is to double down on a losing strategy instead.

Let’s start with the Israeli prime minister. The tell that Netanyahu has gone off the rails — and taken the leadership of the famed Israeli intelligence agency, the Mossad, with him — is reflected in two decisions he made that were flat-out crazy: The first is that Israel could topple the Tehran regime with one big blow from the air, and the second was that it could choose Iran’s new leader.

Before I explain just how crazy that was, some quick background: Ever since I saw up close how the Lebanese Christian militia, the Phalangists, helped sucker the Mossad in 1982 into thinking that through a quick invasion Israel could install the Phalangists’ anti-Palestinian leader, Bashir Gemayel, as president in Beirut, I have held the following rule when it comes to the vaunted Israeli intelligence service: If you want someone assassinated in Beirut or Tehran, call the Mossad. If you want to understand political and social trends in Beirut or Tehran, do not call the Mossad. Because the very reason it is good at the first also leads it to be bad at the second.

The Mossad is very good at hunting and killing Israel’s foes, in large part because it is very skilled at recruiting disgruntled citizens in Lebanon, Iran, the West Bank and elsewhere in the Arab world — that is, people who hate their regimes and are willing to work with Israel to topple them. The problem is that these very same agents, motivated either by grievance or money, tend to exaggerate how weak their regime is and how easy bringing it down would be.

They want Israel to do the dirty work for them. The result is that a dupe like Trump, who doesn’t know any history, assumes that because the Mossad is good at assassinating people, it is equally good at predicting what will happen the morning after they are dead.

That explains why, after the White House meeting in February when Netanyahu and the Mossad’s director at the time, David Barnea, essentially argued that if Israel and the United States assassinated Iran’s top leaders, the government would fall and nice people would take over, Trump did not laugh them out of the room. The president apparently assumed that because the Mossad had super assassination powers it also had super analytical powers, and therefore Iran would tumble into his lap the same way Venezuela did when the U. S. removed its president, Nicolás Maduro.

As my colleagues Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported in their must-read book, “Regime Change,” C. I. A. director John Ratcliffe used one word to describe Netanyahu’s Iran regime change scenarios: “farcical.” Trump, confident that he knew better, ignored him and others — and has been paying the price ever since.

The even bigger tell that both Netanyahu and his intelligence agency had become drunk with power was another incredible story The Times uncovered: that Mossad had been grooming former Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad to take over Iran after the government of the supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was wiped out. As my colleagues reported: “Israel’s decision to build a regime-change plan around Mr. Ahmadinejad is an extraordinary twist in the saga of the country’s relations with the former president, who was known for accelerating Iran’s nuclear program, calling regularly for the destruction of Israel and denying the Holocaust.”

Hello, Israel? Do you know anything about modern Iranian history? Have you ever heard of Mohammad Mossadegh? He was the democratically elected prime minister of Iran from 1951 to 1953 who was ousted by a coup engineered by the C. I. A. and Britain’s MI6 after Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company. Fury over that coup, which installed the West’s man in Tehran, still burns in the heart of many Iranians.

The sheer madness that Israel thought it could install Ahmadinejad — and that the Iranian body politic would not reject him the way a human body rejects an organ implant — is insane. Did Netanyahu and the Mossad really think that proud, nationalistic Iranians, even those who hate the clerics governing them, would say: “Oh, thank you, Bibi, for installing our next leader?” The vanity and overreach in thinking that 7.2 million Israeli Jews could decide who would rule more than 90 million Iranian Muslims is astounding.

Trump and Netanyahu are in good company with Putin, who drank his own Kool-Aid by assuming that Ukrainians were all dying to become part of Mother Russia again and that the democratically elected regime in Kyiv would easily fall.

“Putin’s most fundamental error was believing his own narrative that Ukrainians and Russians were ‘one people’ and that Ukrainian independence was merely an artificial Western construct,” Robbin Laird, a military analyst, noted last year. “This ideological blind spot led him to expect that Russian forces would be welcomed as liberators.”

In a perfect echo of what happened in Iran, Russian intelligence appeared to have relied too heavily “on pro-Russian sources who told Moscow what it wanted to hear,” Laird said, “rather than providing accurate ground truth about Ukrainian sentiment and capabilities.”

Netanyahu, for all his tactical victories over Hamas, Hezbollah and Tehran, has not converted any of it into a new strategic reality for Israel. That would require him to make clear that his military operations in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran were meant to make the region safe for an Israeli-Palestinian peace.

Instead, what the whole world sees is Netanyahu trying to make the region safe for an Israeli annexation of Gaza and the West Bank, and his being ready to throw away everything else — normalization with Saudi Arabia, the support of many young Americans, the support of the Democratic Party, the support of Western Europe and the independence of Israel’s judiciary — to get it.

Meanwhile, Trump has weakened and isolated America by lazily choosing to invade Iran with no allies, no international legitimation and no Plan B to eliminate Tehran’s ability to build a weapon of mass destruction. Instead, Trump enabled Iran to discover two incredibly cheap and effective weapons of mass disruption: controlling the Strait of Hormuz and bombing America’s Persian Gulf allies nearly every time Trump bombs Iran.

And Putin — instead of doing the hard work of making Russia a free and open society that Ukrainians actually might be attracted to — has turned what was a weak Russian democracy into a full-blown police state, with a vulnerable petro-economy. Today, Russia is nowhere to be found in the A. I. revolution. It is as if cars were just invented and Putin said he’d prefer to invest in more horses — and his 19th-century fantasy of a unified Russian Motherland.

What we have today is three leaders all now trying to bomb their way out of a blind alley.

But let us not forget the twisted, cynical, incompetent leaders who have been running Iran since 1979. They, too, are in their own cul-de-sac. Instead of empowering their talented population, Iran’s clerical dictators chose to ensconce themselves in power for 47 years by gunning down opponents, cramming puritanical Islam down the throats of their people and wasting billions of dollars trying to destroy Israel.

Let us hope that one day their people will topple them on their own, maybe with help from a surprising, nonsovereign power. Iran’s leaders recklessly over-exploited their environment and recklessly dammed up too many rivers to reward regime cronies and are now totally vulnerable to a much more powerful foe than Trump or Netanyahu: Mother Nature. The most harrowing report about Iran’s future was put out seven months ago by analysts writing in the highly regarded Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists — and it never mentioned nuclear weapons. It mentioned only the nation’s acute water crisis, which may have shut down more Iranian institutions than Israel and America combined.

“During the summer of 2025, Iran experienced an exceptional heat wave, with daytime temperatures across several regions, including Tehran, approaching 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and forcing the temporary closure of public offices and banks,” the analysts said. “During this period, major reservoirs supplying the Tehran region reached record-low levels. … Officials warned that the capital city may even have to be evacuated if water supplies fail to recover.”

Bottom line, eventually all these conflicts will end in negotiations, because none of these leaders can sustain their stupid wars indefinitely. The only question is when they will have to call the waiter over and say: “Young man, could you please bring me a plate of crow.”

Pentagon Identifies Another Soldier Killed in Iran War

The New York Times July 21, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, the 17th service member to be named, was killed during the disposal of a drone in northern Iraq.

By Jacey FortinPooja Salhotra and Maia Spoto

The Pentagon on Tuesday released the name of a U. S. soldier killed during the disposal of an Iranian drone in northern Iraq.

Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of Fayetteville, N. C., died Saturday during a controlled detonation at Erbil Air Base. The incident is under investigation, the Pentagon said.

Sergeant Swinton had been assigned to the 108th Air Defense Artillery Brigade at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina.

Lt. Gen. John L. Rafferty, the commanding general of U. S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said in a statement that Sergeant Swinton’s death had “occurred during an operation to safeguard fellow soldiers.”

“His service will not be forgotten,” General Rafferty added, “and his sacrifice is not in vain.”

Sergeant Swinton was not involved in the actual detonation, but was killed by flying debris from the blast, said a U. S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters.

The announcement came one day after the Pentagon released the names of two other soldiers killed in the war in recent days. They died in Jordan after an Iranian attack there on Friday. There have now been 17 American military personnel killed since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

The deaths occurred during a week of spiraling clashes between U. S. and Iranian forces in the Persian Gulf, where tensions have worsened since the collapse of a cease-fire reached by the countries last month.

As of Tuesday morning, U. S. forces had been striking targets in Iran, including military command centers and missile and drone launch sites, for 10 straight nights, according to U. S. Central Command. Iran said on Tuesday that it had attacked Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan, countries that host U. S. military bases.

The Iranian attack on Friday that killed two soldiers in Jordan also left another soldier missing, but remains found at the scene are believed to be those of the missing soldier.

In a text message to The New York Times, Sergeant Swinton’s mother, Christel Swinton Andujar, said her son was adventurous, fearless and “the kind of person who could light up any room.”

He grew up in Cumberland County, N. C., and loved basketball and fishing, his mother said. He was married and had two children.

“He had a contagious laugh, an incredible sense of humor and loved making people smile,” Ms. Swinton Andujar said. “He was a true jokester who believed life was meant to be lived to the fullest.”

He enlisted in the Army in 2017 as an air defense early warning system operator, according to the U. S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command.

The Army said in a statement on Tuesday that Sergeant Swinton would receive the Bronze Star, the Purple Heart and the Combat Action Badge, and that he would be posthumously promoted to staff sergeant.

“Sergeant Swinton was an experienced noncommissioned officer who took great pride in his work and the people around him,” said Brig. Gen. John Dawber, who leads the 32nd Army Air and Missile Defense Command. “He answered the call to duty with courage, honor and selfless dedication.”

“He was an amazing man,” Jamiah Gonzalez-Swinton, his wife, said tearfully when reached by phone on Tuesday morning. She was unable to say more.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

A Houthi Blockade Could Worsen an Already Fragile Oil Market

The New York Times July 21, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed, the militant group’s threats in the Red Sea jeopardize Saudi Arabia’s main workaround for oil exports.

By Jenny GrossRebecca F. Elliott and Lisa Friedman

Jenny Gross reported from London, Rebecca F. Elliott from New York and Lisa Friedman from Washington.

Threats from the Iran-backed Houthi militant group this week to block Saudi Arabia’s use of the Red Sea risk cutting off a crucial alternative path for Mideast oil and further destabilizing a global energy market upended by the war in Iran.

Since March, the Saudis have been moving millions of barrels of oil west each day through a pipeline and loading it onto tankers. From there, most of the vessels have navigated the Bab al-Mandab strait, a waterway at the southern end of the Red Sea, mostly to customers in Asia.

Sources: Global Energy Monitor (pipelines); Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute (Houthi-controlled areas)

Samuel Granados/The New York Times

Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Now, another choke point might be turned into a geopolitical weapon, underlining how drastically trade routes have been scrambled. Energy producers that devised workarounds to deliver shipments are now facing the possibility of needing to map new routes.

It was not apparent how or even whether the Houthis, who are based in Yemen, will carry through on their declaration, which they issued on Monday. But there were signs that the threat could be affecting sea traffic. Two oil tankers heading toward the Bab al-Mandab made U-turns and were moving north toward the Suez Canal, according to Kpler, a maritime data company. But that route can be costlier and logistically more complex.

On Tuesday, more than 93 crude oil tankers were operating in the Red Sea, a big increase from the approximately 50 tankers a day before the war, Kpler found, a reflection of the increased use of Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu port on the Red Sea. In recent months, Saudi Arabia has been exporting around 3.6 million barrels of oil and related fuels a day via the Bab al-Mandab strait. Before the war, the Saudis exported fewer than one million barrels per day via that route. Most of the oil shipped from Saudi ports south through the Red Sea is sent to South Korea, Japan, China and other destinations in Asia.

Even though the redirection of oil flows away from the Persian Gulf has allowed Saudi Arabia to continue delivering energy supplies to global markets, its overall exports of crude are running at a fraction of prewar levels.

Note: Data includes exports of crude oil and refined fuels, such as gasoline and diesel.

Source: Kpler.

Rebecca F. Elliott/The New York Times

According to a shipping executive, speaking on the condition of anonymity over concerns about the safety of his seafarers and vessels, shipowners received an email dated Monday from the Houthis warning them against loading cargo at Saudi Arabian ports. A Houthi official confirmed the email.

Oil traders have so far not reacted strongly to the Houthi threat. Brent, the global oil benchmark, is up about 3 percent this week to above $90 a barrel.

Several factors are cushioning oil prices. China is importing much less oil, and the United Arab Emirates is producing more, Ian Bremmer, the president of Eurasia Group, a geopolitical risk consultancy, wrote in a note. At the same time, the United States still has enough stockpiles of gasoline and diesel to meet roughly two months’ worth of demand.

But any attack on ships or infrastructure in the Red Sea would have a chilling effect on the market, analysts said.

“Even if one tanker gets hit by a drone, then that very much sends a signal to shipowners and crews,” said Hamad Hussain, an economist with Capital Economics, a consulting firm. “It would only take a couple to spook ships from making the trip.”

If Saudi Arabia deems shipping oil via the Red Sea’s Bab al-Mandab strait too risky, it has alternatives: It could send oil and fuels north to the Mediterranean via a pipeline in Egypt or the Suez Canal.

That approach, however, would be logistically challenging, not to mention very expensive. The Egyptian pipeline cannot accommodate all the oil that Saudi Arabia is currently sending south, and the Suez Canal is too shallow for fully loaded crude tankers. It would take an extra four weeks to export oil from Saudi Arabia to Asia via the northern route, said Matt Smith, a Kpler analyst.

The Houthis have caused lasting disruptions in the Red Sea in the past, attacking ships in 2023 shortly after the onset of the Gaza war. Today, Red Sea traffic is at only 55 percent to 60 percent of what it was before 2023, according to data from Windward, a maritime data firm.

The latest threats come at a particularly difficult time, with Iran’s attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz prompting many shipowners and operators to decide it is too dangerous to use that waterway. The strait has been practically at a standstill, with the exception of a brief cease-fire, since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. Only 12 ships passed through the critical waterway on Monday, Kpler said, down from about 130 before the war.

The Houthis control a significant part of Yemen. The threat to blockade Saudi Arabia, a U. S. ally, risks opening a new front in the regional war and further disrupting global energy supplies. Last week, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking Yemen’s main international airport in Sanaa.

But Gregory Brew, a senior analyst with the Eurasia Group, said the last time hostilities flared between Saudi Arabia and Yemen in 2023, the Houthis appeared to avoid attacking ships carrying Saudi oil.

That history, he said, has given investors some hope that the newest Houthi threats will not escalate. And yet even a limited offensive by the Houthis would worry markets and raise prices, Mr. Brew said. If that happens, he said, “Oil prices would be likely to climb above $100 a barrel this month unless we get decisive de-escalation between the United States and Iran.”

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

Google Releases Three New A. I. Models

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The models include one that is the company’s most powerful and another that is fine-tuned for cybersecurity, as Google competes with rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic.

By Kate Conger

Reporting from San Francisco

Google on Tuesday released three new artificial intelligence models, including Gemini 3.6 Flash, its most powerful, and Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, which is fine-tuned for cybersecurity.

Google is aiming to compete with rivals such as Anthropic and OpenAI on cutting-edge models and on cybersecurity, an area in which the two start-ups have forged ahead this year with powerful systems that can identify security vulnerabilities in software.

Gemini Flash 3.6 improves on the capabilities of Google’s previous version of Flash, which performed strongly on benchmarks like coding and finance tasks, according to A. I. leaderboards. The new model is also cheaper for users.

Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber can find and patch security vulnerabilities at a lower cost than other larger models, the company said. The third model, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, is designed for tasks like managing A. I. “agents,” which are bots that can act autonomously to function like digital personal assistants.

The new Flash models were built “to meet the sweet spot of efficiency and quality,” Tulsee Doshi, a senior director of product management on Google’s Gemini team, said in a statement.

Google has also been working on a flagship A. I. model called Gemini 3.5 Pro, which is expected to be its highest performing system. The Silicon Valley company had said in May that Pro would be rolled out in June, but it remains unavailable. Google said Pro was still in testing and would be made “broadly available as soon as it’s ready.”

Since OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot kicked off the A. I. boom in 2022, Google has poured money and effort into leading the race. Its Gemini A. I. models soon ranked among the top A. I. tools.

But in recent months, Google has been upstaged by advanced new models from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as new models from Chinese start-ups such as Moonshot AI. This month, Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, also released a model that crept ahead of Gemini’s capabilities, according to several leaderboards.

Cybersecurity has increasingly been a focus for A. I. models. The systems can find flaws in software and fix them more rapidly than humans, but they can also be used to exploit vulnerabilities and carry out cyberattacks.

In April, Anthropic released a cybersecurity-focused model called Mythos, which it said could create a cybersecurity “reckoning.” To prevent the powerful model from falling into the wrong hands, the company made it only available to a small group of organizations so they could defend against cyberattacks. Anthropic later released Fable, a model with similar capabilities and guardrails meant to prevent it from being used for hacking.

OpenAI soon introduced its own cybersecurity model and made it available to only a limited group of organizations to prepare their defenses, before rolling it out more broadly. (The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Google said it was taking a similar approach with Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber. In testing, the model found 55 problems in a complex piece of open-source code known as V8 JavaScript Engine, including 10 vulnerabilities that no other model had uncovered before, the company said.

“The model will be exclusively available to governments and trusted partners,” Ms. Doshi said. “This will give frontline defenders a head start in finding and fixing critical vulnerabilities before they can be exploited, while mitigating against broader misuse.”

Google said the new Flash models would be available for a lower cost than its previous offerings. The systems use 17 percent fewer tokens, which are the units of measurement for A. I. use, than earlier models. That means developers will spend less money to complete the same tasks.

Last week I built a Go game tutor using both Claude Fable 5 and Kimi K3, and they created similar quality output. Kimi took the longest and used the most tokens, but the entire task cost was about 1/2 Fable, because the per-token cost is much less. Today I built the same app, using the same prompt but with Gemini 3,6 Flash. It created an app just as good as the others, but a a little cheaper than even K3 and far, far faster. It was done with the entire app so fast I had to make sure it wasn't the LLM hallucinating completion. I don't remember anything in my professional lifetime that has advanced faster and iterated more frequently than this competition between LLM models.

@mcomfort It is really wild to see how fast these models are changing, even in an industry that's known for rapid development. Why did you choose a Go game tutor as your test? Are there any notable differences between the tutors that the different models create?

I stopped using Google because of the AI thing. Duck, Duck Go is my permanent search engine.

@Joyce I wrote yesterday about how Search is changing as Google incorporates more A. I. tools, and what that means for the open web, which might be interesting to you if you're thinking about how A. I. is being incorporated into more and more products https://www. nytimes. com/2026/07/20/technology/google-ai-open-web. html

A new nonprofit wants to streamline gene therapy for diseases often avoided by pharmaceutical companies — making treatment more like a routine procedure than a bespoke drug.

Nina Frost with her 10-year-old daughter, Annabel, who at age 2 months was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder that affects just 400 children in the United States and has no cure. Credit... Moriah Ratner for The New York Times

Supported by

By Gina Kolata

Without fail, David Liu of the Broad Institute gets at least 20 messages every week from desperate parents. Their child, they’ll explain, has an ultrarare and devastating disorder caused by a mutant gene. Can he help them develop a gene therapy?

Dr. Liu, a gene-editing researcher, answers honestly: Although the science is there — researchers can edit and silence the genes that cause disease relatively easily — the system for developing treatments for rare diseases is just not economically feasible. It typically takes years and hundreds of millions of dollars.

The catchphrase, said Dr. Wendy Chung of Boston Children’s Hospital, is “too rare to care.”

Now, Dr. Liu, Dr. Chung and their colleagues at the Broad Institute, Boston Children’s and the Jackson Laboratory are hoping to change that mentality. On Tuesday, they announced the start of a new nonprofit, the Center for Therapeutic Genetics, to develop gene therapy treatments that can be used and reused in disease after disease.

Treatments developed by the center would be viewed more like routine procedures than drugs. In each case, all that would be changed are the instructions to a gene editor. There would be no need to start anew for every patient.

In principle, with more centers like this one, the new approach could improve the lives of millions of people, Dr. Liu said. About 400 million people worldwide and 25 to 30 million in the United States have a rare disease. Half are children, and a third die before they turn 5.

The project is starting with a $34.5 million contract from the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, a federal agency that supports high-risk, high-reward medical research. It will begin by focusing on neurological disorders that can result in seizures. That work, the researchers hope, will demonstrate how an editing system that fixes mutations in brain cells can be used for more than one genetic brain disease, including ones that strike adults, like Huntington’s.

The first, called alternating hemiplegia of childhood, or AHC, affects just 400 children in the United States. Among them is 10-year-old Annabel Frost. Her parents, Simon Frost and Nina English Frost, who live in Washington, have made getting gene therapy for children with AHC the center of their lives.

When Annabel was 2 months old she started having seizure-like episodes and recurrent bouts of paralysis — her limbs, even her whole body, would be immobile for days or as long as a week. Her parents crossed the country, consulting with neurologists, but no one knew what was wrong.

After they finally received a diagnosis of AHC and learned there was no cure, the Frosts formed a nonprofit and began raising money; they have raised more than $4 million in the past eight years. But expecting families to follow that path — doing fund-raising, organizing golf tournaments, sponsoring 5K races — “is very unfair,” said Dr. Chung, especially when parents are caring for a sick child. And it is still almost never enough to get a company interested in developing a treatment.

Ms. Frost said she and Mr. Frost knew that. So their foundation deliberately supported research that laid the groundwork for a gene therapy for AHC. Then they approached Dr. Liu. “We did not simply bring David a disease and ask him to solve it,” Ms. Frost said. “We brought him a developed scientific opportunity.”

Dr. Liu’s group had extended the life of mice with Niemann-Pick, a genetic brain disease, which gave them hope. For AHC, Ms. Frost said, “we wanted him to target the same cells.”

But it is much easier to get a gene editor to the brain of a mouse than to the brain of a person. With mice, scientists can just inject the editor into their tiny brains. With humans, that won’t work. The challenge is to get a disabled virus carrying gene-editing instructions through the blood-brain barrier, a membrane that protects the brain from infections and toxins.

But researchers at the Broad Institute led by Ben Deverman have found a way. They can hijack a carrier protein that delivers iron into the brain.

That discovery, said Dr. Timothy Yu, a team member from Boston Children’s, “was a real lightbulb moment.”

Treatment will involve an intravenous injection of the engineered virus, which will shuttle through the blood-brain barrier and enter the brain’s intracellular space. From there the editor will enter brain cells where it will slide along the DNA to the mutation. Then the editor will turn the mutated gene into the healthy one.

The plan is to initially treat children most severely affected by AHC. Annabel is not among them, so she will not be first in line.

The method will also be used to treat another neurological disorder, a genetic form of severe childhood epilepsy, Dravet syndrome, which occurs in about one in 15,700 births. Twenty percent of patients die before age 18, said Mary Anne Meskis, the chief executive and co-founder of the Dravet Syndrome Foundation. Many die in their sleep.

“Our parents live in fear every day that when we put our child to sleep at night the child might not wake up,” said Ms. Meskis, who lives near Asheville, N. C.

Ms. Meskis’s 26-year-old son Elliot had his first seizure when he was 6 months old. It lasted an hour before emergency room doctors could stop it. The next month he had another. The next month, another. When Elliot was 18 months old he also began to have thousands of brief seizures every day in which he would blink or suddenly jerk his head. He had episodes of paralysis, which could last for days or even a week.

His parents finally got a diagnosis of Dravet when Elliot was 4. He began taking multiple daily medications that reduced the length of his seizures, but he functions at the level of a 3-to-5-year-old and doesn’t have expressive language.

Dr. Liu and his colleagues have corrected Dravet in mice by injecting a gene editor into the animals’ brains, a proof of principle. Now they will try it in humans.

Elliot’s brain may be too damaged at his age for gene therapy to cure him. The hope, though, is that it might help or cure young children.

The center is not going to solve the problem of getting genetic therapies to patients overnight, its founders emphasized. But the researchers hope the work will lead to methodologies that other doctors can pick up and apply to their own patients.

To achieve that, the center will make its work public whenever possible. That’s something that for-profit companies typically don’t do but that is needed to make real progress, said Dr. Mark Kay, who is the head of the Division of Human Gene Therapy at Stanford University and not involved with the new center. “I really like and support this idea,” Dr. Kay said.

It will be hard at first, Dr. Chung predicted. But she feels a sense of urgency.

“My patients don’t have time to wait,” she said. “We will lose a generation.”

Gina Kolata reports on diseases and treatments, how treatments are discovered and tested, and how they affect people.

Trump Pushes Chinese Election Threat, but Files Show Russia’s Heavy Hand

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Intelligence documents that the White House released to back up President Trump’s claims about China highlight Russian efforts to influence U. S. elections.

By Alan Feuer and Dustin Volz

Alan Feuer has covered the legal battles surrounding the 2020 election. Dustin Volz has covered foreign election meddling since the 2016 presidential race.

President Trump’s prime-time speech last Thursday was intended to shore up his tenacious lies that the 2020 election was stolen from him and leaned heavily on recycled claims that the Chinese government tried to tip the scales against him.

But a trove of intelligence documents that Mr. Trump declassified in hopes that they would bolster his assertions arguably made a stronger case that a different country — Russia — had meddled in the race.

Mr. Trump, nonetheless, barely mentioned Russia during his 25-minute address, in keeping with his longstanding aversion to admitting what criminal and congressional investigators have said for years: Senior Russian officials, including Vladimir V. Putin, the country’s president, worked to undermine Mr. Trump’s opponents in both his 2016 and 2020 campaigns.

“He forgets or just omits that the biggest country that tries to influence on every election is Russia,” Senator Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said on Sunday during an appearance on CBS’s “Face the Nation.” “We’ve documented that time and again.”

The prominence of Russia in the newly declassified documents — and Mr. Trump’s relative silence about the country during his address — was only the latest reminder of how the president has often sought to twist U. S. intelligence to support his falsehoods about elections he has run in. Those efforts have become more worrisome now that Mr. Trump has installed inexperienced loyalists and given them oversight of U. S. intelligence agencies. Bill Pulte, a housing official, is serving as the acting director of national intelligence until Jay Clayton, the U. S. attorney in Manhattan, is confirmed.

The documents that Mr. Trump declassified last week were not the first to highlight efforts by the Russians to influence American elections. In many cases, the new files reflect information that was made public five or six years ago, either in previous disclosures by U. S. intelligence agencies or public statements by senior officials in the first Trump administration.

Most of the allegations about Russian election meddling in the 2020 election were contained in an analysis by the National Intelligence Council dated Aug. 19 that year, less than three months before Mr. Trump lost to Joseph R. Biden Jr. in a defeat that even now he refuses to acknowledge.

The analysis maintained that Mr. Putin and senior officials in his government oversaw efforts to damage Mr. Biden’s campaign.

Moreover, it said, the Russians conspired with officials and “other prominent persons” in the United States to “orchestrate a high-profile corruption scandal” implicating Mr. Biden and the Democratic Party at the peak of the campaign. Republicans have accused Mr. Biden of being involved, while vice president, in corrupt business dealings with his son Hunter and the Ukrainian energy firm Burisma.

“Their aim is to defeat the former vice president” — Mr. Biden — “and ensure the president’s victory,” the intelligence council concluded, referring to Mr. Trump.

The same assessment also made clear that Iran had taken some clumsier but still fairly aggressive efforts to harm Mr. Trump’s electoral prospects, actions that Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the supreme leader, had most likely ordered. But Mr. Trump had little to say on Thursday night about Iranian election meddling, even though the United States is still at war with Iran. He instead highlighted China’s relatively muted actions, which he asserted had been hidden from him and the American people.

The claims surrounding Burisma are among the longest-lasting efforts to smear Mr. Biden. They center on accusations that while serving in the White House under President Barack Obama, he used his power to derail a corruption inquiry into the company to protect Hunter Biden, who sat on its board of directors.

At one point, an F. B. I. informant, Alexander Smirnov, claimed that the oligarch owner of Burisma had paid $5 million to both Mr. Biden and his son. But Mr. Smirnov was ultimately charged with lying about the purported bribes and admitted that he had been fed information by Russian intelligence.

A U. S. intelligence community analysis from March 2021 found that proxies linked to Russian intelligence had promoted false stories about the Biden family “to U. S. media organizations, U. S. officials and prominent U. S. individuals, including some close to former President Trump and his administration.”

Federal prosecutors also undertook an expansive investigation into whether Ukrainian officials had helped orchestrate a plan to damage Mr. Biden’s 2020 campaign, including by using Rudolph W. Giuliani, Mr. Trump’s onetime personal lawyer, to help spread their misleading claims. Mr. Giuliani was never charged in the inquiry.

Russia’s disinformation campaigns, U. S. officials maintain, have included promoting accusations of corruption between the Biden family and Ukraine — as well as a conspiracy theory that Ukraine, not Russia, interfered in Mr. Trump’s 2016 campaign against Hillary Clinton.

Russia-aligned operatives met with people tied to the Trump administration to further seed these narratives. And that dynamic played a role in Mr. Trump’s first impeachment when he urged the newly elected Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky, to investigate the Bidens and then later withheld military funding the country needed in its ongoing conflict with Russian-backed separatists.

Even after Mr. Trump left office in 2021, his congressional allies continued examining the allegations about Mr. Biden and Ukraine but eventually came up empty. In 2023, House Republicans acknowledged that they had not uncovered incriminating material about Mr. Biden, despite their frequent insinuations that he and his family had been involved in criminal conduct and corruption.

Senator Angus King, the Maine independent, seemed to scratch his head about why Mr. Trump had given short shrift to Russian interference during his speech in an opinion article he wrote over the weekend.

“Amazingly,” Mr. King wrote, “Russia was barely mentioned in the speech, even though Russia has consistently been the most aggressive foreign meddler in our elections over the past decade.”

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

A Family’s Daring Escape From North Korea ‘to Live and Stand Tall’

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Their resolve for freedom hardened during the pandemic, when they lived through a crippling food shortage and were forced to witness frequent public executions.

By Choe Sang-Hun

Reporting from Seoul

Rain lashed a flimsy wooden boat as it tossed through a churning sea, its engine straining against the swell. Under the cover of a stormy night three years ago, the vessel was fleeing North Korea.

On board were nine people, including two small children and a woman who was six months pregnant. Only a couple of the passengers had seafaring experience. They eluded a patrol ship, speeding across the world’s most heavily guarded maritime border.

Soon after their boat lurched into South Korean waters, a high-speed warship of the South’s navy bore down on it, tearing the water in aggressive circles. Snipers on the vessel trained their laser sights on the chests of the three adult men on the wooden boat.

Through a loudspeaker, a voice boomed: “Are you lost? Engine trouble?”

The North Koreans shouted: “Please help. We are defecting.”
