The red dots remained stubbornly fixed on their chests. The South Koreans were taking no chances: The three men were clad in North Korean military uniforms, camouflage for a high-stakes escape. Desperate, the men shouted into the boat’s cramped hold for the other passengers to emerge in order to prove that they were civilians. From below, the two children, a 5-year-old girl and 3-year-old boy, were hauled up first, both pale and wasted from seasickness. Only then did the red dots drop off.

The North Koreans, led by Kim Il-hyeok and his younger brother, Yi-hyeok, were bound together by blood and marriage. The brothers, both in their 30s at the time, were accompanied by their mother and their families: Il-heyok’s partner, who was pregnant, and Yi-hyeok’s wife, their two children, his mother-in-law and brother-in-law.

The family, who defected in 2023, were among the few who managed to escape North Korea after its leader, Kim Jong-un, imposed a crushing lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic. They arrived in their adopted country with rare insights into a nation that had been choked off from the outside world. Some details of their escape have not been previously reported.

“That night,” said Yi-hyeok’s wife, Yu-mi, “we crossed from a sea of darkness to a sea of freedom.”

Over several months of interviews in South Korea, Il-hyeok ​spoke with the same swagger that he had developed as a self-described “troublemaker” in North Korea. Yu-mi ​was reserved, pulling her legs tightly to her chest as she spoke. Her mother, who asked not to be named but agreed to be photographed, weighed every word, fearing how her comments might affect relatives left behind in the North. But they all spoke with conviction about why they had to leave North Korea. (The rest of the extended family declined to be interviewed.)

The brothers came from Pyoksong, a county in North Korea’s southwest.

During the famine of the late 1990s, their father, a railway security official, returned with grim accounts from the hardest-hit provinces: The emaciated bodies of children found outside train stations were frozen solid, thumping like frozen fish when they were tossed onto trucks headed to burial grounds. He was the first in the family to lose faith in a ruling class that was unable to feed its people.

One night after his sons reached adulthood, he took them to a hill and pointed toward a cluster of lights across the South Korean border.

“That’s where we should go,” he said. “To live and stand tall.”

Yu-mi lived in the ​nearby coastal town of Kangryong. From there, she could see planes glinting in the sun as they rose from Incheon International Airport, just across the water — a shimmering vision of possibility, yet unreachable for North Koreans barred from travel and cut off from the internet.

“Our country felt like a prison without bars,” she said.

Beginning in kindergarten, children sang the anthem “We Have Nothing to Envy,” even as they were mobilized to haul river water or scour hills for herbs and pine nuts.​ After long workdays, adults attended compulsory “life review sessions,” writing self-criticism and pledges of loyalty. When Kim Jong-un visited ​an island near Yu-mi’s town in 2013, soldiers and villagers swarmed into the sea in jubilation. She knew the scene was staged; ordinary residents, she said, had been banned from leaving home.

In the face of the propaganda, a contraband culture spread. South Korean films and dramas circulated on USB drives smuggled from China. In Kangryong, the devices also arrived inside plastic bottles released by South Korean activists across the water, along with rice and mini-Bibles. Officials warned the bottles contained poison, but South Korean entertainment was winning.

Il-hyeok idolized K-pop groups like Girls’ Generation and styled his hair in a mohawk like BigBang’s Taeyang. He was arrested for “capitalist delinquency” and released only after paying a bribe, his hair razored. He and his friends once secretly watched “Valkyrie,” the Tom Cruise film about the plot to kill Hitler. When the conspirators failed and were executed, his friends wept.

The brothers’ notion of deserting North Korea felt just as perilous. Their father forbade them from marrying, reasoning that the larger the family, the greater the risk of being caught while defecting. He then used connections to transfer Yi-hyeok, his youngest, to Kangryong, where he learned navigation, mapped guard posts, and cultivated ties with officials. Yi-hyeok became a helmet diver, who harvests seafood from the ocean floor, breathing fresh air piped through a surface hose. He eventually met Yu-mi.

Il-hyeok worked in North Korea’s shadow economy, bribing his way into opportunity and out of trouble. He butchered animals for restaurants, ran a small gold mine and bought rice stolen from state granaries, reselling it at a profit. He also grew disillusioned with the system he was gaming.

Then, in 2014, their father died unexpectedly. The South Korean dream seemed to die with him.

Where Il-hyeok, the older brother, was restless, Yi-hyeok was steady. He married Yu-mi in 2017, and the couple soon had their two children. He joined a military-run fisheries company, operating three vessels. Despite a United Nations ban, Chinese buyers worked openly in Kangryong, and on a good day Yi-hyeok could earn more than a typical worker​’s annual salary.

Il-hyeok began dating a kindergarten teacher. Defection was no longer a priority.

“When I mentioned it, my brother told me to watch my mouth,” Il-hyeok recalled.

The pandemic overturned everything.

North Korea imposed one of the world’s harshest lockdowns. In Kangryong, access to the sea was closed off with barbed wire and armed guards. Yi-hyeok’s boats rusted and his debts mounted. Officials claimed that South Korea was dumping infected bodies and waste into border waters. Yet boats supplying seafood to the top tiers of society continued to fish.

“The elites still ate whatever they wanted,” Yu-mi said.

Il-hyeok​ once filmed a gaunt toothless man in rags begging for food. The man said soldiers had shot a villager who tried to gather crabs.

“They are ruthless,” he said in a tired whisper. “Even if you won’t give alms, you shouldn’t break the beggar’s bowl.”

Public executions grew more frequent, targeting those accused of committing violent crimes like murder, which surged during the lockdown, or of distributing “nonsocialist” content such as South Korean dramas. Thousands, including the brothers, were forced to watch as rifle fire cracked across the execution grounds. The crowds dispersed in silence.

“The goal was to instill fear,” Il-hyeok said. “To erase any fantasy about the outside world.”

The authorities were closing in on him, too.

​He wanted to marry his girlfriend, the daughter of a farmer. In a system that claimed to be classless, marrying a woman who worked on a collective farm — even as a teacher — would mean a loss of status for Il-hyeok. Both families opposed the match. The couple moved in together anyway. Then, in 2022, Kim Jong‑un banned unmarried cohabitation. Offenders faced labor camps.

“I had to choose between her and North Korea,” Il-hyeok said. “I chose South Korea — and a true class revolution.”

The brothers no longer argued about whether to leave — only how.

By early 2023, North Korea had begun easing its pandemic restrictions. Yi-hyeok’s boats were among the first permitted back to sea. But the window to escape was already closing. The authorities were preparing to install surveillance cameras along the coast to deter defections.

The brothers spoke in code over the phone. “Good weather” meant a storm was coming, forcing patrol boats back to port. “We’ve got a good catch — come down here” meant Il-hyeok should bring their mother and his girlfriend to Kangryong.

The weather and the catch were ideal the night of May 6, 2023.

Yu-mi’s mot​her, a 52-year-old widow, signed up last, just five hours before departure.

“I could die trying to escape,” she said. “But if my family reached the South and I stayed behind, I’d be as good as dead anyway — the relative of traitors.”

Yi-hyeok’s brother-in-law, his fishing partner, slipped away by boat and waited offshore. The rest of the family crossed a coastal hill strewn with land mines to reach a secluded beach. To carry Yi-hyeok’s two young children more easily, the brothers sealed them inside burlap sacks and hoisted them onto their shoulders. Before they closed the sacks, Yu-mi caught her children looking up at her.

“I thought it might be the last time I’d ever see them,” she said. “I cried, and my husband teared up, too.”

Yi-hyeok’s brother-in-law spotted the prearranged signal — a flashlight blinking three times from the beach — and steered the boat in to pick up the rest of the extended family. Around 10 p. m., the 30-foot-long vessel pulled away, its engine throttled down to little more than a brisk walking pace as it tried to slip quietly toward Yeonpyeong Island in South Korea, just nine miles away.

Below deck, Yu-mi suddenly felt ​the engine roar to full throttle, filling the hold with black exhaust and leaving the women and children seasick. Her youngest child’s eyes rolled back. She carried him up for fresh air — and found the men on deck in a panic.

“That’s when I saw a searchlight from a North Korean patrol boat sweeping across the waves behind us,” she said. “My heart dropped.”

The brothers had already agreed on what to do if they couldn’t outrun a security vessel: strap life jackets and flashlights onto the women and children and send them into the sea, trusting the current to carry them south. The men would steer the boat away as a decoy, making a last stand with 20-inch knives and homemade red-pepper bombs. To lighten the boat, Il-hyeok threw anything heavy overboard — axes, wrenches, fishing net, his brother’s air compressor for helmet diving.

​He ran below deck, fastened a life jacket onto his partner and rushed back outside. She believed he was about to throw her into the sea to save the others. His mother​ thought her son had chosen to save his girlfriend before his mother.

“It gave me endless trouble with them, until I could convince them they’d misunderstood me,” he said.

Gradually, the searchlight behind them faded. The brothers later speculated that the fishing net they had thrown overboard had tangled in the pursuing boat’s propeller.

Their two-hour gamble ended shortly after midnight, after the South Korean vessel stopped them and all nine family members were brought aboard.

An officer greeted them: “Welcome to paradise.”

Before the​y disembarked, the officer raised his fist and shouted, “Fighting!” The English word — common in South Korea as encouragement — was unfamiliar to the North Koreans.

“But he was smiling and shaking our hands,” Yu-mi said, “so we assumed he wished us well.”

​In the South, Yu-mi studied to gain an accounting clerk certificate and found work at a school. Her brother enrolled in college, while Yi-hyeok returned to helmet-diving for seafood.

“My brother joked the diving gear here was so advanced he could fall asleep underwater if he wanted to,” Il-hyeok recalled.

Il-hyeok’s girlfriend gave birth to their first child in the South. The couple married in 2024 and soon welcomed another daughter. Il-hyeok is finding his footing in the South’s capitalist economy, trying part-time jobs at restaurants and operating forklifts and excavators.

The plunge into the South’s noisy democracy was overwhelming. Televisions offered endless channels — so different from the North, where only government broadcasts existed. Back home, Il-hyeok’s ​used motorbike was a prized status symbol​; now he found himself on highways crowded with modern cars. City squares rang with protests.

Yu-mi’s mother marveled at faucets that produced both hot and cold water. On her first day working at a nursing home, ​she faltered when colleagues asked for “napkins” — another English word she had never heard. The brothers’ mother was scandalized by a TV drama in which a wife slapped her husband. And when Il-hyeok first ventured beyond Seoul, the South’s capital, he dutifully called a police detective to ask for permission. The detective only laughed.

And then there were elections.

In the North, ​people lined up in formal dress to receive a ballot with only one name. ​They placed ​their vote in the “yes” box with both hands and bowed deeply to portraits of Kim Jong-un’s father and grandfather, who ruled before him. No one dared approach the “no” box.​ When Il-hyeok and his wife voted in June as South Korean citizens, they found voters arriving in shorts and slippers, earphones in place. The ballot was a bewildering list of names.

Yet, South Korea was no paradise.

After 19 months in the South, Yi-hyeok died in a diving accident in late 2024.​ The brothers’ mother and Il-hyeok’s wife were diagnosed with cancer.

Il-hyeok vented frustration at Seoul’s soaring housing prices. He is saving every penny to move his family out of their cramped, government-subsidized rental apartment. Still, he insisted the defection was “100 percent” the right choice.​ Before his death, Yi-hyeok appeared on television, explaining that he fled to spare his children the indoctrination of North Korean schools. His daughter is now a second grader at a South Korean school, and his son is in kindergarten. The children adapted fastest to their new lives, quickly embracing South Korean staples like fried chicken and pizza.

“My husband gave me and our children the freedom he promised before he died,” Yu-mi said.

The brothers also honored their father’s final wish: When their boat fled North Korea, they carried his ashes with them.

I’ve been captivated by the recent defection of nine North Koreans to South Korea. It is exceedingly rare for an entire extended family to escape together, especially across the heavily guarded maritime border dividing the two Koreas. As it turns out, their escape plan was actually years in the making. I’ve pieced their journey together — a tale of brutal hardships during the pandemic era and a daring search for freedom.

@Choe Sang-Hun This is a beautiful story -- of desperation, great courage, of the bitter-sweetness of "paradise." It also reminded me -- as it should all those who enjoy the luxury of freedom -- of my good fortune. Thanks for sharing this family's journey with NYT readers.

Choe Sang-Hun is the lead reporter for The Times in Seoul, covering South and North Korea.

A Mother’s Crusade to Rid South Africa of African Immigrants

The New York Times July 21, 2026

As immigration surges in the country, activists are going to extreme lengths to expel foreign nationals, often taking the law into their own hands.

As immigration surges in the country, activists are going to extreme lengths to expel foreign nationals, often taking the law into their own hands.

Nozie Khoza and fellow residents marching through the streets of Rosettenville, outside Johannesburg. Credit...

Supported by

By John Eligon and Zimasa Matiwane

Photographs by Joao Silva

John Eligon and Zimasa Matiwane spent months with anti-immigrant activists in Johannesburg to report for this article.

On a clear morning last October, Nozie Khoza and her brigade of self-proclaimed patriots stood at the entrance of a public health clinic in Johannesburg on a quest to shape South Africa in their image.

When the gate opened at 7:30, the group demanded to see IDs from everyone seeking to enter, saying that only South Africans would be allowed inside.

“You belong to Nigeria, sweetheart,” Bongi Nomnganga, one of Ms. Khoza’s allies, told a young woman, turning her away because, even though she had a South African ID, her last name was Nigerian.

“It smells like fraud,” another one of Ms. Khoza’s associates said of a young woman’s South African ID, after the woman told them her parents were from Mozambique.

Ms. Khoza, a 39-year-old mother of two, had no authority to determine who could enter the public clinic.

Rather, she is a foot soldier in a highly organized network of activists going to extreme lengths to harass immigrants in South Africa, most of whom come from other African nations in search of opportunity in the continent’s largest economy.

Polls show a growing number of South Africans share hostility toward immigrants and want the government to do more to thwart the heavy flow of migrants entering the country. There have been nationwide protests and violence. Immigrants have been attacked and even killed, chased from their homes and businesses.

Despite a lack of evidence, many South Africans blame immigrants for crime, for stealing jobs and for taking up valuable public resources in a nation with high unemployment and growing inequality. They say they have lost faith in the government and have taken the law into their own hands.

This wave of anti-immigrant furor echoes movements seen in the United States and Europe. But only 5 percent of South Africa’s 65 million people are immigrants, according to government statistics.

Foreigners accounted for just 3 percent of arrests over the past five years, according to police data. They accounted for just 1.2 percent of arrests for violent crimes over the same period.

Still, officials have ramped up workplace inspections, punishing employers who hire undocumented foreigners. More than 53,000 foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated from South Africa since June, the government said last week.

Cyril Ramaphosa, the president, has announced new investments to secure the nation’s border, and he has repeatedly warned South Africans not to engage in vigilante justice.

But the police have not always intervened when citizens harass foreigners.

“It’s only South Africa that is experiencing such an influx of foreigners every day,” Ms. Khoza told those waiting outside the public health clinic in Rosettenville, a neighborhood in southern Johannesburg.

“The schools are full of your kids. Healthcare is full of you. Workplace is full of you. Restaurants full of you.”

“There’s going to be a war,” she said.

Ms. Khoza was born and raised in Durban, the epicenter of much of the recent anti-immigrant unrest in South Africa. But it wasn’t until she moved to Johannesburg at 23 to work as a television extra and in production that she developed her grim view of immigrants.

She said she watched as the city deteriorated over time and blamed the urban blight on immigrant street vendors. She blamed foreign landlords for not taking care of dilapidated properties.

A construction company she owns stopped getting business. She claims it was because Zimbabweans were underbidding her for contracts. She also says she had to send her daughter to private school because the public schools nearest her home were at capacity. She blamed this on immigrant children overcrowding the school system.

Ms. Khoza’s frustration led her to become an outspoken member of a national anti-immigrant group called March and March. The group targets all foreigners — not just those in the country illegally — and wants them gone.

On a Saturday in May, Ms. Khoza joined a group of about 50 people who marched down a residential street near her neighborhood. Their goal was to raid a home they said had been overrun by illegal Congolese immigrants.

They stopped at a house in the middle of the block to carry out what the group called an eviction. It did not matter that the Congolese family living inside was there legally.

The mob used bolt cutters to break through the driveway gate. They banged on the doors and jostled the burglar bars on the windows. The house was dark and seemed empty.

A few minutes later, the mob breached the front door. Teary-eyed children emerged from a dark corridor, hustling out of the house, shivering.

“We are sorry,” some of them squealed.

Their mother, Sandra, an immigrant from the Democratic Republic of Congo, shuffled out in shock as she cradled her youngest child in a blanket, a two-week-old baby. Tall with her hair braided in cornrows, Sandra’s eyes welled with tears as she confronted the angry crowd.

While all the banging was going on outside, Sandra, 38, had been hiding inside with seven of her eight children. She called her husband, Pierre, who was out at the time, and he went straight to a police station to report a break-in. (Both she and her husband asked that their last names be withheld for their safety.)

Having lived nearly half of her life in South Africa, Sandra knew how dangerous situations like this could be. In 2008, the year she arrived after fleeing civil war in Congo, South Africa experienced its first major spasm of xenophobic violence after apartheid, the era when many Black citizens were forced to flee the country’s violent white-led regime.

Vigilantes killed dozens of immigrants and destroyed many foreign-owned shops, leading tens of thousands of foreigners to flee the country. Violence spiked again in 2015 and 2019.

Other African nations have watched these waves of anti-immigrant violence in disbelief, shocked to see so many South Africans turn their backs on people from countries that provided refuge during apartheid. Nigeria has demanded that South Africa compensate its citizens who have been forced to leave their homes and businesses.

Over the years, Sandra, whose house was raided, had learned how to survive as a foreigner in South Africa. She knew not to answer her cellphone in a crowded taxi so no one would recognize her accent. She knew not to play Congolese music too loudly at home or in the hair salon she owned. She knew how to dress like a South African.

She and her husband said they always keep their immigration paperwork up to date and have legal status as asylum seekers. None of that seemed to matter to the angry mob shoving its way into her house.

The group stormed the family’s home and dumped their belongings on the street.

Pierre, 47, was incredulous when he arrived with the police. He had migrated from Congo in 2008 and met Sandra in Johannesburg. He tried to pacify the crowd by speaking Zulu to them and showing photos of a traditional Zulu wedding ceremony he had with a South African woman he called his second wife.

The mob still wanted them out.

Ms. Khoza has been watching with envy clips of U. S. immigration agents raiding American streets to capture and deport illegal immigrants under the Trump administration.

“The government here should be doing exactly what Trump is doing,” she said, “so that South Africa can have order and South Africans are put first.”

While they wait for the government to act, groups like March and March have asked organizers like Ms. Khoza to be as loud as possible and to make a scene wherever they go.

At Pierre’s house, neighbors flocked to the street to gawk. The block was jammed with police vehicles, a heap of furniture and the mob’s shouting.

Pierre called his landlord, Dermot Connors. When Mr. Connors arrived, he explained that Pierre and his family were lawful tenants and he begged the mob to let the children back inside.

They refused.

Mr. Connors asked the police to intervene, but a police captain told him he was concerned about a potential standoff. “I don’t want to promote violence,” the captain said, adding that the best solution was for the family to find somewhere else to stay for the night.

Sandra stood anguished over her family’s scattered belongings. The keyboard that their eldest child plays at church. The colored pencils that their younger children use for schoolwork. The framed certificate Pierre received from a former employer, praising his “commitment and dedication.”

As the invaders lounged on the family’s furniture, Sandra spotted a familiar face in the crowd. It was Ms. Khoza, whom Sandra said had blocked her several times from getting care at the public health clinic in Rosettenville.

Ms. Khoza later said she did not recognize Sandra but felt remorse about what Sandra’s children endured.

“I felt bad a bit,” she said. “I don’t want to lie.”

Ms. Khoza said the defense of her own children went hand-in-hand with her effort to rid South Africa of immigrants. Last year, she explained to her eldest daughter, Owethu, that foreign nationals were taking over their country.

“I am a victim,” Owethu, 17, said in an interview, adding that she sees her mother and others like her as being on a noble pursuit.

“I think they’re brave because they’re fighting against police, they’re fighting against the government,” she said.

That battle continued the day after a recent nationwide anti-immigrant protest on June 30. The organizers had given that date as a deadline for all undocumented migrants to leave the country, and Ms. Khoza hoped to see fewer immigrants on the streets of Johannesburg.

Instead, she saw many immigrant street vendors selling goods just as before.

“It’s no longer allowed to sell here,” Ms. Khoza told a man selling vegetables. “There are people coming here to check the situation. Pack quickly.”

“We told you to leave by yesterday and you are still here,” Ms. Nomnganga, her associate, chimed in.

As the women went from one stall to another, the vendors were rattled and hustled to pack their onions and cellphone cases and socks.

“I have papers,” one of the vendors said, holding up a plastic bag with her passport.

“Mama, we don’t want your permit,” Ms. Khoza said. “The only thing we want is only South Africans in our country.”

The woman packed up her goods and walked away.

John Eligon is the Johannesburg bureau chief for The Times, covering a wide range of events and trends that influence and shape the lives of ordinary people across southern Africa.

Joao Silva is a Times photographer based in South Africa.

3 Arguments Fueling Anti-Immigrant Sentiment in South Africa

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As the nation convulses with protests and violence, data and research suggest that some of the biggest arguments against foreigners don’t stand up against the facts.

By John Eligon

Reporting from Johannesburg

Foreigners have been forced out of their homes and businesses. Some have been physically attacked. Tens of thousands have fled the country.

Anti-immigrant sentiment is spreading in South Africa, driven by accusations that have become familiar across the world — that foreigners are committing crime, taking jobs and using valuable public resources.

South Africa is the largest economy in Africa, attracting many migrants from neighboring countries. There are about three million documented immigrants living in the country, and many more who are undocumented.

But are the accusations against immigrants in South Africa true? Here is what data and research say about three common arguments used against them.

South Africa reports one of the world’s highest murder rates. But police statistics show that immigrants are arrested at low rates.

While foreign nationals are about 5 percent of the population, they accounted for just 3 percent of arrests over the past five years, according to South African police data that was provided to The New York Times in response to a public records request. They accounted for just 1.2 percent of arrests for violent crime.

The data shows that nearly one in five arrests of foreigners is for immigration violations. At the same time, other statistics show that foreigners occupy South African prisons at a disproportionately high rate.

Last year, South Africa’s corrections department reported that more than 12 percent of inmates serving sentences in the country’s prisons were foreigners.

South Africa’s unemployment rate has hovered over 30 percent for the past several years, and many South Africans say that they haven’t reaped the benefits of living in Africa’s most developed economy.

The sight of foreigners waiting tables at restaurants or running convenience stores has only amplified their disappointment.

Foreigners hold less than 4 percent of formal jobs in South Africa, a rate that has remained mostly unchanged for more than a decade, according to an article published in June by researchers at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. One in five participants in the informal economy — which includes roadside vending — is a foreigner, the researchers said.

As many South Africans turn to the sector because of the high unemployment rate, competition has increased.

But a report by the World Bank in 2018 also found that immigrants tended to take more business risks than South African citizens and that immigrant workers generate jobs for South Africans.

A common refrain among anti-immigrant activists is that foreigners use taxpayer-funded resources, like public health clinics and schools, depriving South African citizens.

South Africa has a school-choice system, and the best public schools fill quickly. Many South Africans argue that immigrant children are taking those prime slots.

Data does not support that argument. Foreigners account for just 2 percent of students in public schools, according to government statistics.

Government officials have raised concerns over the years that foreigners place a significant strain on the budgets of public medical facilities.

A 2023 government report found that at one of the country’s largest medical facilities, Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital in Johannesburg, over 40 percent of the patients were foreign nationals.

The researchers at Witwatersrand found that financial mismanagement by the government had squeezed public services, leading to longer wait times at medical facilities and larger student-to-teacher ratios. Those pressures have the potential to increase anti-immigrant sentiment in the coming years, they wrote.

John Eligon is the Johannesburg bureau chief for The Times, covering a wide range of events and trends that influence and shape the lives of ordinary people across southern Africa.

How the G. O. P. Made Pasta Into a Voter ID Talking Point

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Congressional Memo

Republicans claim that Olive Garden polices its Never-Ending Pasta Bowl more tightly than the United States does its elections. It’s not that simple.

By Michael Gold

Michael Gold reported from the Capitol. His family celebrated most birthdays and holidays at Olive Garden.

Last week, President Trump gave a speech at the White House in which he made exaggerated claims about election vulnerabilities to pressure the Senate to push through a stalled voting restriction bill that would impose strict new voter identification requirements nationwide.

That same week, the pasta behemoth Olive Garden brought back its popular Never-Ending Pasta Pass, and informed customers that a photo ID would be needed to use it.

Thanks to a social media post — what else? — these two separate, seemingly unrelated events became intertwined, as Republicans spun up a buzzy but misleading talking point claiming that Olive Garden polices its bottomless pasta deal more tightly than the United States does its elections.

The claim misrepresents both voter ID laws and the multibillion-dollar casual dining chain’s rules surrounding unlimited breadsticks and limitless spaghetti. But it has nevertheless circulated wildly online, at the Capitol and at the White House, in the latest example of a corroded political discourse that often trivializes the weightiest topics, like comparing voting rights to fettuccine.

Olive Garden’s passes allow the 10,000 Americans lucky enough to purchase one to enjoy 13 weeks of unlimited pasta for 100 bucks. Given those economics, a social media user asked the chain whether families could share a pasta pass. The answer was no; passes could be used only by the individuals who bought them.

“Passholders must present a valid photo I. D. along with the Pass at the time of ordering,” Olive Garden wrote on social media.

And just like that, Republicans had their latest and perhaps most appetizing talking point in their campaign to shame Democrats for opposing strict new measures that would require Americans to provide proof of citizenship to register to vote and limited forms of identification at the polls.

After Congress returned to session on Monday, Olive Garden and its endless pasta deal were invoked seven times in what is a normally dry House committee hearing and once on the Senate floor.

“We are protecting our breadsticks more than our ballots,” said Representative Bryan Steil, a Wisconsin Republican who is the chairman of the Administration Committee, which has jurisdiction over election legislation, and the author of a strict voter ID bill. As it happens, he also worked at the Janesville, Wis., Olive Garden during his senior year in high school.

The comparison is highly misleading. Three dozen states require voters to show identification to vote in person, including 23 that require a photo ID, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The remaining 14 states and Washington, D. C., use other methods to verify voters’ identities, such as requiring a signature on an affidavit or personal information to be provided at the polls.

The Republican bill, known as the SAVE America Act, would establish strict federal limits around what forms of photo identification could be used to verify a voter’s identity at every polling place in the country. It also would require proof of U. S. citizenship to register to vote. Only five states issue photo identification that indicates American citizenship, meaning that in most places, individuals would have to produce a passport or a birth certificate — documents that studies have shown a substantial number of Americans do not have readily at hand — along with their photo ID to be eligible to vote at all under the bill.

Olive Garden would be hard-pressed to sell its bottomless pasta bowl were such documentation required.

Democrats have scoffed, arguing that Republicans are revealing how little they value Americans’ constitutional right to vote by equating it to a promotional card available to customers with cash to spare and the fortune to log onto a restaurant’s website at the right time.

“Voting is not pasta,” said Representative Teresa Leger Fernández, Democrat of New Mexico.

Still, the pasta discourse has even spread to the White House, where a spokeswoman, Abigail Jackson, brought it up in a Newsmax interview the morning after Mr. Trump’s speech.

“I thought, that’s weird,” Ms. Jackson said. “Olive Garden takes pasta pass security more serious than Democrats are taking election security.”

The comparison then simmered on social media all weekend before Republican lawmakers brought it to the halls of the Capitol (which, incidentally, is six miles from the nearest Olive Garden).

Representative Virginia Foxx, Republican of North Carolina and the chairwoman of the Rules Committee, invoked the restaurant at the start of a hearing on Monday about the bills that House G. O. P. leaders are trying to bring to the floor this week.

“Heck,” Ms. Foxx said. “You even need to present a photo ID to utilize the Olive Garden Never-Ending Pasta Pass.”

The restaurant’s promotion also made its way to the Senate floor, where Senator Bernie Moreno, Republican of Ohio and a close Trump ally, brought it up to hammer Democrats for blocking the SAVE America Act.

Democrats have denounced Republicans’ proposed legislation as overly burdensome, arguing that the requirements would make it more difficult for eligible Americans to vote.

They have also dismissed the Olive Garden comparison as overly simplistic, especially given that most Americans can still purchase a standard meal there without showing any identification at all.

“Voting is a constitutional right,” said Representative Jim McGovern, Democrat of Massachusetts. “It is not a lunch special. You have a constitutional right to vote; you don’t have a constitutional right to a breadstick or a bowl of pasta.”

A representative for Olive Garden did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

India’s Young Protesters Are Bloodied but Unbowed

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A day after police forcibly broke up demonstrations, thousands returned to the protest site in New Delhi to keep pushing for action over the country’s failings in education.

By Pragati K. B. Anupreeta Das and Alex Travelli

The reporters were at the main protest site and surrounding streets filled with protesters and security forces.

They flocked to New Delhi by the thousands. Young Indians demanding accountability from their government for a flawed education system, hoping for a promise or a signal from those in power that would reassure them about their futures.

Instead, the throng of protesters who tried to march to Parliament on Monday were confronted by security forces, batons in hand, tear gas canisters ready. As the crowd swelled, the police cracked down, striking people’s shins, calves and backs, swinging their staves overheard. Protesters hurled flip flops and water bottles back. Many rushed to escape through back alleys and side roads. Plumes of tear gas left people choking.

The protesters — mostly young people who chanted slogans, carried posters or stood quietly in solidarity — said they were shocked by the police crackdown and the lack of any real government response. By Tuesday, their sense of anger remained palpable as thousands returned to the protest site near Jantar Mantar, an 18th century observatory, undeterred by spurts of monsoon rain.

Security forces had removed tents and parts of the main stage at the venue. But Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party — a satirical movement that has become a vehicle for the frustrations of millions of young Indians — said that the protest will continue indefinitely. He implored people to keep it peaceful.

Leaders of the C. J. P. said 150 protesters were taken to the hospital from injuries in the protest on Monday. The Delhi Police said 118 of its officers were injured during “violent protests.” Around 70 protesters were detained, according to lawyers’ groups.

Although Prime Minister Narendra Modi has not responded publicly to the protests, on Tuesday he spoke through an emissary. Kiren Rijiju, the parliamentary affairs minister, told reporters, “The safety, security and future of our youth are our priority.”

He also provided assurances that future paper leaks would be prevented.

Mr. Modi rarely responds to critics, so the comments appear to be a sign of the importance the leader has placed on the youth protests and a tacit acknowledgment of the political risk of alienating young voters in a country where more than 40 percent of the population is under the age of 25.

However, the government has said little in response to the specific demands of the C. J. P., which include the resignation of India’s education minister, whom the C. J. P. holds directly accountable for a shoddy education system and leaks in recent entrance exam papers that forced millions of students to retake their tests.

“The government is in no mood to understand us and talk to us,” Chandan Mandal, a 19-year-old high school senior from the state of Rajasthan, said on Tuesday. He said he first protested more than a month ago. According to the C. J. P., at least 21 students have died by suicide since the exam leak, unable to handle the stress.

The police struck him with a baton three times on Monday, Mr. Mandal said. Two reddish bruises, each about three inches long, and an open wound were visible on his back.

“I’m opposing the government itself now,” said Mr. Mandal, who is studying for an entrance exam for engineering school.

A big reason for the frustration millions of young Indians feel is that there aren’t enough jobs, or that there is a mismatch between available jobs and qualifications, according to economists. A recent, widely cited study from Azim Premji University found that 40 percent of young people under 25 are unemployed, even as access to higher education has increased.

The protesters’ most visible slogans as they gathered on Monday morning were less concerned with botched exams than with the government’s overall accountability.

“India is a Democracy! We Need Answers!” read one, in English. “In Search of the Misguided,” read another, in Hindi, next to a hand-drawn sketch of Mr. Modi.

By the afternoon, the police waded in. Cries of pain rose above the shrill police whistles and sirens of riot control vans. A thin, young woman crouched on a median, as her friends dressed a fresh wound on her forearm and rinsed her face, reddened by tear gas.

At the Janpath subway station nearby, a police van lay overturned on its side, its windshield smashed.

Further away from the violence, Wishwas Srivastav, 36, an engine builder, said he had traveled to Delhi from the state of Himachal Pradesh to join the protests.

“It hasn’t been feeling like democracy here for the past 10 or 15 years,” said Mr. Srivastav. Of the government, he said, “I hope they’re listening.”

By Tuesday morning, traffic along Janpath was back to normal, with some of the cross-streets more tightly barricaded. The police van at the metro station had been flipped upright.

At the protest site, volunteers distributed food and drinks to protesters, including burgers from McDonald’s, samosas, water and electrolytes.

Abhishek Kumar, 20, sat in the shade, tired after a roughly eight-hour bus ride from his hometown of Kanpur. After watching the protests on social media on Monday and seeing the police beat protesters, he said, he decided to join in person. Mr. Kumar, who recently took an entrance exam to join the armed forces, said he would stay for a few days.

Many who gathered were parents worried about the future their children stand to inherit. Mina Ganesh, 51, was at the protest site on Tuesday with her son Miher, 17.

“Finally someone in the country is willing to speak up,” Ms. Ganesh said. “It took us long enough. Now that we have begun to speak up, there’s no stopping us.”

Miher, who wants to study either economics or engineering, said he was moved by the actions of Sonam Wangchuk, a prominent education activist who has backed the C. J. P.’s demands and joined its protest with a hunger strike.

Mr. Wangchuk is now 23 days into his fast and was forcibly moved to a hospital on Saturday by the government.

“He doesn’t know any of us,” Miher said. “How can I sit at home knowing he’ll die for me?”

Pragati K. B. is a reporter for The Times based in New Delhi, covering news from across India.

Anupreeta Das covers India and South Asia for The Times. She is based in New Delhi.

Alex Travelli is a correspondent based in New Delhi, writing about business and economic developments in India and the rest of South Asia.

What Happened When Meta Used A. I. to Ban Accounts on Facebook and Instagram

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Camille Hanson built an Instagram business teaching English to nearly 1 million followers. Meta deleted the account earlier this year over false claims of fraud and deception. “It’s like a grieving event, you know,” Ms. Hanson said. “A lot of crying.”

Roberto Suarez, an influencer who wants to make a career on social media, grew his Instagram following to more than 500,000. Meta deleted his account last year. “I was in shock,” he said.

Athenia Rodney runs JuneteenthNY, a group commemorating the end of slavery in the United States. After 17 years of activism, Meta deleted her account, citing child sexual abuse material. “Everything that we do is family friendly,” she said.

Supported by

Users said the technology mistakenly deleted their accounts. To resolve the issue, they still had to rely on A. I.

By Stuart A. Thompson and Eli Tan

The notification startled Camille Hanson awake one night this March. Her Facebook and Instagram accounts, where she had nearly one million followers running a business with her husband teaching English to nonnative speakers, had been flagged for deletion. Meta said she had violated the community guidelines for fraud and deception.

“I’m just an English teacher,” Ms. Hanson, 40, remembered thinking. She was flummoxed by the fraud and deception claims. “What am I doing wrong?” she wondered.

The notice said she could appeal, so she clicked the button to begin the process. A week later, she got another notification: Her appeal was denied.

“All your information will be permanently deleted,” Meta’s response read. “You cannot request another review of this decision.”

It was like having “an actual physical business, and somebody just shuts down your office or your storefront,” Ms. Hanson’s husband, Calvin, 42, said in an interview from their home in Portugal.

What happened to the Hansons was a case of artificial intelligence gone wrong. The technology is increasingly responsible for deciding which accounts broke Meta’s content rules while also managing the appeals for those decisions. Adding to people’s distress, it is often difficult for users like the Hansons to reach anybody at the company to figure out what to do.

In March, Meta announced plans to hand more power to A. I. bots to decide which accounts to ban or harmful images to remove. Months later, the company laid off thousands of employees, including those who did those jobs.

Users have organized online, with more than 60,000 recently signing a petition asking Meta to provide more information about account bans and to let humans review appeals. Several communities on Reddit and elsewhere have been bombarded with complaints from Meta users about the company’s A. I.

Daniel Roberts, a Meta spokesman, disputed that A. I. was worse at handling accounts than humans, and said the company’s new A. I. moderation tools make 13 percent fewer mistakes than human employees and find 10 percent more violations. Of the five accounts The New York Times flagged to Meta, all were banned by the company’s old A. I. moderation tools, Mr. Roberts said.

“We’re committed to making fewer enforcement mistakes and helping individuals protect their accounts — and A. I. is delivering on both,” he said.

Meta has grappled with several instances of A. I. going awry. In May, hackers exploited its A. I. customer service chatbot to attack 34,000 Instagram accounts, including a former White House account of Barack Obama’s. That same month, employees revolted over a program that tracked their keyboard movements to train A. I., leading Meta to pause the effort.

Last week, 26 former Meta employees said in a lawsuit that the company had laid them off using an A. I. algorithm that targeted them for having disabilities. A Meta spokesman said that “workforce management and organizational decisions were and are made by people, not A. I.”

People Over Platforms, a user advocacy group that sells account recovery services, created the online petition this year to compel Meta to change its account moderation policies. Meta had accused many of the signers of sharing child exploitation material — a charge that users said added insult to injury — and then banned them.

That was the accusation Meta made against Athenia Rodney, the owner of JuneteenthNY, a group commemorating the end of slavery in the United States, when the company banned all of her personal and professional accounts on Facebook and Instagram last year.

“Our technology found your account, or activity on it, doesn’t follow our rules,” the notice from Meta read. “As a result, our technology took action.”

Ms. Rodney said she did not understand Meta’s rationale because her group’s content is “family friendly.” After her accounts were banned, she sifted through JuneteenthNY’s photo archives to search for potential posts that could have triggered the A. I. bots, but found nothing.

Then Ms. Rodney recalled that shortly before Meta canceled her accounts, the company had alerted her about suspicious logins from Seattle and Singapore — even though she lives in Atlanta. It was a sign that her accounts had been hacked.

Ms. Rodney had quickly changed her passwords, but six of her Instagram and Facebook accounts for various businesses and personal profiles were banned.

To get those accounts back, Ms. Rodney said she had submitted identification documents, filed complaints with the Better Business Bureau and Federal Trade Commission, reached out to state consumer protection offices and messaged Meta employees on LinkedIn. Nothing worked.

Since then, JuneteenthNY has had to convince sponsors that it is a legitimate organization that has been around for nearly two decades.

“Our sponsors go to our social media page to confirm that we are a valid organization, that we have been doing this for 17 years,” Ms. Rodney said. “So now, when they go to our account and they see 500 people, they’re like, ‘You haven’t been doing this — y’all are a fraud.’”

After The Times flagged the five banned accounts to Meta, the company said it investigated and found that two were the result of hacks and one was for a legitimate reason. The hacked accounts were rightfully banned because the hackers violated child safety policies, Meta said.

Meta then restored the two hacked accounts, including Ms. Rodney’s JuneteenthNY account. Two of the five accounts flagged were mistakenly banned, including those of the Hansons, the company said.

Roberto Suarez, an Instagram influencer who had built a following of more than 500,000 users before he was banned this year, was one of those who received an email from Meta that his account was restored — along with his photos, followers, messages and more. He started posting content again to fans who had not heard from him in months.

A few weeks later, Meta sent him another email. “Your account has been suspended,” it read, claiming he had violated copyright laws on his content. “If you don’t take action, your account will be permanently disabled.”

Mr. Suarez denied violating any copyright. Shortly after The Times asked about the new ban, his account was restored again.

Ms. Hanson also received an email from Meta that her account was back. “We reviewed your account and found that the activity on it does follow our community standards on fraud and deception, so you can use Instagram again,” the message read. “We’re sorry we got this wrong.”

This article began with a tip I got from a reader, saying that his Facebook account was randomly banned. When he tried to figure out what happened, he came across the petition we mention in the story with over 60,000 signatures. Meta has always had a problem with mistakenly deleting accounts or removing content. But the company has enthusiastically embraced A. I. to moderate more and more of its products, including the appeals process. It was very telling when we flagged the accounts with Meta and they reinstated most of them: when a human finally took a look, it was immediately clear that a mistake was made. The people we spoke with seemed fine with A. I. playing a role in moderating Facebook and Instagram, but they wanted a human in the loop when it came to appeals. Curious if anyone here has faced a wrongly ban?

Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.

Eli Tan covers the technology industry for The Times from San Francisco.

Restaurant Review

The Bay Area farm-to-table classic changed the American restaurant scene. Now it has opened a dynamic new place right next door.

Credit... Video by Kelsey Mcclellan For The New York Times

Supported by

By Tejal Rao

Tejal Rao is a chief restaurant critic for The New York Times.

Sit down at Chez Panisse and dinner starts, just like that. No scripted introduction, no mission statement, no spiel. Not even a little, “Have you dined with us before?”

If you didn’t already know that Alice Waters opened this place 55 years ago in Berkeley, Calif., that it became one of the most important restaurants in the country, mothering the modern farm-to-table movement and an era of rustic, ingredient-obsessed American cooking that leaned heavily on France, well, you could wrap up dinner and polish off your pluot galette without anyone tipping you off

You might expect Chez Panisse to hammer home the values of building education and community through fresh local food that Ms. Waters has been promoting for decades, that it would pause now and then to flex. But dinner here is never didactic. It flows in the quiet, straightforward way of a bistro that’s been around forever. Service is calm, self-possessed, attentive, sometimes a little detached in the way that makes Americans complain about Parisian restaurants.

Chez Panisse is still devoted to pristine seasonal ingredients from small farms and to preparing them like a romantic home cook from another century. Its aesthetic was imitated until it became an inescapable cliché, but was also pushed forward by more expressive and experimental kitchens.

As a result, a meal here can now feel both wonderfully timeless and oddly stuck in time, so much so that it came as a surprise when Bar Panisse opened in December — a new act, directly next door. How would a modern restaurant interpret the culinary ethos that, half a century ago, transformed American food culture?

Chez Panisse opened in 1971, rebelling against both mainstream industrial food and healthy-ish hippie counterculture.

It’s now divided in two, the restaurant downstairs run by the chefs Amy Dencler and Martin Fabre, and the cafe upstairs run by the chefs Nathan Alderson and Ann Cromley. Downstairs, there’s a set menu that isn’t a tasting, but a pleasant, sensible, unfashionably tight four courses. (Add a cheese course if you like.)

Recently, I had an excellent dish of pork, roasted on a spit then sliced very thinly, with cherries and fried herbs, with a splash of pan sauce. I did worry at first glance about a salad that resembled a fairy crown, weighed down with mounds of chopped salmon — it looked both out of proportion and underdressed on the plate, but it surprised me with a woven sense of texture and bursts of acidity.

Over the course of a few meals, I also had a couple of dishes that were technically proficient but forgettable, hazy even as they arrived. Dessert, overseen both upstairs and down by the pastry chefs Carrie Lewis and Eriko Yahiro, was consistently a joy. Dishes like an oversize profiterole with a moat of summer fruit, or a medley of sorbets with a curved tuile, were a reminder of how the most banal classics can bring so much pleasure when they’re made with care and superlative ingredients.

Upstairs, where salads and beautiful, airy pizzas are always on the menu, I ordered “Lindsey’s almond torte.” It’s a simple cake, and I’ve made it more times than I can remember, following a recipe from Lindsey Shere’s classic cookbook, “Chez Panisse Desserts.”

There is a Chez way to do everything — to buy lettuces, wash lettuces, dry lettuces, dress lettuces — and this happens to be the Chez way to bake an almond cake. With a deeply golden top that had bubbled right at the center, the cake was served that day with early blueberries in thick, dark syrup and such softly whipped cream, it could barely hold its shape.

The dessert was extremely straightforward in both flavor and presentation, a little restrained, but it reinforced the lasting power of Chez Panisse, a restaurant that finds meaning by continuously looking into the past — specifically, its own.

No, this is not a recipe for thrills, but there’s something reassuring about the way everyone at Chez Panisse seems to share an unshakable house style, built as much on ephemeral ingredients as on the kitchen’s own half-century-deep archive. Maintaining it is how the restaurant has endured, even as generations of servers and cooks have come through its doors.

Amelia Telč, the chef at Bar Panisse, is not one of them. She hadn’t worked for the group before she got the job, but like so many chefs, she had studied the restaurant’s cookbooks and absorbed its reverence for ingredients.

Ms. Telč buys from the same purveyors, approaches techniques and recipes from the same point of view, though in some ways, Bar Panisse is less technically ambitious. (It’s in the name, it’s a bar!) The menu is short, easy to share, and plates tend to have few components, but this works to bring the food closer to the kind of provincial French cooking that Chez Panisse once idealized.

Service is sharp and fast-paced and the room has energy, particularly at the bar where the drinks shift with the seasons, too. Ms. Telč writes a new menu each week, and it involves small, snacky things along with a few dishes you can make into a meal. Specials come and go, like tiny fried squash blossoms, still attached to the young zucchini, with little more than a heap of finely chopped and exceptionally sweet peperonata.

A fluffy and finely calibrated green salad is usually on the menu, as are the puffy gougères you should order alongside it. But I most looked forward to the changing platters of fat, creamy-centered butter beans, served in a shallow pool of cooking broth, which might be topped with a glug of olive oil and a halved hard-boiled egg; or braised winter greens; or slabs of smoked eggplant and garlic and a few fuzzy leaves of minty nepitella.

These platters looked like what you might put on the table at home, simple to the point of being almost unremarkable, but there was beauty and confidence in that.

The Gulf shrimp on the bar menu, so small they would usually wind up flavoring the stockpots at Chez Panisse, are fantastic. Ms. Telč might fry these shrimp and serve them whole with a splotch of lemon aioli. They’re sweet, their carapaces so delicate that you can eat them shell and all.

Strawberries from Swanton Berry Farm recently appeared ripe and raw in a Pavlova layered with a properly tenderhearted meringue and devastatingly soft whipped cream, the whole thing so fragile, it seemed to be collapsing continuously into a soupy custard until the very last bite. It was a dessert that wanted to be eaten, and fast.

Much as at Chez Panisse, there is a gentle touch to the preparations: No dish will be the most intense or loudest version of itself. At its best, this gentleness can be clarifying — particularly if you’ve gotten bored with kitchens where the salt, fat, acid and heat dials are turned all the way up, all the time. But occasionally, it’s disappointing.

On one visit, my table shared a lamb pie served with a bouquet of young, particularly tender fava leaves. The pastry was beautifully browned and crisp all over, with a thick, pinched rim, and the plate projected a kind of springy abundance. But once I dug inside, the filling was surprisingly plain, a bit dry. It was a rare misstep from a kitchen that understands that simplicity requires precision.

Bar Panisse does not take reservations, and a chatty line of locals starts outside before it even opens. Standing on the sidewalk, catching the laughter and gossip, it doesn’t feel like a destination, but a neighborhood spot — the kind of self-effacing restaurant where you know you’ll be taken care of while you eat and drink well.

In its warmth and spontaneity, its scrappiness and sprightliness, Bar Panisse is somehow both attuned to the way we dine now and true to the restaurant’s original spirit. Chez Panisse might have forever changed the way we think and talk about food, but it also seems less interested in its own mythology than the ordinary, unglamorous work of being a good restaurant. That’s not revolutionary, but it’s still rare.

Tejal Rao, our chief critic based in Los Angeles, writes starred reviews of restaurants nationwide. Ligaya Mishan, our chief critic based in New York City, writes starred reviews of restaurants in New York and beyond. Briefer starred reviews of New York restaurants are written by our contributing critics Mahira Rivers and Ryan Sutton, and first appear weekly in the Where to Eat newsletter (subscribe here).

Cyclospora Spreads Through Human Feces. How Did It Get Into Our Food Supply?

The New York Times July 21, 2026

Cyclospora Outbreak

Advertisement

Supported by

The large number of cases suggests that excrement entered the food system on a “surprising scale.”

By Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi

The hard, and nauseating, truth about cyclospora is that it’s spread through human feces. Over decades of research, scientists have not found a single place aside from the human gut where the parasite grows. So now that we’re in the midst of the largest recorded outbreak in United States history, one has to ask: How did human excrement get into our food?

As infections surge across much of the United States, public health investigators are working to figure out how this microscopic parasite contaminated the produce eaten by so many people.

The current case numbers — more than 6,000 people sickened in Michigan alone — suggest that human feces somehow got into our food system on a “surprising scale,” said Matthew Moore, a food safety microbiologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

An understanding of the parasite’s life cycle — and of what happened in previous outbreaks — offer clues about how it might have gotten there.

Cyclospora infects the small intestine, causing frequent watery diarrhea that carries the parasite’s oocysts, or eggs. If those oocysts then contaminate produce — such as from a worker’s unwashed hands (alcohol-based hand sanitizer does not kill the parasite) or through water used to irrigate fruits or vegetables — they can cause illness in a person who consumes the food days or weeks later. In a global food system, where a lot of fresh produce is shipped across the world, inadequate hand-washing facilities or a leaky latrine on a single farm could sicken many people, even thousands of miles away.

Many of the standard techniques for disinfecting the water used in agriculture, including adding chlorine, are geared toward killing bacteria, not parasites, Dr. Moore said. This means that water that appears “clean” on a test might still contain cyclospora from human feces.

For most cyclospora outbreaks that investigators have successfully solved, the source has turned out to be either the water used for irrigation or the hygiene of the people harvesting the crops, said John Guzewich, who worked on food-borne disease outbreaks at the Food and Drug Administration from 1997 to 2011.

Previous outbreaks have been linked to lettuce and salad mixes, raspberries, basil, cilantro, fruit mixes, snow peas and snap peas — all of which are often consumed raw. Cooking produce to at least 158 degrees kills the parasite.

Researchers have found that cyclospora oocysts are particularly “sticky,” clinging to certain types of produce more than other microbes do. That’s especially true of foods like raspberries and cilantro, which have tiny hairs that can harbor the parasite, said Kalmia Kniel, a microbiologist at the University of Delaware who studies cyclospora. This also helps to explain why rinsing herbs or berries with water at home is not entirely effective at removing the oocysts.

Several cyclospora outbreaks linked to raspberries in the late 1990s illustrated one way the parasite can contaminate fresh produce, said Melvin Kramer, an epidemiologist who worked in several state and local public health departments before founding a food safety consulting group.

In 1996, after collecting detailed food histories from people sickened with cyclospora, investigators traced the illnesses to raspberries from a few farms in Guatemala. There, investigators determined it was likely that the insecticides and fungicides sprayed onto the berries had been mixed with contaminated water. The farms had sourced the water from wells or a nearby river, both of which were vulnerable to runoff from latrines, especially during the rainy season. Although the water was filtered, the filter removed only debris, not microbes like cyclospora.

Before this year, the largest outbreak in the United States in recent history occurred in the summer of 2020, sickening 701 people in 14 states and hospitalizing 38. Federal officials linked it to Fresh Express bagged salads containing iceberg lettuce, red cabbage and carrots. They traced at least some of that produce to a farm in South Florida and detected cyclospora in a nearby water canal that had been used to irrigate crops on the farm. Later, genetic analysis confirmed that the cyclospora found in the canal water matched that found in people sickened in the outbreak, said Frank Yiannas, who was a top official at the F. D. A. from 2018 to 2023.

That was the only cyclospora outbreak occurring during his tenure for which investigators were able to find the source of contamination, Mr. Yiannas said. “It’s very rare for F. D. A. to be able to point with specificity to the sources of contamination, whether it’s a farm, a field or a ranch.” And, he added, it’s even rarer for investigators to figure out how the produce was contaminated in the first place.

But, he said, tainted irrigation water is the most likely route of contamination for most large cyclospora outbreaks.

Given the size of the current outbreak, Dr. Kniel said, it is unlikely that a single sick person who didn’t wash his or her hands properly before harvesting produce could have caused such widespread illness.

Instead, the parasite might have spread to multiple farm workers, causing many to shed oocysts in their waste. Then, a leak in a septic system or heavy rainfall might have somehow allowed human waste to seep into water that was used to irrigate crops. The same type of contamination could also affect water used to wash fresh produce, or could be spread on harvesting or processing equipment.

“You’d have to have a lot of produce being irrigated with a lot of water that was contaminated by a lot of cyclospora to see this number of cases,” said Keith R. Schneider, a professor of food safety at the University of Florida.

Chopped and bagged lettuce is particularly vulnerable to contamination, Dr. Kniel said, because many heads of lettuce from multiple fields may mingle before processing.

If federal investigators want to find the cause of the current outbreak, Mr. Yiannas said, they will need to “get out there and sample the heck out of the environment.” Otherwise, he added, “they’re not going to be able to determine it.”

That degree of sampling — as with the rest of the steps in the cyclospora investigation — requires resources, expertise and time.

“Some people think that outbreak investigations can be solved in 50 minutes just like murder mysteries in TV detective shows,” Mr. Guzewich said. “I would love if it happened that way.”

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi is a Times reporter focusing on nutrition and sleep.

This Lifesaving Genetics Tool Works Best if You’re White

The New York Times July 20, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Genetic prediction models are poised to revolutionize medicine. But because they have been trained on European DNA, they threaten to widen health care disparities.

By Emily Baumgaertner Nunn

The National Institutes of Health recently announced a remarkable achievement: the world’s largest database of human genomes, a repository of information that the agency says will help usher in a new era in personalized medicine.

Scientists are already developing clinical tools and techniques based on genomic information gathered from the agency’s All of Us program. One of the most promising? Polygenic risk scores. These can help predict a person’s likelihood of developing complex diseases, like cardiovascular disease and breast cancer, from as early as infancy.

But there’s a glaring problem: The tools were trained overwhelmingly on the DNA of people of European descent, so they often fail to accurately assess risks for anyone else. For some conditions, the forecasts for people of color are almost no better than flipping a coin.

Researchers are racing to correct the biases through advancements in modeling and widespread recruitment of minority groups. They fear that failing to close the gaps could worsen health care disparities — and prevent the technology from realizing its promise of helping to decrease chronic disease.

“It really warrants attention,” said Eimear Kenny, the director of the Institute for Genomic Health at Mount Sinai and a principal investigator in a national consortium that tests the genetic scores.

Geneticists measure a polygenic risk score by aggregating hundreds or thousands of tiny variations across the genome, many of which might nudge a person’s disease risk by only a fraction. By bundling them together, they can generate a cumulative score, ranking a person’s predisposition to common killers.

For patients at the extremely high end of the risk distribution, the scores can offer a medical advantage, potentially giving doctors a decades-long runway to intervene. Those in the highest percentiles for a cardiovascular disease score, for instance, can be prescribed cholesterol-lowering statins earlier, potentially helping prevent some heart attacks and strokes.

But the entire premise rests on the data used to train the model in the first place. The UK Biobank — established in the early 2000s and widely considered a leading genomic trove — is overwhelmingly homogenous; roughly 94 percent of its participants are white. The Million Veteran Program, a repository run by the U. S. Department of Veterans Affairs, is almost three-quarters white.

The cohort in the All of Us program, built by the N. I. H. with the goal of diversifying data, is still about 50 percent European, according to Alicia Martin, a statistical geneticist at the Broad Institute. The effort’s future is also at risk: One of its major funding streams, the 21st Century Cures Act, is set to expire at the end of this fiscal year. (The program’s budget has already been reduced by 72 percent since 2023.)

“You can’t just snap your fingers and overnight have a biobank from Africa, a biobank from India, a biobank from China that are all as large and open and comprehensive as the UK Biobank,” Dr. Martin said. “We can develop all the fancy statistical methods we want, but still not be able to overcome without more diverse representation.”

Other clinical tools could be affected by the ancestry bias, such as integrated artificial intelligence models that draw upon genomics and other biomedical data. Doctors who sequence a genome to look for rare mutations may also find genetic variants in patients of color that researchers have not studied enough to understand.

Genetic blind spots can also cause scientists to miss discoveries that benefit everyone. One example: the PCSK9 gene. Scientists found that a rare mutation that occurred mostly in a small proportion of Black people could naturally reduce the risk of developing coronary heart disease by 88 percent. That set off a race to develop drugs that mimic the mutation for people of all races and ethnicities. But scientists only found the variant because one study in Dallas had ensured that its participant pool was more than half Black.

Major demographic events in history, like mass migrations, explain why genetic findings from people in Africa or of African descent are vital to study. Communities there have accumulated great genetic diversity over hundreds of thousands of years. By contrast, present-day Europeans descend from a small group of Africans who expanded out of Africa about 50,000 years ago. As a result, they have much less diversity.

“If you’re going to pick a population to study for the sake of everybody’s good, the Europeans are the worst you could choose,” said Jay Kaufman, an epidemiologist at McGill University who has written about race and genomics.

The most obvious solution is to recruit more people of color, something the All of Us program says it has prioritized. The group works with local partner organizations like churches and community health centers to host discussion sessions and enroll rural communities through a mobile clinic. It also returns individualized health findings and genetic risks to the participants to establish a sense of reciprocity.

Still, recruitment can be an upstream endeavor, particularly in the United States, which has a history of mistreatment of people of color, from the Tuskegee Syphilis Study to discriminatory sickle-cell screening to the story of Henrietta Lacks, a Black patient whose cancer cells were used for research without her knowledge or consent.

“Why would you contribute if you’ve been wronged in that way in the past?” Dr. Martin said. “There is some earned mistrust that needs to be addressed — to have that level of trust to be willing to say, ‘Take my data, monitor it for decades, do whatever you want with it.’”

In the meantime, researchers designing polygenic risk scores have found technical ways to diversify data. Modeling tools can now pull weighted information from a variety of sources simultaneously, rather than drawing only from the largest European cohorts and then forcing their algorithms onto other groups. Mount Sinai Health System in New York and U. C. L. A. in Los Angeles, for example, have both established more diverse biobanks than the UK Biobank, with each of them containing tens of thousands of genomes.

Scientists also draw from rapidly growing biobanks in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, which bolster the accuracy of polygenic risk scores for East Asian groups. Localized initiatives are underway in Peru, Mexico, Qatar and elsewhere. And a continentwide program called H3Africa is collecting genetic data in African populations and supporting efforts by scientists there to study how genes and environments cause diseases.

Academic networks have also tapped sources beyond biobanks, integrating data from large, disease-specific cohort projects, including the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Study, or ARIC, which intentionally enrolled thousands of Black participants from North Carolina and Mississippi.

For breast cancer, a project called Confluence aggregates data from over 300 individual studies across 62 countries, providing information from 400,000 breast cancer cases and more than 1.5 million controls. The influx of data from minority groups is being used to sharpen breast cancer polygenic risk scores for everyone.

Private genomics companies and start-ups looking to develop and sell polygenic risk scores do not typically have access to those vast networks. Until recently, they relied almost exclusively on data from the UK Biobank. But the All of Us program recently expanded its policies so that companies can use its more diverse data.

Will all of these efforts, taken together, be enough? It depends on whom you ask. Some experts argue that even an ethnically representative data pool is still imperfect, since variations in other factors — socioeconomic status, health access, age or even sex — can still cause a score’s accuracy to decay. Others believe that the statistical issue was overblown in the first place.

Dr. Kenny, who has been helping to test existing polygenic risk scores for 11 common conditions in racially and ethnically diverse patients, argues that the bias is too complex to resolve quickly.

“I don’t think these things are perfectly portable yet — and maybe never will be perfectly portable,” she said. “But there are things that are starting to narrow that gap.”

Emily Baumgaertner Nunn is a national health reporter for The Times, focusing on public health issues that primarily affect vulnerable communities.
